cases.implementation: The ProFound Detection V4.0 software allows an interpreting physician to quickly identify suspicious soft tissue densities and calcifications by marking the detected areas in the tomosynthesis images. When the ProFound Detection V4.0 marks are displayed by a user, the marks will appear as overlays on the tomosynthesis images. Each detected finding will also be assigned a “score” that corresponds to the ProFound Detection V4.0 algorithm’s confidence that the detected finding is a cancer (Certainty of Finding). Certainty of Finding scores are a percentage in range of 0% to 100% to indicate computer-assisted detection and diagnosis' (CAD) confidence that the finding is malignant. ProFound Detection V4.0 also assigns a score to each case (Case Score) as a percentage in range of 0% to 100% to indicate CAD’s confidence that the case has malignant findings. The higher the Certainty of Finding or Case Score, the higher the confidence that the detected finding is a cancer or that the case has malignant findings.

cases.problem: Patients exposed to opioid drugs often have complex medical needs and are at risk of multiple negative outcomes, including overdose, suicide, development of addiction, and other behavioral health challenges.
cases.task: Stratification Tool for Opioid Risk Mitigation (STORM)
cases.context: Department of Veterans Affairs; VHA: Veterans Health Administration; Health and Medical; United States
cases.implementation: The STORM predictive model provides an estimate of the likelihood of an overdose, suicide event, or death in the next year, documented in a health care system.
cases.outcome: UNKNOWN; 원천의 기대효과와 별도 관측 성과는 구분해야 합니다.
cases.reported_benefits: The effectiveness of the targeted prevention program was tested during a randomized staged roll-out of the targeted prevention program using a stepped wedge evaluation design. The targeted prevention program utilizes the STORM model to identify patients for interdisciplinary case review (i.e. by a team of clinicians which includes those with pain, behavioral health and recovery expertise). Inclusion in the mandate for team-based case review of patients, the predictive model estimated that "very high" risk of overdose or suicide events in the next year was associated with a significant 22% reduction in all-cause mortality within 4 months of inclusion (Strombotne et al., 2023). https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC9060407/ Inclusion in the case review program was also found to reduce all-cause mortality and reduce likelihood of opioid analgesic discontinuation, in the subpopulation of patients on long-term opioid analgesics (Li et al., 2023).
cases.source_description: Patients exposed to opioid drugs often have complex medical needs and are at risk of multiple negative outcomes, including overdose, suicide, development of addiction, and other behavioral health challenges. Numerous strategies have been developed to minimize risks and treat conditions that underly them, but coordination of care across patient treatment providers and conditions can be challenging and interventions to reduce risk can be time consuming. Decision support to systems are needed to ensure recognition of a patient’s current conditions and consideration and tracking of recommended interventions. Risk estimation is needed to ensure that the most complex and at-risk patients receive adequate clinical attention in time-constrained health care environments.

cases.task: REACH VET Suicide Risk Prediction and Recovery Engagement
cases.context: Department of Veterans Affairs; VHA: Veterans Health Administration; Health and Medical; United States
cases.implementation: The REACH VET 2.0 predictive model provides an estimate of the likelihood of dying of suicide in the next month for all active VHA Veterans.
cases.outcome: UNKNOWN; 원천의 기대효과와 별도 관측 성과는 구분해야 합니다.
cases.reported_benefits: The REACH VET 2.0 model is expected to identify a population of Veterans at elevated risk of suicide and other adverse outcomes for review by providers. Providers conduct outreach to identified Veterans when appropriate. This model and the targeted prevention in which it is used (i.e. the REACH VET clinical program), is used to augment VHA's extensive clinical suicide prevention program. While VHA conducts universal screenings for suicide risk by asking patients structured questions regarding suicidality, this screening process does not identify all Veterans at elevated risk. The REACH VET model is intended to supplement clinical screening and assessments and support identification of changes in risk. The REACH VET model supplements clinical practices by identifying Veterans at statistical risk of suicide, given similarities in their health care data with prior suicide decedents. After identification, reevaluation of care and outreach are completed to support risk mitigation. This targeted prevention program was nationally implemented in VHA in 2017 and there was an evaluation of the effects of the REACH VET program. This evaluation found that REACH VET implementation was associated with greater treatment engagement, new safety plan documentation, and fewer mental health admissions, emergency department visits, and documented suicide attempts. Full findings of this program evaluation are available at: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC8524305/.
cases.source_description: Suicide is a low frequency event, but clinical attention and intervention can reduce the risk of suicide and other adverse behavioral health outcomes. REACH VET offers a targeted suicide prevention approach to focus attention on Veterans with the greatest risk/need. This AI system is designed to support identification of Veterans at an elevated risk of suicide or other preventable adverse outcomes to support mitigation of risks, if indicated.

cases.task: Velacur
cases.context: Department of Veterans Affairs; VHA: Veterans Health Administration; Health and Medical; United States
cases.implementation: The Velacur Determined Fat Fraction combines ultrasound attenuation and backscatter coefficient measurements. The device is indicated to determine liver tissue stiffness, attenuation, and Velacur Determined Fat Fraction in a non-invasive way. VDFF is not intended to be used in pediatric patients. This device's outputs are meant to be used in conjunction with other clinical indicators in order to aid in clinical management of patients with liver diseases, including hepatic steatosis. The device is intended to be used in a clinical setting and by trained medical professionals.
cases.outcome: UNKNOWN; 원천의 기대효과와 별도 관측 성과는 구분해야 합니다.
cases.source_description: Velacur is a portable device intended to measure the stiffness and attenuation of the liver in a non-invasive way, via measurement of liver tissue shear modulus and ultrasound attenuation. This is done by measuring the wavelength or wave speed of mechanically created shear aves within the organ of the patient. Attenuation is measured directly via the loss in power of the ultrasound beam. The device is designed to be used at the point of care, in clinics and hospitals. The device is used by a medical professional, an employee of the clinic/hospital. The activation unit is placed under the patient, while lying supine on an exam bed. The activation unit vibrates at frequencies of 40, 50, and 60 Hz, causing shear waves within the liver of the patient. The ultrasound transducer is placed on the patient’s skin, over the intercostal space, and is used to take volumetric scans of the liver while shear waves are occurring. The device includes two algorithms designed to help users detect good quality shear waves and identify liver tissue. From the scan data, the device calculates tissue stiffness and attenuation. Minor hardware and software changes were made to the device. The organ guide (cleared in K223287) was also extended to add more optional overlays on top of the liver overlay to help with optimizing the scan and training users to obtain adequate images. The significant change is the addition of a new output measure for Velacur, an ultrasound derived fat fraction (VDFF).

cases.reported_benefits: Accelerate ultrasound workflows: the R-trigger algorithm is expected to be implemented as workflow enhancement for transthoracic clinical applications on EPIQ and Affiniti Ultrasound Systems in the VM13 software release. The Auto-Measure and AutoStrain features, cleared on Philips EPIQ and Affiniti systems (K211597, K190913 resp.) support users during B-mode (2D), CW-, PW- and TDI-Doppler measurements by automating some of the measurements needed to complete a routine transthoracic echo (TTE) exam for adult patients.
cases.source_description: The R-Trigger algorithm software feature on Philips EPIQ and Affiniti Ultrasound System is intended to support detection of R-wave peak (R-trigger) as an input to certain transthoracic echo (TTE) clinical applications, initially including AutoStrain LV, AutoEF, 2D Auto LV (collectively referred to as “AutoStrain”), and AutoMeasure applications. The R-trigger algorithm is expected to be implemented as workflow enhancement for transthoracic clinical applications on EPIQ and Affiniti Ultrasound Systems in the VM13 software release. The Auto-Measure and AutoStrain features, cleared on Philips EPIQ and Affiniti systems (K211597, K190913 resp.) support users during B-mode (2D), CW-, PW- and TDI-Doppler measurements by automating some of the measurements needed to complete a routine transthoracic echo (TTE) exam for adult patients. The current AutoMeasure and AutoStrain applications require input from physio signal (ECG), using electrodes, because the modules and their detectors work on single cardiac cycles, starting and ending with the End Diastole (ED), or more precisely, with delimiting R-trigger events as a good approximation. Determining the R-triggers is currently done on the EPIQ and Affiniti Ultrasound Systems by a dedicated physio board. To enable clinical users to be able to use AutoMeasure and AutoStrain application without the R-trigger (ECG based) input, R-trigger feature (non-ECG-based) has been developed.

cases.context: Department of Veterans Affairs; VHA: Veterans Health Administration; Health and Medical; United States
cases.implementation: The QVCAD CAD engine employs several image pattern recognition processes and artificial neural networks to detect suspicious areas of breast tissue 5mm or more in diameter that have characteristics similar to breast lesions. It inspects every tissue location in the 3-D ABUS images it processes with dedicated algorithms. These algorithms characterize the volumetric region surrounding each location by automatically extracting features that have been determined to represent suspicious signs. These features include typical ultrasound image features described in the radiological literature, such as region boundary, margin, echo pattern, orientation, posterior enhancement, architectural distortions, etc. Using those features, the QVCAD CAD engine generates a score for each suspicious area to distinguish potential breast lesions from normal breast tissue.

Genius AI Detection packages all CAD findings derived from the corresponding analysis of a tomosynthesis exam into a DICOM Mammography CAD SR object and distributes it for display on DICOM compliant review workstations. The interpreting physician will have access to the CAD findings concurrently to the reading of the tomosynthesis exam. In addition, a combination of peripheral information such as number of marks and case scores may be used on the review workstation to enhance the interpreting physician’s workflow by offering a better organization of the patient worklist.

The device intends to aid in the interpretation of digital breast tomosynthesis exams in a concurrent fashion, where the interpreting physician confirms or dismisses the findings during the reading of the exam.

Target Audience: The target audience mobile application developers and other internal stakeholders who may be interested in analyzing and understanding the sentiment and feedback from these reviews. cases.reported_benefits: With a single capture, CLARUS 700 produces a 90º high definition widefield image. Widefield images are automatically merged to achieve a 135º ultra-widefield of view. The CLARUS 700 makes use of a deep learning algorithm for Optic Nerve Head (ONH) detection. The ultra-widefield montage on CLARUS 700 is no longer dependent just on the patient accurately fixating their gaze on the internal fixation. With the ONH detection, the software will find the optic nerve and determine based on the image(s) captured where the patient was gazing at the point of capture. The CLARUS 700 device allows clinicians to easily review and compare high-quality images captured during a single exam while providing annotation and caliper measurement tools that allow in-depth analysis of eye health. CLARUS 700 is designed to optimize each patient’s experience by providing a simple head and chin rest that allows the patient to maintain a stable, neutral position while the operator brings the optics to the patient, facilitating a more comfortable imaging experience. The ability to swivel the device between the right and left eye helps technicians capture an image without realigning the patient. Live Infrared (IR) Preview allows the technician to confirm image quality and screen for lid and lash obstructions, prior to imaging, ensuring fewer image recaptures.
cases.source_description: The CLARUS 700 angiography imaging aids in the visualization of the vascular structures of the retina and the choroid.

cases.problem: While humans can generate word lists for text-matching approaches, the generated word lists are likely to be limited and biased by the vocabulary, language habits, population exposure, and local dialects of the human generating the list. Deep learning methods can help to augment candidate term lists to help overcome some of these challenges.
cases.task: Deep-Learning approaches to develop candidate lists of terms for use in text searches
cases.context: Department of Veterans Affairs; VHA: Veterans Health Administration; Health and Medical; United States
cases.implementation: The outputs of this use of AI is a candidate list of terms related to a concept of interest. This candidate list is combined with suggestions generated by human experts and then these are reviewed by a subject matter expert to generate a final list of terms for use in text-matching algorithms to extract medical record free text mentions of interest. For the pre-trained Large Language model approach, the input is a query prompting for synonyms of terms related to the concept of interest. The output is the answer provided by the LLM, including the suggested candidate terms and the original terms that were stated in the query. For the word and phrase embedding models, the input is an initial list of terms that are relevant to the concept of interest and the output are the suggested candidate terms, ranked by their statistical similarity to the original terms, based on the transformation of a clinical corpus into vector space or an “embedding model”. Regardless of the type of model used, all suggested candidate terms are reviewed by subject matter experts to ensure quality term lists are used in all text searches.
cases.outcome: UNKNOWN; 원천의 기대효과와 별도 관측 성과는 구분해야 합니다.
cases.reported_benefits: Here we (1) query pre-trained large language models (e.g., ChatGPT or Llama) through a user interface that allows prompting (such as the OpenAI API or CodeLlama) and/or (2) query word and phrase “embedding” models (e.g., Word2Vec and Phrase2Vec) to expand candidate term lists for review by subject matter experts. Our team has found both approaches effective for expediting the generation of more comprehensive term to concept mappings for use in text-matching algorithms that increase the accuracy of clinical concept extraction. We expect this use of AI to improve initial brainstorming of terms related to a given concept, resulting in a more sensitive approach to finding information of interest in free-text clinical notes. Experience to date has found that this approach enriches term sets in ways that increase sensitivity for identification of text of interest in clinical TIU notes when used in our CLEVER natural language processing pipeline.
cases.source_description: The intended use is to increase the comprehensiveness of term lists to be used in text-matching approaches to identifying concepts of interest in free-text medical record notes. Text-matching approaches are an efficient method for identifying text of interest in medical notes. The success of text-matching approaches depends on the quality of term lists used to search for a concept of interest. While humans can generate word lists for text-matching approaches, the generated word lists are likely to be limited and biased by the vocabulary, language habits, population exposure, and local dialects of the human generating the list. Deep learning methods can help to augment candidate term lists to help overcome some of these challenges. Once generated these augmented candidate terms are reviewed by subject matter experts for appropriateness and accuracy of the suggested terms for the concept and use case of interest.

cases.task: Use of Large Language Models to improve classification of identified text snippets from the CLEVER natural language processing pipeline
cases.context: Department of Veterans Affairs; VHA: Veterans Health Administration; Health and Medical; United States
cases.implementation: This AI use case adds additional LLM-derived classification labels to text snippets from free-text clinical notes identified by the CLEVER NLP pipeline. These labels indicate the LLMs classification of the text snippet as being related to a concept of interest. For example, in our first deployed use of this method, an LLM model was used to improve classification of text snippets identified as including the term “xylazine” in the note text. The LLM classified identified text snippets into one of three labels: (1) "Other" (OTH) for snippets without evidence of suspected xylazine exposure, (2) "Suspected-Positive" (SUS-P) for snippets with positively asserted evidence of suspected exposure, and (3) "Suspected-Negative" (SUS-N) for snippets where the suspected exposure was negated. The OTH category included, for example, the many cases in which providers educated patients about the presence of xylazine in the illicit drug supply. The LLM-derived classification labels were used to narrow down text snippets for display as mentions of “possible xylaxine exposure” on the STORM decision support display (to help clinicians find information of relevance to opioid risk management across VA medical records) and in maps of possible xylazine exposures for strategic planning. In both cases, only those text snippets labeled as “SUS-P” were included on the displays.
cases.outcome: UNKNOWN; 원천의 기대효과와 별도 관측 성과는 구분해야 합니다.
cases.reported_benefits: Improved classification of text snippets from clinical notes will increase clinician and management efficiency in use of decision support to summarize and review information extracted from free-text clinical notes. For example, improved filtering of text snippets for clinical risk factors of interest will reduce clinician time in obtaining clinically needed information about risk factors of interest by filtering out text snippets that are unlikely to be meaningful to their immediate clinical decision. In short, the clinician will have fewer candidate text snippets to read through to get the information they need. Likewise, summary views of identified possible concept mentions will be more accurate, reducing noise in views to support strategic decisions.
cases.source_description: Use of text matching approaches like CLEVER to identify clinical information of interest in free-text clinical notes is an efficient approach but can be over-inclusive (e.g. including terms when used with an alternative meaning, for example, a search for “arms” may pick up mentions of forearms and firearms). A variety of approaches can be used to further filter identified text snippets to those more likely to be of interest for a given use case. Here we use large language model queries to classify text snippets as being relevant to a concept of interest.

cases.task: AMS – Algorithmic Profiling in the Austrian Public Employment Service
cases.context: Public Employment Service Austria; Central-Government; Unemployment.; Austria
cases.implementation: The system applies statistical modelling techniques to historical labour market data, incorporating variables such as education, employment history and demographic indicators to generate probability scores.
cases.outcome: UNKNOWN; 원천의 기대효과와 별도 관측 성과는 구분해야 합니다.
cases.source_description: Public employment services aim to allocate counselling resources and labour market programmes efficiently while supporting diverse jobseekers with varying employment prospects. In Austria, the Public Employment Service (AMS) introduced an algorithmic profiling system to assist counsellors in classifying jobseekers according to their predicted likelihood of re-entering employment. Stakeholders include jobseekers, employment counsellors, programme administrators and oversight authorities. The objective was to improve the effectiveness of active labour market policies by tailoring support intensity to statistically estimated prospects. The system applies statistical modelling techniques to historical labour market data, incorporating variables such as education, employment history and demographic indicators to generate probability scores. Based on these outputs, individuals are categorised into high, medium or low employment prospects, which inform differentiated support pathways. Expected impacts included more targeted allocation of training resources, improved programme efficiency and data-informed counselling decisions; however, concerns emerged regarding fairness, transparency and potential discrimination in automated classifications.

cases.source_description: Businesses often need rapid, reliable guidance on economic measures, employment rules, subsidies, and administrative obligations, especially during periods of disruption such as the coronavirus crisis, when demand for official information rises sharply and questions become more varied. In this context, the Federal Ministry for Digitisation and Business Location introduced Mona through the Company Service Portal to give companies a simpler and more accessible way to obtain practical support on economic matters. The objective is to reduce information barriers for firms, improve access to official guidance across web and mobile channels, and help users navigate complex topics such as financial support, labour law, short-time work, teleworking, and research-related measures. The implementation combines a public-facing conversational interface with structured information flows, enabling both free-form questions and guided step-by-step navigation through key thematic areas. At a conceptual level, the service uses natural language understanding to interpret user requests, retrieve relevant information, and deliver responses through a chatbot integrated into the national business portal. The impact includes faster access to official information, lower demand on traditional support channels, and a more user-friendly experience for companies. It also improves service scalability, strengthens consistency of communication, and creates operational value by making critical business information available in a more efficient and responsive way.

In the Youth for Climate context, thousands of contributions were gathered in a short period, creating a need for a systematic way to analyse multilingual input without losing sight of recurring themes, priorities, and actionable insights. It also enhances scalability, reduces manual analysis effort, and increases the value of public engagement by making it easier to convert diverse ideas into usable strategic input.

cases.task: Walloon - Agricultural subsidy monitoring with the use of GeoAI
cases.context: Département de l'Agriculture; Local Government; Agriculture, forestry, fishing and hunting; Belgium
cases.implementation: This creates challenges for public authorities seeking to ensure compliance, use public funds efficiently, and maintain consistent oversight across large agricultural areas. The objective of this use case is to improve the accuracy, reach, and efficiency of subsidy monitoring by replacing sporadic manual checks with continuous and comprehensive observation.
cases.outcome: UNKNOWN; 원천의 기대효과와 별도 관측 성과는 구분해야 합니다.
cases.source_description: Monitoring whether agricultural subsidy conditions are met is traditionally a labour-intensive process, often based on limited field inspections that cover only a small proportion of parcels and crops. This creates challenges for public authorities seeking to ensure compliance, use public funds efficiently, and maintain consistent oversight across large agricultural areas. The objective of this use case is to improve the accuracy, reach, and efficiency of subsidy monitoring by replacing sporadic manual checks with continuous and comprehensive observation. The implementation uses geospatial analysis and image-processing techniques applied to satellite imagery in order to verify whether land use and crop conditions comply with subsidy requirements. At a conceptual level, geo-enabled analytical models process remote sensing data to assess agricultural parcels continuously, enabling authorities to monitor 100 per cent of parcels and crops rather than relying on field visits to only around 5 per cent. The solution is integrated into compliance monitoring workflows to support more timely and evidence-based verification. The impact includes broader coverage, reduced need for costly site inspections, and more effective stewardship of public money. In addition, it improves reliability, scalability, and consistency in agricultural oversight, while enabling authorities to identify potential issues earlier and allocate inspection resources more strategically.

cases.task: AcPaas - Technical procurement documents comparison
cases.context: Digipolis & city of Antwerp; Private sector; General public services n.e.c.; Belgium
cases.implementation: The objective of this use case is to support more efficient procurement preparation and solution design by identifying whether in-house technology components can satisfy requirements described in procurement or offer documentation. The implementation uses natural language processing to compare the text contained in technical files with metadata describing existing IT components, including APIs and applications.
cases.outcome: UNKNOWN; 원천의 기대효과와 별도 관측 성과는 구분해야 합니다.
cases.source_description: Public procurement processes often involve reviewing complex technical documents and determining whether existing internal digital components could already meet some of the stated requirements. This task can be time-consuming and fragmented, particularly in large organisations where APIs, applications, and other reusable assets are documented across multiple repositories and formats. The objective of this use case is to support more efficient procurement preparation and solution design by identifying whether in-house technology components can satisfy requirements described in procurement or offer documentation. The implementation uses natural language processing to compare the text contained in technical files with metadata describing existing IT components, including APIs and applications. For APIs, descriptive content is extracted and pre-processed from metadata files to improve matching, while an experimental extension also compares technical diagrams against component metadata. Conceptually, the solution links document analysis, metadata enrichment, and semantic comparison within the Antwerp City Platform as a Service environment. The impact includes faster identification of reusable digital assets, reduced duplication of development effort, and more informed procurement decisions. It also supports better use of existing technology investments, improves consistency in technical assessment, and enhances organisational efficiency by making internal component knowledge easier to access and apply in procurement and architecture processes.

Traditional enforcement methods rely heavily on manual observation by police, limiting detection rates and scalability. This use case aims to enhance enforcement capabilities by automating the identification of such violations and supporting road safety policies. The system uses roadside camera infrastructure to capture images of passing vehicles, which are then processed using computer vision techniques to detect whether a driver is holding and using a mobile phone. Images not indicating violations are automatically discarded, while detected cases are anonymised to protect privacy before further review. Law enforcement authorities validate flagged cases before issuing fines. The solution integrates image recognition models trained on annotated datasets to distinguish relevant behaviours. The pilot demonstrates the feasibility of augmenting enforcement through automated pre-selection of violations, improving efficiency and enabling more consistent monitoring. It contributes to increased deterrence, optimised use of police resources, and enhanced road safety outcomes.

cases.context: Corti; Private sector; Public health services.; Denmark
cases.implementation: This use case addresses that operational problem by supporting dispatchers and call-takers during emergency calls so that out-of-hospital cardiac arrests can be recognised faster and with fewer errors. The implementation uses real-time speech analysis on live emergency calls, applying predictive models trained to detect linguistic and behavioural patterns associated with cardiac arrest.

cases.source_description: Emergency call handlers must identify cardiac arrest within seconds, yet callers often describe symptoms unclearly and high-pressure conditions can lead to delayed recognition or missed warning signs. This use case addresses that operational problem by supporting dispatchers and call-takers during emergency calls so that out-of-hospital cardiac arrests can be recognised faster and with fewer errors. The broader objective is to improve emergency medical response, reduce avoidable mortality, and strengthen the reliability of call-centre decision-making in time-critical situations. The implementation uses real-time speech analysis on live emergency calls, applying predictive models trained to detect linguistic and behavioural patterns associated with cardiac arrest. At a conceptual level, the system listens to the call as it unfolds, analyses speech signals and conversational content, and produces immediate decision support for human operators. The approach is intended to work alongside dispatch professionals rather than replace them, feeding alerts and clinical suggestions into the emergency response workflow. Reported performance from the original deployment described detection accuracy of up to 95 per cent, and the Copenhagen implementation was sufficiently promising to support wider piloting with the European Emergency Number Association. The impact includes quicker diagnosis, reduced error rates, faster dispatch decisions, and stronger overall service quality, with clear public value in improving survival chances during medical emergencies.

SATIKAS was developed for the Estonian Agricultural Registers and Information Board to automate this monitoring task and improve oversight of grassland management using remote sensing. cases.task: OTT - Predicting employment pathways
cases.context: Estonian Unemployment Insurance Fund; Central-Government; Unemployment.; Estonia

cases.source_description: Employment services must decide how best to support jobseekers with very different skills, histories, and barriers to work, yet this can be difficult to do consistently when advisers are handling large caseloads and labour market conditions are changing. OTT was developed by the Estonian Unemployment Insurance Fund to improve understanding of client needs and to help identify the most suitable employment pathways for individual jobseekers. The objective is to support more accurate job recommendations, better targeting of retraining or reskilling measures, and more effective allocation of staff attention across client groups. The implementation uses machine-learning methods trained on more than 100,000 client records to estimate the probabilities of different employment outcomes and suggest appropriate positions or interventions based on qualifications and profile characteristics. At a conceptual level, the system combines client data, pathway prediction, and recommendation logic within a tool used by civil servants rather than as a fully autonomous public-facing service. It helps structure client segmentation, identify likely needs, and distribute workload more effectively among advisers. cases.source_description: SyRi was introduced by the Dutch government in 2014 to address a longstanding administrative challenge: municipalities wanted a more systematic way to identify possible welfare fraud and misuse of public benefits across fragmented public-sector datasets. Before SyRi, several municipalities had been developing their own approaches, creating inconsistency and duplication in fraud-detection practices. The use case involved municipalities, civil servants and national authorities, with the objective of improving the targeting of further investigations by identifying addresses considered at higher risk of irregularities in welfare claims. SyRi did not make formal decisions itself, but was designed to support civil servants by generating recommendations for additional scrutiny based on aggregated signals from existing governmental systems. The solution was implemented by combining risk indicators from multiple sources, including tax records, health-insurance data, residence information and education-related datasets, to generate risk profiles for possible fraud or misuse. At a conceptual level, the system used cross-dataset matching and risk-scoring techniques to highlight cases for further human review. However, the system became highly controversial because of concerns over privacy intrusion, lack of transparency and discriminatory effects on poorer and more vulnerable citizens. Following legal challenge, a Dutch court ruled in early 2020 that SyRi’s use breached Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights, and the system was prohibited. Its impact therefore includes not only lessons on administrative targeting, but also a major cautionary example regarding legality, transparency and rights-based governance.

The impact was a clear improvement in control efficiency, better targeting of investigative effort and stronger use of public funds, with measurable gains in detection performance and a more scalable approach to compliance monitoring.

cases.source_description: During the COVID-19 pandemic, the Polish government needed a way to monitor compliance with mandatory quarantine orders while limiting in-person checks and at the same time offering practical support to people confined at home. The operational challenge was to verify that quarantined individuals remained at the required location without relying solely on repeated police visits, which would have been resource-intensive and harder to scale during a public-health emergency. The use case therefore involved quarantined residents, police authorities and public-health institutions, with the objective of improving quarantine enforcement, reducing administrative burden and giving users access to relevant information and support. The solution was implemented through the free Home Quarantine app for iPhone and Android, connected to the official database of phone numbers associated with quarantine orders so that only eligible users could activate it. After registration using a phone number and SMS code, users submitted a reference photograph, and the app then sent unscheduled prompts requiring a new image within 20 minutes. At a conceptual level, the system combined facial-recognition checks with location verification to confirm identity and presence, effectively replicating the function of an in-person control. The app also included health information and access to a hotline. The impact was improved scalability in quarantine monitoring, reduced dependence on physical inspections and more integrated support for quarantined individuals, while also raising broader questions about proportionality, privacy and emergency digital enforcement.

The expected impact was better crowd management, improved public information and faster response to unsafe density levels. More broadly, the initiative created value by improving public-space management, supporting safer tourism and demonstrating a scalable model for real-time occupancy monitoring in high-footfall environments.

cases.source_description: Upplands-Bro Municipality began using Tengai in June 2019 to address a persistent challenge in recruitment: reducing bias in candidate selection while maintaining a structured and efficient hiring process. Traditional interviews can be influenced by subjective impressions, inconsistent questioning and uneven evaluation practices, which may affect fairness and the quality of shortlist decisions. The use case therefore involved the municipality’s recruitment and staffing agency, hiring managers and job candidates, with the objective of making recruitment more impartial, standardised and evidence-based while preserving a final human assessment of motivation and fit. The solution was implemented through Tengai, one of the first social interview robots, developed in collaboration between municipal staff and Furhat Robotics. At a conceptual level, the system first identifies candidates with the highest general performance scores to create a shortlist, then conducts structured interviews in which it assesses behaviour, problem-solving ability and other competencies, including the ability to ask follow-up questions where needed. These interview outputs are combined with competency scores and passed on to recruiters, who then carry out the final interview stage. The first results were regarded as successful, and the service was adopted permanently within a week of release. The impact included a more standardised interview process, reduced exposure to bias in early screening and significant reputational value through national and international media attention to the municipality’s innovative recruitment approach.

Heart and lung diseases place a major burden on health systems, yet earlier and more individualised risk identification requires data on a scale and depth that routine care alone cannot easily provide. The use case brought together all six Swedish healthcare regions, university hospitals and a broad group of scientific stakeholders, with the objective of building a national evidence base to improve understanding of cardiovascular, pulmonary, epidemiological and genetic risk factors. The study began with a pilot in 2012 to confirm feasibility, followed by the major study launch in 2014, building on work initiated in 2007. The impact lies in creating a world-leading research resource that supports earlier prevention, more precise risk stratification and stronger scientific understanding of heart and lung disease. In broader terms, SCAPIS improves the foundation for long-term public-health planning, supports clinical innovation and strengthens the ability of the health system to move from reactive treatment towards prevention.

cases.source_description: Hackney Council introduced the Early Help Profiling System to support earlier intervention for children and families considered vulnerable, in a context where public services were under pressure to identify risk sooner and target limited support resources more effectively. The system was intended to help social workers prioritise households that might require attention by drawing on patterns across education, housing and economic records. Each month, practitioners received a shortlist of 20 families assessed as high risk, with the objective of enabling preventive action before harm escalated. The solution was implemented by combining administrative datasets such as school attendance, housing information and financial records to generate risk profiles and ranked recommendations for frontline teams. At a conceptual level, the system used predictive modelling and cross-dataset analysis to flag cases for further human review rather than making decisions automatically. It was reported to be more than 80% accurate and projected to save around €1 million annually, suggesting potential gains in targeting and efficiency. However, the initiative attracted strong criticism over secrecy, commercial control of data and its perceived relationship to austerity-era service pressures. In the end, Hackney Council discontinued the system after it failed to deliver the expected benefits, making it a notable example of the gap that can emerge between technical promise, public trust and operational value.

The operational challenge is especially acute where invoice volumes are high and staff must interpret coding requirements repeatedly under time pressure. This use case was introduced to improve efficiency and reduce error in financial administration by supporting more accurate posting decisions from the outset. The expected impact is faster invoice handling, fewer posting errors and reduced risk of additional costs from interest and charges. More broadly, the use case creates value by improving operational efficiency in financial management, increasing consistency in accounting processes and supporting more scalable processing of incoming invoices across public-sector organisations.

The pilot involved twenty older residents already supported by the City Council’s Area for Social Rights and was launched in the context of a broader challenge focused on improving quality of life for senior citizens through technology. The operational problem was social isolation and the difficulty of maintaining regular reminders, wellbeing monitoring and day-to-day support for people who may be vulnerable but still living independently. The implementation used the Misty II social robot as an in-home interaction platform, capable of providing reminders, supporting simple monitoring functions and engaging users in daily routines. At a conceptual level, the solution combined conversational interaction, scheduling support and basic assistive features within a real-world pilot setting so that user acceptance and practical value could be evaluated directly. The expected impact included better user experience, reduced feelings of isolation and improved support for routine health and wellbeing tasks. More broadly, the pilot explored a scalable model for complementing social-care services and extending support for older people living alone.

cases.source_description: Family benefits offices in Germany face a recurring administrative burden because, to maintain eligibility for child benefit, a student’s current certificate of enrolment must be submitted twice a year. The problem is compounded by the lack of a uniform certificate format across German universities, which means that large volumes of heterogeneous documents must be checked manually. This use case was introduced to reduce processing effort, improve consistency and accelerate validation while retaining staff oversight. The stakeholders include applicants, family benefits offices and case-handling staff, with the objective of making the verification of study certificates faster, more reliable and less labour-intensive. The solution is implemented through a workflow in which the applicant uploads the certificate via a web portal, the text is extracted using optical character recognition, and the resulting content is classified automatically. At a conceptual level, the system checks four points: whether the document is a study certificate, whether it relates to the correct child, whether the semester or validity period is correct, and whether the issuing institution is a recognised German university. The result is displayed within the specialist procedure and must be actively accepted by an employee. The training base currently includes 60,000 semi-automatically annotated certificates, anonymised with a dedicated algorithm, and the classification combines Naive Bayes, Support Vector Machine, Logistic Regression, natural language processing and named-entity recognition. The impact is improved efficiency, reduced manual workload and more scalable certificate processing.

cases.source_description: Public prosecutors and investigators face the operational challenge of reviewing very large volumes of seized digital material in cases involving the distribution, acquisition or possession of child and youth sexual abuse imagery. Much of this material may be entirely irrelevant to the offence under investigation, yet it must still be assessed carefully to identify evidential content. The use case was therefore designed to support case workers by accelerating the initial sorting of suspicious images so that the most potentially relevant material could be prioritised for detailed review. Its objective was to reduce the burden of manual screening, improve consistency in the handling of digital evidence and support more efficient investigative and prosecutorial workflows while preserving human judgement in the final assessment. The implementation used automated image-recognition techniques to analyse visual material and identify items most likely to depict illegal content involving children or adolescents. At a conceptual level, the system functioned as a triage mechanism, separating likely irrelevant material from images requiring closer investigation and forwarding flagged content to case handlers and, where appropriate, to the public prosecutor for decision. The impact was faster evidence screening, reduced manual effort and improved focus of investigative resources on the most relevant material. In operational terms, the approach enhanced scalability, supported reliability in evidence handling and improved the efficiency of highly sensitive prosecutorial work.

cases.source_description: When an accident at work, or on the journey to or from work, is caused by a third party, the Employer’s Liability Insurance Association must assess whether recourse proceedings against that third party are likely to succeed. Previously, suspected cases were forwarded through a standardised document flow to a central office, where they were manually pre-checked, creating a slow and resource-intensive process across large case volumes. This use case was developed to improve prioritisation and support case handlers with more structured evidence before they decide whether to pursue recourse. The stakeholders include the insurance association, recourse departments and case officers, with the objective of increasing efficiency, improving the quality of triage and strengthening decisions on whether legal recovery is worthwhile. The solution is implemented using a model trained on around one million completed recourse and subrogation proceedings, both successful and unsuccessful. At a conceptual level, the system estimates the plausibility of a potential recourse action, forecasts the likely probability of success and predicts the level of total costs. In parallel, text-mining methods identify critical keywords, such as whether the police were called or whether an assault occurred, to provide additional decision support. These outputs are delivered through a web interface for the recourse department. The impact is faster pre-assessment, better-informed case selection and reduced manual effort, with broader value in improving consistency, focusing resources on higher-potential cases and making recourse management more scalable.

cases.source_description: This use case addresses the need to extend rehabilitation support beyond conventional clinical sessions by introducing an assistive robot that can complement therapists’ work in hospitals, rehabilitation gyms and patients’ homes. The context is one in which patients recovering from injury or managing long-term functional limitations often require frequent support with exercises, daily activities and safety monitoring, while clinical staff must balance intensive care needs with limited time and resources. The stakeholders include patients, rehabilitation professionals, ward staff and carers, with the objective of improving continuity of support, reinforcing therapy routines and assisting with everyday tasks that help preserve autonomy and safety. The implementation uses the humanoid robot R1, developed as part of the ETAPAS H2020 project, combining advanced mechanics, sensors and intelligent control capabilities to operate as a low-cost assistive-rehabilitation platform. At a conceptual level, the system supports traditional rehabilitation treatments, assists staff in clinical environments and provides in-home functions such as fetching or locating objects, reminding patients about appointments or medication, and detecting falls to support emergency management. The expected impact includes improved continuity of care, better patient experience and stronger support for independent living. More broadly, the solution offers scalability through lower-cost deployment, reduces pressure on clinical staff and strengthens rehabilitation outcomes by extending assistance into everyday environments.

cases.source_description: Kari was created to help local municipalities manage large volumes of citizen enquiries about public services in a faster and more consistent way. In many councils, residents need clear answers on procedures, rights and local services, yet frontline teams often face repetitive requests that absorb time and slow response delivery. The use case therefore involves municipal administrations and citizens, with the objective of improving access to information, reducing pressure on service staff and strengthening the quality of digital interaction with local government. The solution is implemented through a virtual-agent platform integrated into municipal service channels and supported by a knowledge base containing more than 6,000 intents, covering a very broad range of local-government questions. At a conceptual level, the system uses conversational language-processing and intent-recognition techniques to interpret citizen requests, match them to the relevant service information and return standardised answers that can be maintained centrally and reused across municipalities. Kari is currently available in 80 Norwegian municipalities, covering about 30% of the Norwegian population, and is being introduced in Sweden, Finland and Denmark. The result is improved user experience, faster access to information and greater scalability in handling routine enquiries, while municipalities benefit from more efficient service delivery, better consistency of responses and reduced administrative workload.

Public authorities must respond in an environment where inaccurate online content can spread rapidly, undermine trust and complicate communication with citizens. The use case therefore involves municipal decision-makers, communication teams and public-sector organisations seeking to manage information risks more effectively, with the objective of detecting problematic content early and handling it in a way that is operationally useful and socially responsible. The expected impact is improved responsiveness to misinformation, better prioritisation of public communication efforts and stronger institutional trust. cases.task: Home Quarantine App - Supporting the use of electronic control for home quarantine
cases.context: Hungarian government; Central-Government; Health n.e.c.; Hungary
cases.implementation: In early May 2020, a government decree enabled the use of electronic control to support home quarantine, responding to the practical challenge of monitoring compliance during the COVID-19 pandemic without relying solely on manual enforcement. The solution was implemented through a mobile application developed by Asura Technologies, a Hungarian company with experience in facial-recognition and GPS-location technologies.
cases.outcome: UNKNOWN; 원천의 기대효과와 별도 관측 성과는 구분해야 합니다.
cases.source_description: In early May 2020, a government decree enabled the use of electronic control to support home quarantine, responding to the practical challenge of monitoring compliance during the COVID-19 pandemic without relying solely on manual enforcement. The app was introduced in a context where authorities needed a scalable mechanism to check whether quarantined individuals remained at home, while also attempting to encourage uptake by linking participation to lower fines for breaches of quarantine rules. The stakeholders included quarantined citizens, state authorities and the developer company Asura Technologies, with the objective of strengthening compliance monitoring and supporting pandemic-control measures. The solution was implemented through a mobile application developed by Asura Technologies, a Hungarian company with experience in facial-recognition and GPS-location technologies. At a conceptual level, the system linked identity verification with geolocation checks, while personal data formally remained with the state and the company’s role was described as establishing the connection between the relevant data points rather than accessing the data itself. Although use of the app was voluntary, the incentive structure created practical pressure to adopt it. The impact lay in providing a digital alternative to more labour-intensive monitoring, but the case also raised broader issues around proportionality, governance and the role of private operators in public enforcement technology. The app is no longer in use, but it remains significant as a pandemic-era example of digitally supported quarantine control.

cases.task: Estimation of income of self-employed and SMES who pay taxes by module
cases.context: Agencia Tributaria; Central-Government; Economic affairs n.e.c; Spain
cases.implementation: This use case was designed to estimate the likely income of those taxpayers more accurately so that official statistical and analytical work can be based on more robust information. The solution is implemented through predictive estimation based on a wider comparison population of taxpayers with similar characteristics who do declare exact income, as well as taxpayers who switch between the modular system and direct declaration from one period to the next.

cases.source_description: In Spain, certain self-employed workers and small and medium-sized enterprises may opt to pay taxes under a modular system rather than declaring their exact income. While this simplifies compliance for taxpayers, it creates an analytical challenge for the tax administration because exact income figures are not directly available for this group, yet they are still needed for the calculation of ratios, statistics and broader economic analysis. This use case was designed to estimate the likely income of those taxpayers more accurately so that official statistical and analytical work can be based on more robust information. The stakeholders include the tax administration, statistical and analytical teams, and indirectly the wider policy community that relies on income-based indicators, with the objective of improving the quality of tax-based estimates without changing the underlying tax regime. The solution is implemented through predictive estimation based on a wider comparison population of taxpayers with similar characteristics who do declare exact income, as well as taxpayers who switch between the modular system and direct declaration from one period to the next. At a conceptual level, the system uses these comparable datasets to infer likely income levels for the target population and feeds the resulting estimates into the calculation of income-related indicators. The impact is improved statistical reliability, stronger analytical precision and better consistency in fiscal reporting, creating value through more accurate measurement and more useful evidence for policy and administration.

cases.context: Hungarian police; Central-Government; Police Services; Hungary
cases.implementation: This use case therefore aims to streamline enforcement by linking roadside capture, data verification and administrative processing in a single workflow. The solution is implemented through the Véda intelligent camera network, which feeds data into KAFIR, the Traffic Safety Automated Processing and Information System, and then into the police’s broader Robotzsaru records and case-management platform.

cases.source_description: Hungary’s road-safety enforcement authorities needed a faster and more integrated way to process large volumes of traffic violations with minimal delay and consistent evidential handling. Manual processing of speeding and related road-traffic offences can be time-consuming and vulnerable to bottlenecks, particularly when evidence must be matched against vehicle registries and then transferred into case-management systems. This use case therefore aims to streamline enforcement by linking roadside capture, data verification and administrative processing in a single workflow. The stakeholders include the police, responsible enforcement authorities and road users, with the objective of improving traffic-safety enforcement, accelerating case handling and reducing administrative friction in the imposition of fines. The solution is implemented through the Véda intelligent camera network, which feeds data into KAFIR, the Traffic Safety Automated Processing and Information System, and then into the police’s broader Robotzsaru records and case-management platform. At a conceptual level, the cameras capture the vehicle registration number, speed, location coordinates, date and time, after which KAFIR cross-checks this information against the traffic registry, for example to determine whether a vehicle is stolen, and uploads the data into Robotzsaru. The files are then classified and sent to the competent authority without human intervention at that stage, followed by an ex post administrative check. The impact is highly automated enforcement, faster transmission and classification of cases, and more consistent processing of no-fault traffic infringements.

cases.task: Predicting sick leave duration
cases.context: Norwegian Labour and Welfare Administration (NAV); Central-Government; Unemployment.; Norway
cases.implementation: The use case therefore focuses on improving prioritisation in sickness-absence management by estimating how long the current period of sick leave is likely to continue. The solution is implemented through a random-forest model that predicts the remaining duration of an ongoing sick-leave episode.
cases.outcome: UNKNOWN; 원천의 기대효과와 별도 관측 성과는 구분해야 합니다.
cases.source_description: The Norwegian Labour and Welfare Service needed a more structured way to support case workers dealing with people on sick leave, particularly when deciding which cases require closer follow-up and which may need less attention. Without predictive support, such decisions depend heavily on individual judgement and can make it harder to allocate case-management effort efficiently across large caseloads. The use case therefore focuses on improving prioritisation in sickness-absence management by estimating how long the current period of sick leave is likely to continue. The stakeholders include case workers, people on sick leave and the wider set of actors involved in return-to-work dialogue, with the objective of improving the quality of follow-up decisions and making case management more targeted. The solution is implemented through a random-forest model that predicts the remaining duration of an ongoing sick-leave episode. At a conceptual level, the prediction is integrated into the information available to the case worker when deciding whether to call a dialogue meeting between the relevant parties. To strengthen interpretability, the outputs are explained using Shapley values, allowing case workers to understand which factors contributed most to the prediction. The use case does not aim to detect perpetrators directly at the initial stage, but to help authorities identify potential victims more effectively and trigger further investigation where justified. The stakeholders include labour inspectors, banks, researchers, the Financial Intelligence Unit and, ultimately, prosecutors and judges, with the objective of strengthening early detection while preserving human control over escalatory decisions. The solution is implemented through pattern-recognition scripts applied to banking data using risk patterns supplied by the Inspectorate. At a conceptual level, the scripts search for relevant transactional connections, after which human reviewers check the output for false positives. If a pattern is validated, it may justify a further FIU investigation into suspicious transactions, which can then support legal escalation and, where authorised, access to address and transaction details for tracing potential victims. Machine-learning refinement and expansion to four other major banks are under consideration. The impact lies in earlier and more targeted identification, improved investigative efficiency and stronger inter-institutional cooperation in combating labour exploitation.

cases.source_description: Legal and policy rules are often difficult to interpret consistently, particularly when different professional groups or affected citizens need to understand how norms should be applied in practice. This creates challenges not only for legislative drafting and legal analysis, but also for the legitimacy and acceptance of decisions made under complex regulatory frameworks. Calculemus FLINT was developed to address this problem by making normative legal texts more understandable, more formally interpretable and easier to test for executability. The stakeholders include policymakers, legislative lawyers and citizens subject to legal rules, with the objective of improving the exchange, interpretation and explanation of norms across different groups while supporting more transparent and accountable implementation. The solution is implemented through a paired method and language framework: Calculemus as a roadmap for solving normative questions, and FLINT as a formal domain-specific language for interpreting judicial and normative sources. At a conceptual level, the approach translates legal norms into structured formal representations that allow rules to be analysed, compared and tested more systematically. This can help explain whether laws are operationally executable and whether decisions made under them can be justified clearly. The impact is primarily qualitative, centred on greater interpretability, improved legal transparency and stronger normative grounding for automated or assisted decisions. More broadly, the method creates value by increasing confidence in rule-based public administration and supporting clearer communication between legal experts, policymakers and citizens.

cases.source_description: Amsterdam introduced the 1.5 metre monitor during the COVID-19 pandemic to support enforcement of public-health guidance on social distancing in busy public spaces. The operational problem was that authorities needed a way to observe crowd behaviour and communicate distancing risks in real time, particularly in locations where pedestrian density could change quickly and manual oversight alone was insufficient. The stakeholders included municipal authorities, public-space managers and pedestrians, with the objective of encouraging safer distancing behaviour, monitoring crowding and helping manage public areas under emergency regulations. The solution was implemented through camera-based monitoring that measured the distance between pedestrians and displayed anonymised visual feedback using green, orange and red smileys, accompanied by audio warnings. At a conceptual level, the system used computer-vision techniques to estimate interpersonal distance and produce immediate behavioural cues without storing photographs, while still recording pedestrian counts to track crowd levels. This allowed the city to test a form of real-time public-space monitoring that combined behaviour feedback with crowd measurement. The impact was primarily operational and situational: it offered a way to promote distancing and understand crowding patterns during the pandemic, while limiting data retention by avoiding image storage. Once COVID-19 restrictions ended, the monitor was discontinued. Although temporary, the case remains an important example of how public-health rules were supported through live behavioural monitoring in urban environments.

cases.source_description: Public organisations working with large volumes of unstructured information on IT security need better ways to search, interpret and reuse textual content that is often fragmented across news, reports and background material. The operational challenge is that pure text alone is difficult to query with precision, especially when words have multiple meanings or when users need systems to support more advanced reasoning rather than simple keyword lookup. This use case therefore focuses on improving the metadata attached to unstructured textual information so that search quality and automated reasoning can be strengthened. The stakeholders include the BSI, analysts and users of IT-security information, with the objective of creating cleaner, more structured and more semantically useful text resources for retrieval and analysis. The solution is implemented by first creating a corpus of publicly available IT-security news and background texts, pre-processing it to remove artefacts and technical noise, and then enriching it through a combination of semantic and statistical methods. At a conceptual level, manually created taxonomies and ontologies, using standards such as SKOS, are combined with machine-learning approaches that capture local context and support named-entity extraction, while transformer-based NLP models are applied to tasks such as entity recognition, classification and question answering. The impact is expected to include higher-quality search, more reusable metadata and better support for automated interpretation, creating value through improved information access and stronger analytical capability in cybersecurity knowledge management.

cases.implementation: The use case involves residents, the IRIS service and the municipal departments responsible for resolving reported incidents, with the objective of speeding up response times, reducing classification errors and improving the overall quality of citizen service. cases.source_description: Barcelona City Council relies on IRIS as the channel through which citizens report incidents, submit complaints and suggest service improvements, yet the effectiveness of the process depends heavily on the initial thematic classification chosen by the user. If an incident is assigned to the wrong category, it can be routed to the wrong department, causing delays and reducing service quality. The operational problem was therefore to simplify classification for citizens while improving routing accuracy inside the council. The use case involves residents, the IRIS service and the municipal departments responsible for resolving reported incidents, with the objective of speeding up response times, reducing classification errors and improving the overall quality of citizen service. The solution is implemented through MARIO, a machine-learning-based module developed as part of the IRIS update. At a conceptual level, the module analyses the free text entered by the user and suggests the most likely categories into which the incident fits, allowing the citizen to choose the most appropriate option with guidance from the system. This creates a more intelligent classification layer at the point of submission and reduces the reliance on later manual correction. The reported impact is substantial: whereas previously around 50% of communications had to be reassigned, MARIO now achieves a hit rate of over 85%. More broadly, the project creates value by improving routing efficiency, reducing rework and making citizen reporting more reliable and user-friendly.

cases.source_description: Sigma served as the chatbot for Portugal’s public-services portal, ePortugal.gov.pt, helping users navigate state services and complete certain simple interactions through a digital conversational interface. The operational challenge was that citizens often need quick answers about administrative procedures but may struggle to navigate large service portals or understand where to find the right transaction. Sigma was introduced to improve access to public-service information and make some routine interactions more convenient, such as changing an address on the Citizen Card or checking polling stations during elections. The stakeholders included portal users, public-service administrators and the teams managing the national digital-services platform, with the objective of simplifying first-line access to administrative information and tasks. The solution was implemented through a combination of three Microsoft technologies: LUIS for intent recognition, QnA for service and chat content, and Cognitive Services APIs for keyword-based interpretation. At a conceptual level, these components enabled the chatbot to recognise user questions, retrieve relevant content and guide people towards the appropriate service or action. This created a conversational access layer over the wider ePortugal portal rather than requiring users to rely solely on menus and static pages. The impact was improved convenience, quicker access to routine information and broader experimentation with conversational public services. Although Sigma is no longer in use, it remains a useful example of multi-platform chatbot deployment in government digital services.

cases.task: Tool to optimise self-consumption in residential sectors
cases.context: Aiguasol; Private sector; Housing and community amenities n.e.c.; Spain
cases.implementation: Households and residential communities increasingly want to make better use of locally generated renewable electricity, but optimising self-consumption is difficult because it depends on understanding both generation patterns and highly variable consumption behaviour. This use case was therefore designed to help residential users and energy planners develop more efficient self-consumption scenarios and better align local renewable generation with actual demand.
cases.outcome: UNKNOWN; 원천의 기대효과와 별도 관측 성과는 구분해야 합니다.
cases.source_description: Households and residential communities increasingly want to make better use of locally generated renewable electricity, but optimising self-consumption is difficult because it depends on understanding both generation patterns and highly variable consumption behaviour. In practice, selecting the right system size and managing hourly distribution of photovoltaic output across users requires forecasting that most available tools do not support well. This use case was therefore designed to help residential users and energy planners develop more efficient self-consumption scenarios and better align local renewable generation with actual demand. The stakeholders include energy users, installers, planners and potentially grid operators, with the objective of improving self-consumption rates, supporting system sizing and enabling more efficient use of distributed renewable energy. The solution is implemented through a set of tools built around three modules: recruitment, planning and execution. At a conceptual level, the platform combines consumption forecasting, photovoltaic production forecasting and optimisation techniques to calculate hourly distribution coefficients and recommend self-consumption scenarios. In addition, automatically generated statistical profiles by user type help determine the optimal number of PV panels during earlier planning stages. The expected impact is better use of renewable generation, more accurate system sizing and reduced difficulty in planning residential self-consumption schemes. More broadly, the tool creates value by helping users adapt consumption habits, supporting future grid-stability services and enabling a more data-driven, scalable approach to distributed energy management.

cases.context: The National Library of Finland; Central-Government; Cultural services.; Finland
cases.implementation: The Stanford NER system was trained using 220 annotated pages and evaluated using 34 pages. Using the trained model, it was possible to classify images into the following groups: advertisements, drawings, notes, pictures, paintings, maps or garbage.

cases.source_description: Two AI tools have been integrated into the IT system of the National Library of Finland (digi.nationallibrary.fi): 1. Named entity recognition (NER) -Stanford NER software to recognize persons and place names from the Finnish historical newspapers. The first training and evaluation data set was created that consists of pages of both journals and newspapers from the time period 1836–1918. The Stanford NER system was trained using 220 annotated pages and evaluated using 34 pages. The results that were achieved were mostly good: 71 % of person names and 79 % of place names were recognized from the evaluation data. 2. Image classification -Google TensorFlow was used to classify images. A training dataset was created that was used to train the classifier model with TensorFlow. Using the trained model, it was possible to classify images into the following groups: advertisements, drawings, notes, pictures, paintings, maps or garbage. -The trained model was used to classify 50 000 images and its accuracy was about 70-75% when about 10 000 classified images were manually observed. -A graphical user interface was created that enabled an easier way to observe achieved results.

cases.task: IMMS (Intelligent Material Management System) for the entire library collection.
cases.context: Helsinki City Library; Local Government; R&D general public services.; Finland
cases.implementation: Implemented in May 2019, IMMS complements the existing library management infrastructure by adding a more detailed layer of collection, space and logistics management. The system uses data collection tools to track materials at granular locations, including shelves, shelving carts, transport bins and storage areas, thereby creating greater transparency across the material flow.
cases.outcome: UNKNOWN; 원천의 기대효과와 별도 관측 성과는 구분해야 합니다.
cases.source_description: Helsinki City Library introduced the Intelligent Material Management System during its transition from separate library-specific collections towards one shared collection serving the whole city network. The operational problem was that materials needed to move more flexibly between branches, while library staff required better visibility over where items were located, how they circulated and how available space could be used. The objective was to support a “floating” collection model, in which books and other materials are no longer tied permanently to a single branch but can circulate according to user demand and operational needs. Implemented in May 2019, IMMS complements the existing library management infrastructure by adding a more detailed layer of collection, space and logistics management. The system uses data collection tools to track materials at granular locations, including shelves, shelving carts, transport bins and storage areas, thereby creating greater transparency across the material flow. It supports decision-making on stock distribution, item movement, collection balance and physical space use across the library network. As a result, Helsinki City Library has been able to move towards a model in which most of the collection floats between libraries. The main benefits include more efficient use of the overall collection, improved staff control over logistics, better alignment between material availability and user demand, and a more scalable approach to managing public library resources across multiple branches.

cases.context: La Poste; Central-Government; Transport; France

cases.outcome: UNKNOWN; 원천의 기대효과와 별도 관측 성과는 구분해야 합니다.
cases.source_description: La Poste’s truck-scheduling use case addresses the difficulty of managing loading operations when incoming trucks arrive early, on time or late because of congestion and other disruptions. The operational problem is that uncertain arrival times reduce loading-bay utilisation and force logistics operators to make costly rescheduling decisions. The solution combines a machine-learning classifier with an optimisation model: the classifier estimates the probability that each truck will arrive early, on time or late, and these probabilities are then used to proactively adjust loading slots. At a conceptual level, the system links real-time truck-location information, historical traffic data, predictive classification and mathematical rescheduling. The expected impact is more efficient loading-bay management, lower disruption costs and better transport-flow optimisation. Research on the case reported that the combined predictive and proactive approach reduced rescheduling costs by around 42% compared with a baseline schedule without real-time arrival predictions. This indicates that predictive information can materially improve operational planning when integrated with optimisation rather than used only as a passive forecast.
