cases.source_description: The Bibliothèque nationale de Luxembourg implemented this use case to improve the accessibility, usability and long-term management of textual documents held in its collections. National libraries are responsible not only for preserving documentary heritage, but also for making it discoverable and usable for researchers, public institutions and citizens. The operational challenge addressed here concerns the conversion of scanned or image-based materials into structured, searchable and better-organised digital resources. The objective is to enhance the quality of digitised content by correcting errors, identifying meaningful information within texts and improving the organisation of associated image content. The implementation uses optical character recognition as a foundation for transforming scanned documents into machine-readable text, followed by correction processes to improve the reliability of the extracted content. Entity extraction is then applied to identify relevant names, places, organisations or other significant references within the material, while image-content organisation supports better structuring and retrieval of visual components. Together, these techniques make the digitised collections easier to search, classify and reuse. The impact is a stronger digital library service, improved discoverability of national documentary resources, higher-quality metadata and text outputs, and better support for research and public access. Over time, the approach contributes to more scalable digitisation workflows and strengthens the National Library’s capacity to preserve and disseminate Luxembourg’s cultural and documentary heritage.

cases.source_description: The City Municipality of Kranj launched this use case in 2021 to explore how a residential district could be managed through more integrated, data-informed urban services. The pilot focused on Mlaka pri Kranju and was carried out with a consortium of local companies, including RIKO d.o.o., 3fs d.o.o., Iskraemeco d.d., Komunala Kranj d.o.o., Domplan d.o.o., Elektro Gorenjska d.d. and Vigred d.o.o. The main operational need was to obtain a clearer, more timely picture of how neighbourhood infrastructure performs, particularly in relation to utilities, environmental conditions, traffic and connectivity. Rather than managing these domains separately, the municipality aimed to create a smart-neighbourhood model that could later be extended to other parts of the city. The technological implementation centres on a digital twin approach, combining data from smart electricity, gas and water meters with environmental and traffic sensors, supported by a telecommunications backbone. These inputs are collected, visualised and analysed to create a digital representation of selected neighbourhood functions and infrastructure conditions. The resulting model can support monitoring, planning and service coordination at local level. Its value lies in giving the municipality and service providers a more coherent operational view, improving evidence for infrastructure decisions, enabling future scalability across Kranj, and establishing a practical foundation for broader smart-city development.

cases.source_description: AuroraAI was launched in Finland as a national service model intended to support more human-centric public services and more informed public-sector management. The underlying challenge was that services were often organised in silos, making it harder for citizens and businesses to receive timely support aligned with real-life situations and harder for authorities to allocate services in a coordinated way. AuroraAI sought to respond to this by creating a “well-being snapshot” and linking it to service provision across different life events, with the objective of improving relevance, timing and coordination in public support. The stakeholders included citizens, companies, responsible authorities and public-service organisations, with the broader aim of reshaping how government worked across institutional boundaries. The solution was implemented through a decentralised network architecture designed to connect service providers and allocate services more effectively based on identified needs. At a conceptual level, the model combined distributed data use, service-matching logic and ethical-governance principles, with responsible organisations coordinating the application of the model to selected life events. This was intended to enable knowledge-based management as well as more timely support for end users. The anticipated impact included better cross-service coordination, less fragmented service supply and stronger conditions for ethically functioning digital support in government. Although the service model is no longer in use, AuroraAI remains significant as an ambitious attempt to redesign public services around life events, wellbeing and coordinated digital governance.

cases.source_description: Civocracy provides public authorities with an online participation environment designed to improve dialogue between citizens, businesses, civil-society organisations and governments. The use case addresses a recurring challenge in public consultation: traditional participation processes can be fragmented, limited in reach and difficult to analyse systematically once large volumes of feedback are collected. By offering a structured digital space for discussion, debate and idea generation, the platform aims to make consultation more transparent, inclusive and continuous. It has been used by cities in Germany, the Netherlands, Belgium and France, supporting local authorities that want to involve communities in policy development, urban planning or service improvement. Its implementation combines online discussion-board functionality with tools for crowdsourcing ideas, tracking participation, producing statistics and monitoring the impact of engagement activities in real time. Data analytics and machine-learning capabilities support the analysis of group sentiment and help public bodies understand how participants respond to proposals or policy themes. This makes consultation outputs easier to interpret and compare, particularly where feedback is broad or diverse. The platform’s main benefits include wider participation, clearer evidence from citizen input, more transparent follow-up on public discussions and stronger trust-building between institutions and communities. For administrations, it also creates a reusable and scalable channel for managing participatory processes across multiple policy areas.

cases.source_description: This use case focuses on reducing avoidable deterioration and hospital admissions among patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and heart failure by identifying warning signs early enough for preventive treatment to begin. In routine care, exacerbations can escalate quickly, and delayed intervention may result in emergency admission, worsening health status and higher pressure on clinical services. This allows preventive treatment to be initiated before the event fully develops and integrates monitoring with clinical decision support. The expected impact is fewer admissions, better prevention of deterioration and a more proactive model of care for vulnerable patients. More broadly, the use case improves service responsiveness, enhances patient safety and experience, and creates business value through more efficient use of healthcare resources and better continuity of care.

cases.implementation: This use case addresses the operational need for faster, more reliable early assessment of emergency patients, particularly in distinguishing non-critical cases from those requiring urgent hospital care. cases.source_description: In emergency departments, clinicians must decide quickly whether a patient can be safely discharged or needs immediate admission, often while facing incomplete information, time pressure and high patient volumes. This use case addresses the operational need for faster, more reliable early assessment of emergency patients, particularly in distinguishing non-critical cases from those requiring urgent hospital care. The stakeholders include emergency physicians, nurses, laboratory services and hospital managers, all of whom need better decision support to improve triage, reduce delays and allocate beds and clinical attention more effectively. The objective is to strengthen the initial diagnostic process so that patients receive the right level of care sooner and hospital resources are directed where they are most needed. The solution is implemented through a diagnostic-support tool that analyses blood and urine samples and applies predictive models to identify the 15 most common acute illnesses and infections seen in emergency settings. At a conceptual level, the system combines laboratory data, probabilistic ranking methods and workflow integration to produce a prioritised list of likely diagnoses within 60 minutes of the patient’s arrival. This enables clinicians to incorporate rapid analytical insight into admission and treatment decisions. The expected impact is quicker diagnosis, more accurate triage and improved use of emergency capacity. In practice, the tool supports better patient flow, a more consistent clinical response and greater value through safer, more efficient acute-care delivery.

This creates an administrative burden that can reduce the time available for direct patient care and increase the risk that urgent findings are not prioritised as quickly as they should be. The use case therefore focuses on supporting physicians in general practice by improving the handling of incoming test results and helping surgeries manage clinical information more efficiently. This means routine or low-risk results can be handled more efficiently, while urgent cases are surfaced promptly for review. The impact is expected to include lower administrative effort, quicker response to clinically significant findings and better use of time in primary care. More broadly, the approach improves reliability, enhances workflow efficiency and strengthens the overall quality and responsiveness of general-practice services.

cases.source_description: Prostate cancer is frequently identified at an early stage, when the disease has not yet spread beyond the prostate, yet many patients still undergo surgery that may later prove unnecessary and can cause complications or long-term discomfort. This use case addresses the clinical and operational challenge of determining which patients genuinely need intervention and which can be managed more conservatively without compromising outcomes. The stakeholders include urologists, oncologists, multidisciplinary cancer teams and patients, with the objective of improving treatment decisions, reducing overtreatment and ensuring that surgery is reserved for cases where the risk of progression is sufficiently high. The solution is implemented through a risk-assessment model trained on historical disease patterns and clinical outcome data to estimate the likelihood that the cancer will spread from the prostate. At a conceptual level, the system analyses patterns in previous patient trajectories and produces an individualised risk estimate that can be incorporated into medical assessment and treatment planning. This supports clinicians in distinguishing patients who may require surgery to prevent metastases from those who may safely avoid surgical treatment. The expected impact is more precise diagnosis-related decision-making, fewer unnecessary operations and a better balance between clinical benefit and treatment burden. In practical terms, the use case improves patient experience, supports more efficient use of surgical resources and creates value through more personalised and proportionate cancer care.

cases.source_description: PET imaging is an important tool in cancer diagnosis and treatment planning, but it requires the injection of a radioactive tracer, and higher tracer doses generally produce clearer images. The operational challenge is therefore to maintain diagnostic image quality while reducing the radiation exposure faced by patients, particularly when repeated scans may be required over time. The stakeholders include radiologists, nuclear-medicine specialists, oncology teams and patients, with the objective of making imaging safer and more cost-effective without undermining its clinical usefulness. The solution is implemented through image-processing models that work on scans acquired using a reduced radiation dose. At a conceptual level, the system addresses the increased noise created by lower-dose imaging by applying denoising and reconstruction techniques that enhance image clarity sufficiently for diagnostic use. This allows the scan to retain its practical value while lowering the quantity of tracer administered. The expected impact is a reduction in radiation exposure and, consequently, a lower long-term risk associated with imaging, alongside savings linked to reduced use of radioactive tracer. In broader terms, the use case improves patient safety, supports more sustainable imaging practice and enhances service efficiency by preserving diagnostic quality while lowering both clinical risk and material cost.

cases.source_description: Turing addresses the challenge of managing motorway lighting in Flanders in a way that balances energy efficiency, climate objectives, road safety and operational workload. The Agency for Roads and Traffic had already adopted a lighting strategy in 2011 in response to the European Union’s objective of reducing energy consumption by 20% by 2020, and the number of illuminated road sections has since fallen by almost half. However, the existing control approach relies mainly on historical traffic intensities and weather forecasts at provincial level, which limits the precision of decisions on whether lighting is necessary for a specific road segment. The Turing use case aims to make lighting control more localised, timely and evidence-based. Its implementation combines rule-based algorithms with machine-learning techniques to integrate internal and external data sources into the current road-lighting control system. Local and real-time information on traffic intensity and weather conditions can be processed to determine more accurately when lighting should be switched on or off. This allows the system to move from broad assumptions towards segment-level operational decisions. The anticipated results include lower energy consumption, stronger contribution to climate targets, maintained or improved road safety, and a significant reduction in manual workload for operators. The use case also demonstrates how existing infrastructure-management systems can be upgraded through data-driven automation.

The Agency for Roads and Traffic is responsible for controlling slippery road conditions on the roads it manages, but spreading decisions depend on local interpretation of real-time measurements, weather forecasts and staff experience. The expected impact is better spatial representation of forest resources, improved support for monitoring and stronger evidence for policy and economic planning. cases.source_description: Estonia’s courts needed a faster and more efficient way to produce hearing transcripts, since manual transcription of court sessions is slow, labour-intensive and places a heavy burden on clerks. According to the Estonian courts, a single criminal case containing about 14 hours of hearings could require an average of 112 working hours to transcribe manually. The use case therefore involved the courts, the Centre of Registers and Information Systems and judicial staff, with the objective of reducing transcription effort, speeding up protocolling and improving the handling of spoken courtroom data in both physical and remote hearings. The solution is implemented through Salme, a speech-recognition tool developed with CGI Estonia and Tilde and integrated into the Court Information System via X-Road. At a conceptual level, Salme supports both real-time and offline transcription, assigns microphones to speakers, returns transcript text with only a short delay and links recordings, transcripts and notes back into court workflows. The system was trained using more than 800 hours of transcribed audio for acoustic models and over 800 million words of textual data for the custom language model, producing reported word-error rates between 8% and 15% and overall precision of about 92%. The impact includes major time savings, faster transcript production and better integration of courtroom recordings into digital judicial processes, creating value through efficiency, accuracy and secure operation on authorised court infrastructure.

cases.source_description: Monitoring sea-ice conditions in the Gulf of Riga is important for understanding winter dynamics, environmental conditions and maritime risks, yet consistent large-scale observation is difficult to achieve through field methods alone. This use case addressed the need for a more systematic way to characterise ice extent, ice occurrence probability and ice-season length across different winter scenarios in the Baltic Sea. The stakeholders include researchers, environmental analysts and organisations concerned with marine observation, with the objective of generating a reliable statistical picture of sea-ice behaviour over time and across locations. The solution was implemented using optical remote-sensing data from the MODIS instrument at 250 m resolution, covering the period from 2002 to 2011. At a conceptual level, the method relied on bimodal histogram analysis of remote-sensing reflectance data to distinguish ice from water, then used the resulting classifications to calculate sea-ice extent, occurrence probability and season length. The outputs were compared with official ice charts and multi-sensor products, showing strong agreement with reference data, with R² values above 0.83. The study found large year-to-year variation: the ice season ranged from 68 to 146 days and maximum ice extent from 329 to 15,350 km², with higher ice occurrence in waters shallower than 15 m. More broadly, the work creates value by providing a robust analytical basis for regional ice monitoring and winter-scenario classification.

Border authorities face the dual challenge of processing travellers quickly while also verifying identity and right of entry with a high level of reliability. Manual control remains essential, but alone it can slow throughput and leave less room for automated support in detecting document misuse. cases.source_description: Monitoring occupational exposure to ionising radiation is a critical public-health and workplace-safety responsibility, particularly for workers whose roles involve repeated or potentially high-risk exposure. The challenge is not only to collect exposure data, but also to interpret it in a way that supports personalised follow-up and allows unusual patterns or potential anomalies to be detected early. This use case therefore focuses on strengthening the SISERI monitoring system so that exposure oversight becomes more targeted, responsive and effective. The stakeholders include occupational-health professionals, radiation-protection specialists, regulatory bodies and exposed workers, with the objective of improving individual monitoring and supporting earlier identification of cases that may require investigation or intervention. The solution is implemented using data from the ionising radiation exposure monitoring information system itself. At a conceptual level, the system applies analytical models to historical and current exposure records in order to profile normal and abnormal patterns, support personalised monitoring of worker exposure and flag cases that diverge from expected ranges or trajectories. These outputs can then feed into occupational-health and regulatory workflows for review and follow-up. The expected impact is improved detection of anomalies, more tailored exposure monitoring and better use of specialist oversight capacity. More broadly, the approach strengthens safety governance, improves the reliability of monitoring processes and creates value by enabling a more scalable and preventive model of radiation-risk management.

cases.source_description: Environmental monitoring depends on the ability to identify contaminating substances accurately and to understand whether different samples point to the same pollutant source or to distinct pollution events. In practice, chemical analyses generate complex spectral outputs whose similarities and differences can be difficult to assess consistently at scale, especially when many compounds or trace signatures must be compared across multiple samples. This use case addresses that challenge by improving how analysts detect polluting molecules and interpret the relationships between molecular spectra. The stakeholders include environmental laboratories, pollution-monitoring authorities and investigators responsible for tracing contamination sources, with the objective of strengthening environmental surveillance and making the identification of pollutants more precise and operationally useful. The solution is implemented by applying analytical models to the results of chemical analyses in order to compare spectra and objectify their proximity or divergence. At a conceptual level, the system uses pattern-recognition techniques on molecular signatures to highlight recurring forms, distinguish substances more reliably and support the identification of contaminants present in environmental samples. This can also help investigators infer whether pollution may stem from similar or distinct origins. The expected impact is more accurate detection of polluting molecules, faster interpretation of analytical results and stronger support for source identification. In practical terms, the approach improves the reliability and scalability of environmental analysis and creates value by enabling more targeted pollution control and remediation efforts.

cases.implementation: This use case addresses that challenge by helping the Directorate General of Public Finances target tax audits more effectively and allocate investigative resources where they are most justified. The solution is implemented within the CFVR system through large-scale processing and cross-checking of data collected by different administrations.

cases.source_description: Tax administrations must process very large volumes of information from multiple public sources in order to identify cases where individuals or companies may not be complying with their fiscal obligations. The difficulty lies in distinguishing the truly high-risk situations from the mass of ordinary declarations, especially where discrepancies may result from error, omission or deliberate fraud. This use case addresses that challenge by helping the Directorate General of Public Finances target tax audits more effectively and allocate investigative resources where they are most justified. The stakeholders include tax auditors, compliance teams and public-finance authorities, with the objective of improving the efficiency, fairness and consistency of fiscal controls. The solution is implemented within the CFVR system through large-scale processing and cross-checking of data collected by different administrations. At a conceptual level, the system analyses patterns such as abrupt changes in income, inconsistencies between declared situations and other indicators of risk in order to generate prioritised signals for tax-control teams. These signals support audit selection and case valuation while leaving the final judgement to tax professionals. The expected impact is more accurate targeting of audits, reduced time spent on low-yield controls and better recovery of irregular situations. In operational and public-value terms, the approach increases scalability, strengthens the credibility of tax enforcement and creates value through more efficient use of control resources and fairer treatment of compliant taxpayers.

cases.source_description: The Government’s Information and Press Service of Luxembourg implemented this use case to improve the management of a large media library of political photographs belonging to the Luxembourg State. The operational problem was the manual indexing of extensive photographic collections, a process described as laborious and time-consuming. Without efficient metadata, the value of the media library is reduced, as photographs are harder to retrieve, identify and reuse by public institutions. The objective was to accelerate the identification of politicians appearing in government photographs and to improve the quality and completeness of metadata associated with the collection. The AI project uses facial-recognition technology to identify political figures in images and generate enhanced metadata for the media library. At a conceptual level, the system analyses visual features in photographs, compares them with authorised reference material and supports the tagging of individuals appearing in the images. The resulting metadata makes the collection easier to search and manage, while reducing the manual effort required from staff. The impact has been to facilitate and accelerate metadata production, improve the usability of the State’s photographic resources and enable better exploitation of the media library’s content across government. The use case delivers administrative efficiency, strengthens information management and supports more consistent reuse of public visual records.

cases.source_description: Historical archives contain vast quantities of handwritten material that remain difficult to exploit because older manuscripts are often challenging to read, search and interpret at scale. For the Luxembourg National Archives, this limits the accessibility of important seventeenth- and eighteenth-century sources and constrains the extent to which researchers can use them effectively. The CLAVIS project addresses this documentary bottleneck by improving the legibility and usability of digitised manuscript collections. The stakeholders include archivists, historians, researchers and cultural-heritage institutions, with the objective of making historic documents more accessible, searchable and useful for future generations while also improving archival description processes. The solution is implemented by submitting digitised manuscript images to Transkribus, a platform for automated handwriting recognition, transcription and search in historic documents. At a conceptual level, the system processes scanned archival pages, converts handwritten text into machine-readable transcriptions and enables downstream uses such as content search, structured retrieval and the automated generation of inventories or indexes of people and places. This transforms previously difficult-to-use archival sources into a more navigable digital resource. The expected impact is greatly improved accessibility to historical records, reduced manual transcription effort and stronger support for archival research and discovery. More broadly, the project improves the scalability of document processing, enriches cultural-heritage services and creates value by opening complex manuscript collections to much wider scholarly and public use.

cases.source_description: Arnhem’s 3D scan project focuses on preventing accidental damage to critical underground infrastructure during construction work. The operational issue is that sewer infrastructure is often located below ground in ways that may be difficult for construction teams to visualise accurately from the surface, creating a risk of costly damage, service disruption and safety hazards. The municipality’s approach combines a precise 3D scan of the main sewer with an application that visualises the sewer’s location above ground. The implementation therefore links geospatial surveying, three-dimensional infrastructure modelling and field-based visualisation, allowing users to understand the position of underground assets before or during works. Conceptually, the system turns hidden sewer infrastructure into a digital and spatially interpretable layer that can be consulted by staff or contractors. The expected impact is fewer accidental strikes, better planning of construction activities, reduced repair costs and improved protection of essential municipal infrastructure. By making underground assets more visible and usable in operational settings, the project supports safer, more data-driven public works management.

The operational problem is that people may drop out of programmes when support is not aligned with their personal motivation, behaviour, context or barriers. The system seeks to make clear who needs what type of attention by monitoring and adjusting more than 80 factors related to internal drivers. Its implementation uses profiles, behavioural data and contextual indicators to plan automatic or semi-automatic interventions, such as measurements, encouragement and targeted support activities intended to keep people engaged in class or training. cases.source_description: ProRail’s agent system is designed to support train traffic controllers when disruptions or delays occur on the Dutch rail network. The operational challenge is that small delays can propagate quickly through interconnected railway services, requiring rapid decisions on routing, prioritisation and recovery measures. Train traffic controllers must assess complex operational conditions under time pressure, balancing passenger disruption, infrastructure capacity and the need to prevent knock-on effects. cases.source_description: Rijkswaterstaat needed a more efficient and affordable way to inspect national roads and waterways, since traditional inspection approaches often depend on expensive professional camera equipment and limited collection capacity. Routine infrastructure inspection is essential for maintaining safety and service quality, but manual processes and specialist hardware can restrict coverage and raise costs. The use case therefore focused on expanding inspection capability while lowering the barriers to large-scale visual data collection. The stakeholders include Rijkswaterstaat, inspection teams and infrastructure managers, with the objective of automating a larger share of road and waterway inspection and improving the timeliness and consistency of asset monitoring. The solution is implemented through standard Android smartphones mounted on cars and ships, each running an application that captures an image every second. At a conceptual level, these images are combined with geographic data and used to train a cloud-based neural network that can recognise relevant infrastructure conditions and support automated inspection tasks. By using inexpensive, widely available devices instead of specialist cameras, the system creates a more scalable and flexible inspection model. The expected impact is lower equipment cost, broader inspection coverage and faster collection of infrastructure data. More broadly, the project creates value by modernising public-asset monitoring, improving operational efficiency and demonstrating how low-cost sensing combined with cloud-based analysis can reshape large-scale infrastructure inspection.

In many cases, however, decision-makers must interpret large volumes of information under pressure, making it difficult to determine the optimal deployment strategy quickly and consistently. This use case addresses that challenge by helping users prevent flooding through more precise and operationally relevant guidance. The stakeholders include flood-risk managers, emergency planners and operational users responsible for preventive action, with the objective of minimising risk through better real-time deployment choices and more tailored decision support. The solution is implemented through smart algorithms that combine live risk information with knowledge of the resources available. This means the output is not simply descriptive, but directly linked to the operational choices that can still be made in time. The expected impact is more effective preventive deployment, quicker and better-targeted decisions and improved use of limited resources in flood-risk situations. More broadly, the approach enhances reliability, supports scalability in operational prevention and creates value by turning real-time information into practical, context-sensitive action for those managing water-related threats.

The implementation uses Earth observation data, with satellite imagery analysed across time to identify changes in vegetation cover. The main impact is broader territorial coverage, faster identification of potential illegal logging, better targeting of field checks and stronger evidence for environmental enforcement. Local authorities, transport operators and travellers require accurate, timely information to support better travel choices and reduce pressure on the city centre. The objective of this pilot is to improve accessibility and sustainability by guiding users to appropriate parking facilities or encouraging a shift towards public transport based on real-time conditions. cases.source_description: Tax administrations must identify fraud and recovery risks across very large volumes of declarations and receivables, while using enforcement capacity in a targeted and proportionate manner. Business Intelligence and Analytics (BI&A) supports the Dutch Tax Authority by using self-learning models to indicate where risks may exist, based on previously inspected declarations and feedback from inspection outcomes. The broader operational objective is to move from uniform or purely rule-based selection towards more refined risk identification, allowing the administration to focus attention where available data suggest a higher probability of non-compliance or recovery opportunities. One example is Dynamic Monitoring, which links outstanding receivables to possible sources of redress, such as wages, cars, real estate or other assets, and generates lists of claims where new recovery options may be available. The implementation combines machine-learning methods with administrative tax data, inspection histories and feedback loops from previous control results. Models are progressively refined as additional outcomes become available, improving their capacity to identify relevant risk patterns. The potential impact is more efficient allocation of inspection and recovery resources, faster identification of actionable cases and improved use of existing administrative data. At the same time, such systems require careful governance to ensure transparency, legality, non-discrimination and appropriate human oversight in tax decision-making.

cases.source_description: Prosecutors and legal researchers face significant information-management challenges when preparing criminal cases, as relevant case law, procedural material and hidden connections may be dispersed across large and complex legal datasets. Case Law Engine was developed by LexIQ for the Dutch Public Prosecution Service to reduce research time and improve the quality of case preparation. The Public Prosecution Service had explored how advanced digital tools could support daily working procedures, particularly where professionals need to search, analyse and draw insights from criminal-case information. The tool, also described as a “Jurisprudentierobot”, supports prosecutors and researchers in identifying relevant case law, understanding patterns and making better use of information during preparation. Its implementation combines machine-learning algorithms with intuitive search functions, data visualisations and analytical features that help users navigate large volumes of legal and case-related data. Rather than replacing legal judgement, the system provides indications, connections and possible outcome-related insights that professionals can assess within their own legal reasoning. The impact is reduced time spent on manual research, better handling of information overload and improved ability to detect relevant or previously hidden information. For the Public Prosecution Service, the tool offers business value by strengthening preparation quality, supporting consistency and enabling staff to approach criminal-case analysis in a more structured and evidence-informed way.

cases.source_description: Busy pedestrian areas in Amsterdam require reliable crowd-management capabilities to safeguard public safety, maintain comfort and support evidence-based operational decisions in high-density urban spaces. The CityFlows initiative, developed as an EIT Urban Mobility flagship project, brought together the Municipality of Amsterdam, AMS Institute and a wider consortium of partners to address the need for better monitoring and management of pedestrian flows, particularly in locations affected by congestion, events, tourism and changing mobility patterns. The objective was to provide public authorities with a decision-support capability that helps them understand crowd dynamics and take timely measures to improve the use of public space. The emerging technology implementation centres on the Crowd Management Decision-Support System, a software-based platform licensed through City Analytics to government authorities. At conceptual level, the system combines pedestrian-flow data, urban analytics and operational decision-support functions to help authorities assess crowding conditions, anticipate risks and select appropriate interventions. Its deployment supports integration between urban data sources, monitoring tools and municipal crowd-management processes. The main impact is improved situational awareness for public authorities, enabling safer, more comfortable and more responsive management of busy pedestrian spaces. The creation of City Analytics as a dedicated start-up also strengthens scalability and reuse, allowing the solution to be offered beyond the original project context and supporting cities seeking reliable tools for managing public space during normal operations and crisis situations.

cases.source_description: The municipality of Rijswijk tested CrossWalk to address a concrete accessibility and road-safety challenge: standard pedestrian crossing times are often insufficient for older people, people with disabilities or citizens with reduced mobility. This can create unsafe situations at intersections and reduce the autonomy of residents who require more time to cross the road. The pilot involved the Municipality of Rijswijk and Dynniq, with the objective of making pedestrian infrastructure more responsive to the needs of vulnerable road users while avoiding permanent changes to signal timing for all pedestrians. The emerging technology implementation is based on a mobile application connected to traffic signal systems. When a registered user with mobility difficulties approaches or waits at a crossing, the app uses location data to communicate with the traffic control software and signal the user’s presence. The traffic light system can then automatically extend the green phase, allowing additional time for a safe crossing. At conceptual level, the solution integrates mobile positioning, traffic-light control logic and intersection management systems. Its impact lies in improving pedestrian safety, accessibility and user experience for residents who walk more slowly. It also demonstrates how smart-city infrastructure can provide targeted support without redesigning the entire traffic system, making the approach potentially scalable to other intersections and municipalities with similar accessibility objectives.

cases.task: Algorithm Impact monitor bridge openings
cases.context: Province of South Holland; Regional Government; Transport; Netherlands
cases.implementation: The smart bridge addresses this challenge by using digital monitoring and predictive analytics to support more informed bridge-operation decisions across an infrastructure portfolio that includes more than 100 bridges.

cases.source_description: The Province of South Holland must manage the movement of both road traffic and shipping across a region where bridge openings can create delays, congestion and competing demands between transport modes. The smart bridge addresses this challenge by using digital monitoring and predictive analytics to support more informed bridge-operation decisions across an infrastructure portfolio that includes more than 100 bridges. The initiative forms part of South Holland’s wider work on smart shipping and focuses on linking up-to-date road-traffic information with live shipping information, so that the impact of bridge openings can be better understood and anticipated. In the project “impact monitor bridge openings”, the province has taken an important step towards predicting traffic intensities around several key bridges. The technological implementation combines sensor-based data collection, traffic information and algorithmic analysis, including Long Short-Term Memory neural networks designed to forecast traffic conditions up to 21 minutes ahead. These models are suited to time-series prediction because they can learn from sequential patterns in traffic behaviour and bridge-operation data. The reported correlation-efficient accuracy of 60–80% indicates that the approach can provide useful short-term forecasts for operational planning. The main value is improved anticipation of congestion, better coordination between road and waterway mobility, more evidence-based bridge management and a stronger basis for reducing disruption while keeping both transport networks accessible and safe.

cases.source_description: This pilot investigates whether smart-camera analytics can support earlier recognition of aggression, panic and abnormal behaviour in crowded public environments. The operational problem is that incidents in stations, airports, city centres or entertainment districts can escalate quickly if security teams identify them too late. Traditional monitoring relies heavily on human operators observing multiple camera feeds, which can be demanding, inconsistent and slow. ViNotion develops technology that analyses the behaviour of individuals and detects signs of panic, aggression or deviant conduct at an early stage. The implementation uses video analytics and behaviour-recognition models to process visual information from cameras, identify movement or interaction patterns associated with abnormal events, and generate alerts for security or assistance personnel. Conceptually, the system combines computer vision, behavioural classification, anomaly detection and real-time alerting. The expected impact is faster deployment of staff, reduced harm to the public, more efficient incident response and better management of safety risks in large public areas. Its value depends on accuracy, proportionality and careful governance, because behavioural interpretation in public spaces can raise concerns around false positives, surveillance intensity and the treatment of individuals whose conduct is incorrectly flagged.

cases.task: Firework nuisance detection system - AI to determine if bangs are firework
cases.context: Municipality of Amersfoort; Local Government; Police Services; Netherlands
cases.outcome: UNKNOWN; 원천의 기대효과와 별도 관측 성과는 구분해야 합니다.
cases.source_description: Dutch municipalities face recurring public order and safety issues linked to illegal fireworks, particularly during evenings and festive periods, placing strain on enforcement capacity and generating resident complaints. The firework nuisance detection system was introduced to help municipalities such as Amersfoort identify when and where fireworks are being set off, enabling more targeted enforcement. Stakeholders include municipal authorities, enforcement officers, residents and public safety services. The objective is to distinguish fireworks from other loud noises, identify nuisance hotspots and optimise patrol routes and response times without relying solely on citizen reports. The system combines a distributed network of acoustic sensors placed in public space, which capture sound events and triangulate their location when multiple sensors detect the same bang. Signal-processing and classification techniques analyse acoustic signatures to distinguish fireworks from other impulsive sounds such as slamming doors or vehicle backfires. When a sound is classified as fireworks, alerts are automatically sent to municipal enforcers via mobile devices, alongside spatial and temporal data. The pilot has improved situational awareness and allowed more selective deployment of enforcement resources. Qualitatively, municipalities report faster response times, better evidence-based planning and improved transparency around nuisance patterns, while residents benefit from more visible and timely enforcement.

In complex housing situations, case officers faced difficulties in deciding when a home visit was justified, leading to inconsistent practices and inefficient use of limited inspection capacity. The objective of this use case was to support more consistent, evidence-based prioritisation of cases where discrepancies between declared circumstances and observed living conditions suggested elevated risk, while preserving human decision-making authority. However, concerns regarding transparency, proportionality and potential bias prompted increased regulatory scrutiny, and similar profiling tools have since been restricted or discontinued in several municipalities

The objective was to assess feasibility, risks and governance requirements rather than to deploy an operational system. cases.source_description: Organisations that generate residual materials often lack efficient mechanisms to identify potential reusers, assess the value of surplus flows and close material loops across sectors. Excess Material Exchange (EME) addresses this problem by creating a digital trading platform where supply and demand for excess materials can be matched at scale. The initiative involves organisations such as ProRail, Schiphol and other public and private actors seeking to reduce waste and improve circular-economy performance. The operational objective is to move residual materials away from disposal or low-value treatment and towards productive reuse by making information about available materials more visible, comparable and actionable. The technology implementation relies on artificial intelligence to read, interpret and structure data on material streams, including information on composition, availability, quality, location and potential applications. Matching algorithms then identify possible links between suppliers and buyers, including combinations that may not be obvious through manual brokerage. The platform’s intelligence lies not only in listing materials, but also in actively bringing together parties whose residual flows and needs may align. The expected impact is faster matching, greater scalability in circular-material exchange, reduced transaction costs and improved resource efficiency. For participating organisations, EME can support waste reduction, lower procurement or disposal costs, and contribute to broader sustainability and circular-economy objectives.

cases.source_description: Street managers need reliable information on how different road users move through public space, especially where cyclists, pedestrians and vehicles interact in ways that are not fully captured by traditional traffic counts. FlowCube responds to this need by using compact camera-based modules to generate traffic intelligence for local mobility management. The system is intended to give authorities and transport planners a clearer picture of flows, routes and travel times without relying on manual observation or intrusive data collection. Its implementation combines compact video sensors with image-recognition algorithms that distinguish cyclists, pedestrians and, where configured, other types of traffic. At a conceptual level, the modules detect objects, classify road-user categories, track local movement and aggregate observations into usable mobility data. Multiple FlowCubes can also combine data to infer commonly used cycling routes and corresponding travel times. The expected impact is more accurate insight into active mobility, better evidence for infrastructure planning, improved monitoring of cycling and walking policies, and safer management of mixed-use streets. Technolution presents FlowCube as an operational product and emphasises privacy compliance, because the system generates mobility indicators rather than functioning as an identity-based surveillance tool. This makes it relevant for municipalities seeking granular traffic intelligence while remaining within data-protection constraints.

cases.source_description: The bridge-inspection drone pilot explores how unmanned aerial vehicles can reduce reliance on manual inspection capacity for bridges and viaducts. The operational problem is that infrastructure inspections are often labour-intensive, require specialist access arrangements, and may expose inspectors to safety risks when structures are difficult to reach. Public infrastructure managers need reliable ways to detect deterioration, document structural conditions and prioritise maintenance without closing assets unnecessarily or deploying extensive human resources for every inspection. The implementation uses drones to capture visual data from bridges and viaducts, allowing inspection teams to review high-resolution imagery of structural elements that would otherwise require physical access. At a conceptual level, the approach can combine UAV-based image capture, georeferenced inspection records, visual analytics and, where developed further, computer-vision models for recognising cracks, corrosion, deformation or other signs of damage. The expected impact is faster inspection, lower operational burden, improved safety for inspection staff and more consistent documentation of asset condition. If validated, the pilot could support more risk-based infrastructure maintenance by helping authorities identify which structures require closer expert review and which can be monitored remotely.

cases.context: Province of Gelderland; Local Government; Transport; Netherlands
cases.implementation: The objective was to move beyond fixed or locally reactive signalling by using digital information from road users and connected systems. cases.source_description: Urban traffic intersections must balance the needs of private vehicles, buses, emergency services, cyclists and pedestrians while reducing congestion and improving journey reliability. In Gelderland, existing traffic lights at eight intersections in Arnhem and Velp were replaced with intelligent traffic-control systems, or iVRIs, to support better traffic flow. The objective was to move beyond fixed or locally reactive signalling by using digital information from road users and connected systems. The implementation uses mobile data and vehicle-to-infrastructure communication so that road users and traffic-control installations can exchange information. Buses and emergency services can receive priority when approaching an intersection, while other road users may receive up-to-date information about routes and speed advice. At a conceptual level, iVRIs combine connected traffic-light controllers, data exchange standards, road-user messages, priority rules and adaptive signal control. This allows the intersection to respond more dynamically to current traffic conditions and to support policy priorities such as public transport reliability or emergency response. The expected impact is smoother traffic flow, reduced waiting times, better journey predictability and more efficient use of existing road infrastructure. Dutch public portals continue to provide national visibility on iVRI deployments, while Gelderland’s own public material refers to implementation and execution documents for the Arnhem and Velp iVRIs.

cases.source_description: Police investigations increasingly involve large volumes of online information, making manual monitoring of digital sources time-consuming and inconsistent. iColumbo was developed within the Dutch police’s Internet Research & Investigation Network (iRN) to support systematic online searches for suspicious material. Stakeholders included law enforcement investigators, digital forensics units and judicial authorities. The objective was to enhance investigative capacity by automating parts of open-source intelligence collection while preserving legal oversight. The service crawled publicly accessible online sources and forums using predefined search strategies, keywords and behavioural patterns. Collected material was indexed and presented to investigators for assessment, rather than triggering automatic enforcement actions. The project improved consistency and speed in early-stage investigations and reduced reliance on ad hoc manual searches. Although the specific iColumbo project has since been concluded, its concepts informed later police tooling for digital investigations. The main impact lies in professionalisation of online investigative practices and improved methodological consistency in handling internet-based evidence.

cases.source_description: The Artificial Intelligence Knowledge System for the judiciary was developed to support legal professionals in identifying comparable lawsuits more efficiently. The operational challenge is that courts and judicial staff work with large volumes of case material, and finding relevant precedents or similar disputes can be time-consuming when searches rely only on keywords or manual legal knowledge. The District Court of East Brabant tested a system that allows users to enter text and receive the ten most similar lawsuits. The implementation is based on textual similarity search, likely combining natural language processing, document representation and ranking techniques to compare an input text with a database of past cases. Conceptually, the tool transforms legal documents into searchable representations, calculates similarity between the user’s text and available case records, and returns a ranked list of relevant results. The expected impact is faster legal research, more consistent retrieval of comparable cases and better support for judicial preparation. By assisting users in navigating case material, the system can improve internal efficiency without replacing judicial reasoning. Its value depends on the quality of the underlying case database, the transparency of similarity criteria and careful use by trained legal professionals.

cases.context: Ministry of Interior; Central-Government; Executive and legislative organs, financial and fiscal affairs, external affairs.; Netherlands
cases.implementation: LAA - Address quality in Personal Records Database (BRP) supports the Dutch Ministry of Interior in improving address quality by using data analysis to recognise patterns that may indicate incorrect addressing. The technological implementation applies analytical methods to administrative data in order to detect combinations, deviations or patterns associated with possible address-registration problems.
cases.outcome: UNKNOWN; 원천의 기대효과와 별도 관측 성과는 구분해야 합니다.
cases.source_description: Public authorities depend on accurate address records to deliver services, administer rights and obligations, and prevent misuse of public systems, but incorrect registrations in the Personal Records Database can undermine these functions. LAA - Address quality in Personal Records Database (BRP) supports the Dutch Ministry of Interior in improving address quality by using data analysis to recognise patterns that may indicate incorrect addressing. The underlying problem is that inaccurate address data can affect administrative decisions, public-service delivery and fraud prevention, particularly where residence information is used to determine eligibility, correspondence, enforcement or access to benefits. The initiative aims to help bring the BRP into better order by identifying records that may require verification or correction. The technological implementation applies analytical methods to administrative data in order to detect combinations, deviations or patterns associated with possible address-registration problems. These outputs can then guide further checks by competent authorities, who assess whether a registration is indeed incorrect and what follow-up is required. The system therefore functions as a risk-identification and prioritisation tool within a broader governance process. The expected impact is improved data quality, more targeted verification work, stronger reliability of the population register and better support for fraud prevention. Given the sensitivity of population data, the value of the system depends on clear legal safeguards, proportionality, transparency and appropriate human oversight.

Eindhoven’s use case focused on mapping “unknown” companies that could pose a potential environmental risk by using data more intelligently. This creates the risk that environmentally relevant businesses are not prioritised for supervision or included in the appropriate regulatory process. The implementation uses data matching and analytical screening to identify companies that may fall outside established inspection lists but show characteristics associated with environmental risk. At a conceptual level, the system combines business-register information, location data, sector classifications, permit or enforcement records and risk indicators to generate candidate companies for further human review. cases.source_description: Municipalities administering welfare benefits face pressure to prevent fraud while ensuring fair and lawful treatment of beneficiaries. The Municipality of Nissewaard introduced a predictive model to identify cases with a higher likelihood of unlawful behaviour in the housing market, such as undeclared cohabitation or subletting. Stakeholders included social services, case officers and welfare recipients. The objective was to prioritise investigations and reduce random or unnecessary checks. The model analysed historical administrative data, identifying patterns associated with confirmed fraud cases and assigning risk scores to current clients. These scores informed decisions on whether further investigation was warranted, always requiring human review. While the system aimed to improve efficiency, concerns emerged around transparency, bias and legal safeguards. Following national scrutiny of similar systems and evolving legal standards, Nissewaard discontinued the model in 2021. The case significantly influenced Dutch policy discussions on automated risk profiling, reinforcing the need for strict governance, explainability and proportionality in data-driven public services.

cases.source_description: The Deventer and Goirle welfare-fraud detection pilot used risk profiling to identify welfare recipients whose files might require additional investigation. The administrative problem was the need to target limited enforcement capacity towards cases considered more likely to involve irregularities, while managing public funds and ensuring compliance with welfare rules. The stakeholders included the municipalities of Deventer and Goirle, welfare recipients, municipal social-service staff, enforcement teams and citizens affected by decisions based on risk scores. The implementation generated risk profiles for welfare recipients, with the resulting score used to decide whether a dossier should be examined more closely. At a conceptual level, such a system links administrative datasets, applies risk indicators or algorithmic scoring rules, and routes selected cases to additional human investigation. The intended impact was more efficient fraud detection, better prioritisation of municipal control resources and earlier identification of possible unlawful behaviour. However, because SyRI-style systems involve sensitive personal data and profiling of welfare recipients, they raise significant concerns around transparency, discrimination, proportionality and legal accountability. These concerns are particularly relevant given the broader Dutch SyRI judgment, where the system’s legal basis was found incompatible with privacy protections.

cases.source_description: Large municipalities need to enforce parking rules across dense urban areas efficiently, while limiting manual checks and maintaining consistent treatment of vehicles using paid or restricted parking spaces. Parking control in various Dutch municipalities - Parking control by means of scan cars supports parking enforcement in Amsterdam, The Hague, Rotterdam and Utrecht through vehicles equipped with cameras that inspect parked cars while driving through city streets. The operational problem is that conventional on-foot inspection can be labour-intensive and difficult to scale across large numbers of parking spaces, particularly in cities with high vehicle turnover and complex parking regimes. The scan cars capture licence plates and use an image-recognition algorithm to identify registration numbers. These readings can then be checked against parking-payment or permit databases to determine whether a vehicle appears to be compliant. Cases that require further verification can be reviewed before enforcement action is taken, depending on local procedures. The technology therefore combines mobile sensing, automated number-plate recognition and integration with municipal parking-administration systems. Its impact is greater inspection coverage, faster detection of possible parking violations, more efficient deployment of enforcement staff and improved consistency in parking control. For municipalities, the approach can also generate better operational data on parking behaviour and support more responsive management of urban parking policy.

cases.source_description: City centres increasingly require reliable insights into pedestrian flows to support economic development, urban planning and public safety. The municipality of Nijmegen introduced passer-by counting to better understand how people move through the city centre, how busy specific areas are at different times, and how these patterns relate to retail performance and public space use. Stakeholders include municipal planners, economic development teams, local businesses and event organisers. The objective is to generate continuous, objective data on footfall without relying on manual counts or surveys, enabling evidence-based decisions on zoning, infrastructure investments and city marketing. The system uses fixed sensors placed in public space to detect and count passers-by while avoiding direct identification of individuals. The sensors process visual or signal data locally to extract movement counts and directional flows, which are then aggregated and transmitted to municipal dashboards. Data is anonymised at source and integrated with other urban indicators, such as time of day, weather and events. The solution has improved the municipality’s ability to monitor urban vitality in near real time and to evaluate the impact of interventions such as street redesigns or events.

The emerging technology implementation combines augmented visual intelligence with targeted online research capabilities. It also helps combine report data with relevant online sources at an investigative-support level. The impact is faster, more efficient and more complete processing of referrals, allowing law-enforcement officers to focus their attention on high-priority cases, victim identification and perpetrator detection. The case provides clear operational value by improving triage, reducing repetitive workload and supporting more targeted investigative action.

The system structures legal documents, extracts relevant concepts, and presents ranked jurisprudence results to users through an interface integrated into existing prosecutorial workflows. Human decision-making remains central, with the tool acting strictly as an advisory aid rather than an automated decision-maker. According to publicly available judicial documentation, the Jurisprudence Robot has been tested in controlled environments and limited operational settings, with no evidence of nationwide deployment or discontinuation. Reported benefits include faster legal research, improved consistency in case preparation, and reduced administrative burden, while maintaining judicial accountability and professional autonomy.

cases.source_description: The Municipality of Rotterdam needs to keep neighbourhood waste collection reliable and clean while avoiding both overflowing containers and unnecessary collection trips to bins that are not yet full. This use case addresses this operational problem by installing sensors in waste containers to measure filling levels and support more efficient collection planning. In dense urban areas, conventional waste collection based on fixed routes or schedules can result in two opposite inefficiencies: waste accumulating beside overcrowded containers when emptying is too late, and staff time and vehicle kilometres being wasted when containers are emptied too early. The system uses “filling degree meters” that transmit the status of containers every hour, providing regular information on how full each bin is. This data is made available to collection teams, and drivers can use a tablet to see which route should be taken next. The technological implementation combines sensor-based monitoring, data transmission and route-support tools that translate container-level information into operational guidance for waste-collection services. The expected impact is cleaner public space, fewer complaints about overflowing containers, more efficient use of collection vehicles and reduced unnecessary driving. For waste-management staff, the system improves day-to-day planning by showing where intervention is actually needed. For the municipality, it supports a more responsive and resource-efficient approach to urban waste services.

The operational issue is that investigations can involve lengthy recordings with multiple voices, requiring officers or analysts to listen manually to identify who is speaking and when. This is time-consuming and can also expose investigators to conversations unrelated to the subject of interest, creating unnecessary privacy intrusion. Spraaklab develops technology that can largely disassemble, distinguish and label speech from different speakers, allowing police teams to work more efficiently and with higher analytical quality. The implementation uses speech-processing techniques, likely including speaker diarisation, voice-separation, audio segmentation and speaker-labelling models. Conceptually, the tool structures raw audio into speaker-specific segments, helping analysts locate relevant parts of recordings without reviewing unrelated material repeatedly. The expected impact is faster audio review, improved investigative productivity, better-quality evidence handling and stronger privacy protection for people whose conversations are not relevant to the investigation. Its value depends on accuracy in difficult acoustic conditions, careful validation and appropriate human review, since mistaken speaker attribution could affect investigative interpretation.

The Municipality of The Hague developed a road safety model to assess and compare risk levels for all road sections and intersections within the city. Stakeholders include municipal traffic engineers, urban planners, and road safety policymakers. The objective is to move from reactive accident analysis to preventive, data-driven traffic safety management. The model combines historical accident records with a comprehensive dataset describing traffic conditions, infrastructure characteristics, environmental factors, and usage patterns. According to official government documentation, the model is actively used as a decision-support instrument rather than an automated enforcement mechanism. cases.source_description: Residents experiencing debt, care needs or social vulnerability often interact with multiple services, but early warning signs may remain fragmented until problems become acute. Twenterand’s reported use case concerns profiling residents to map debt and care-related problems, with the aim of identifying people who may need help earlier. The operational problem is that social problems often develop gradually and may only become visible once enforcement, crisis care or intensive support is required. A predictive system can bring together administrative indicators and historical patterns to identify households or individuals whose situation resembles earlier cases of debt escalation or care need. At a conceptual level, the system would classify or prioritise residents according to risk signals, enabling municipal professionals to consider preventive outreach or support. The expected impact is earlier intervention, better coordination between social services, reduced crisis escalation and more efficient targeting of limited municipal capacity. The use case must be handled carefully because it involves potentially sensitive social and financial data, and because predictive profiling can unintentionally stigmatise residents or neighbourhoods. Its legitimacy depends on clear purpose limitation, strong human oversight, transparency to affected people and safeguards ensuring that the system is used to offer support rather than punishment.

cases.task: Early school leavers in the municipality of Amersfoort - Estimation of students at risk
cases.context: Municipality of Amersfoort and Dordrecht; Local Government; Education n.e.c.; Netherlands
cases.implementation: The Amersfoort and Dordrecht use case concerns the use of an algorithm to estimate which students may be at risk of becoming early school leavers. The expected impact is better targeting of support, lower dropout rates, more efficient use of guidance capacity and improved educational outcomes.
cases.outcome: UNKNOWN; 원천의 기대효과와 별도 관측 성과는 구분해야 합니다.
cases.source_description: Preventing early school leaving requires timely identification of pupils whose educational trajectory suggests a higher risk of dropping out before completing their programme. The Amersfoort and Dordrecht use case concerns the use of an algorithm to estimate which students may be at risk of becoming early school leavers. The operational problem is that schools and municipalities may hold relevant signals, such as school changes, grade repetition or attendance-related patterns, but these signals may not be systematically combined for early intervention. At a conceptual level, the algorithm compares current pupils with patterns observed among previous early school leavers and assigns an indication of risk. Professionals can then decide whether additional guidance, counselling or follow-up is appropriate. The intended value is preventive: the model is meant to help education and youth-support services act before disengagement becomes irreversible. The expected impact is better targeting of support, lower dropout rates, more efficient use of guidance capacity and improved educational outcomes. However, the case also raises important governance issues because educational-risk profiling can affect young people’s opportunities and may be difficult to understand or contest. It should therefore be presented as decision support for human professionals, with transparent explanation of the indicators used and safeguards against discriminatory effects.

cases.source_description: The municipality of The Hague needed a more efficient way to manage the intake of environmental-permit applications governed by the Environmental Law General Provisions Act, known as Wabo. Permit procedures in this area can involve large volumes of documents and varied applicant questions, creating an administrative burden at the earliest stages of the process and slowing the movement of cases into proper review channels. The use case therefore focused on improving intake efficiency and reducing repetitive administrative work, while helping the municipality process environmental permits more consistently. The stakeholders include municipal permit teams, applicants and environmental-administration staff, with the objective of automating part of the intake process and improving the speed and quality of early-stage handling. The solution is implemented through a Wabo assistant that uses natural language processing to support permit-related tasks. At a conceptual level, the system analyses incoming textual information, identifies relevant content and helps structure or route permit applications so that initial handling requires less manual intervention. This creates a more standardised intake workflow and allows staff to spend less time on repetitive front-end processing. The expected impact is faster handling of permit submissions, reduced clerical burden and improved efficiency in the administration of environmental permits. More broadly, the Wabo assistant creates value by modernising a document-heavy municipal process, supporting better service for applicants and enabling a more scalable model for managing regulatory intake under environmental law.

cases.task: Water fields - purification system for rainwater
cases.context: Municipality of Breda and I-SAGO; Local Government; Waste water management.; Netherlands
cases.implementation: The City of Breda implemented “water fields”, a nature-based purification system that collects, buffers, and treats rainwater at district level. The objective is to optimise water use, reduce pressure on drinking water supplies, and improve climate resilience.

cases.source_description: Cities increasingly face pressure to manage water sustainably while reducing reliance on potable water for non-drinking purposes. The City of Breda implemented “water fields”, a nature-based purification system that collects, buffers, and treats rainwater at district level. Stakeholders include municipal water managers, urban planners, and local residents. The objective is to optimise water use, reduce pressure on drinking water supplies, and improve climate resilience. Rainwater from the surrounding area is collected and filtered through a series of natural purification layers before being stored for reuse. Sensors continuously monitor system performance, rainfall volumes, and storage levels. Operational data is analysed to optimise purification processes and forecast water availability, supporting adaptive system management. According to reporting on the project, the water fields are fully implemented and integrated into Breda’s water infrastructure. The initiative has improved water efficiency, reduced operational costs, and enhanced resilience to drought and heavy rainfall. It also demonstrates how data-driven monitoring can support sustainable urban water systems while maintaining transparency and reliability.

The Water management system supports Hoogheemraadschap De Stichtse Rijnlanden, Tauw and HAL24K in applying data science to complex water-management challenges. The case focuses on improving how real-time operational data can be used to understand conditions at water treatment plants and anticipate changes in water levels, rather than relying only on periodic checks or reactive maintenance. The technological implementation is based on HAL24K’s Dimension data-intelligence platform, demonstrated through the use of live sensor data. The expected impact is more efficient maintenance, faster detection of emerging problems, better use of real-time information and improved capacity to manage water systems proactively. For the responsible organisations, the value lies in strengthening operational resilience, reducing avoidable interventions and creating a more data-driven basis for water-level control and treatment-plant management.

cases.implementation: Welfare administrations need to ensure that people who are entitled to benefits receive support while also detecting improper use or abuse of public funds. cases.source_description: Welfare administrations need to ensure that people who are entitled to benefits receive support while also detecting improper use or abuse of public funds. WIL Lekstroom, a cooperation of municipalities in the Utrecht region, was reported as using algorithms to support detection of abuse and improper use of social-assistance benefits. The operational problem is that benefit-control processes are labour-intensive, and staff may need to identify which cases deserve additional review without checking every file manually. At a conceptual level, the system would use historical benefit, case-management or administrative data to detect patterns associated with previous improper use, then generate signals or risk scores for officials. The expected impact is more targeted investigation, reduced unnecessary checks, improved administrative efficiency and better protection of public resources. However, welfare-fraud prediction is a high-risk area because historical data may reflect biased enforcement patterns and flagged residents may not know that an algorithm influenced additional scrutiny. The system should therefore be understood as decision support only, not as automatic sanctioning or benefit withdrawal. Any responsible use would require clear documentation, explainability, human review, appeal routes and monitoring for discriminatory impact, especially because the affected population may already be socio-economically vulnerable.

cases.source_description: Nexus is designed to support community police officers who require timely, structured and locally relevant information before engaging with neighbourhoods. Officers often need to review recent incidents, local risks and operational context, but conventional briefing processes can be fragmented, time-consuming or dependent on manual searches across different systems. The case involves Brightlands Techruption, the Open University’s CAROU, Maastricht University’s BISS and the Dutch Police iLAB, with the objective of providing officers with an accessible expert system that delivers detailed neighbourhood briefings through speech interaction. The emerging technology implementation consists of a speech-operated expert system that allows officers to request and receive information verbally. At conceptual level, the system combines speech recognition, knowledge retrieval and expert-system logic to transform operational data on recent incidents into a concise briefing tailored to a specific neighbourhood. The interface reduces the need for manual interaction and supports use in operational contexts where officers may benefit from hands-free access to information. The impact is improved situational awareness, more efficient preparation and a better user experience for community police officers. By making local incident information easier to access and interpret, Nexus can support more informed decision-making, strengthen neighbourhood policing and reduce the time spent searching for relevant background information before field activities.
