cases.task: Alexacert: Voice application on Alexa for requesting a birth certificate
cases.context: Municipality of Turin; Local Government; General services.; Italy
cases.implementation: The solution uses an Alexa voice application activated through the phrase “Alexa, speak with Torino certificates”. After recognition, the system uses the email address associated with the Amazon profile, asks the user to confirm the request and, once consent is given, retrieves the PDF certificate from the Registry or ANPR and sends it to the registered inbox.
cases.outcome: UNKNOWN; 원천의 기대효과와 별도 관측 성과는 구분해야 합니다.
cases.source_description: Alexacert was developed by the Municipality of Turin as a proof of concept to test whether citizens could request registry certificates through a voice assistant rather than through traditional online portals or physical offices. The administrative problem is that even standard registry procedures can create friction for users, particularly when they require navigation across multiple interfaces, authentication steps and back-office systems. The prototype focuses on birth certificates, which are well suited to experimentation because they are exempt from stamp duty. The solution uses an Alexa voice application activated through the phrase “Alexa, speak with Torino certificates”. The user is identified once by linking the Amazon account with a recognised digital identity, such as SPID, and this authorisation remains valid until explicitly revoked. After recognition, the system uses the email address associated with the Amazon profile, asks the user to confirm the request and, once consent is given, retrieves the PDF certificate from the Registry or ANPR and sends it to the registered inbox. The expected value is a simpler, faster and more accessible interaction with municipal registry services. The prototype also demonstrates how voice interfaces, digital identity, consent management and public back-office integration can be combined in a citizen-facing service.

cases.source_description: Medication non-adherence among elderly and chronic patients leads to poorer health outcomes and higher healthcare costs. At the University Hospital Miguel Servet (HUMS) in Zaragoza, outpatient pharmacy processes were fragmented, manual, and prone to dispensing and coordination errors. The SAMPA project was implemented to improve treatment adherence, streamline medication management, and enhance patient experience. Stakeholders include hospital pharmacists, clinicians, outpatient staff, and elderly patients. The solution involved a comprehensive digital transformation of the outpatient pharmacy unit. Core components include an integrated electronic prescription platform, automated storage and dispensing robots, full traceability across prescribing and dispensing stages, appointment scheduling, and adherence monitoring systems. These components are interconnected with hospital information systems, enabling end-to-end visibility of medication flows and patient interactions. Supporting tools such as a patient app, improved web services, and dedicated communication points facilitate engagement and follow-up. The project has been implemented at HUMS and has reduced dispensing errors, improved workflow efficiency, and enhanced accessibility for patients. SAMPA demonstrates how integrated digital systems can deliver measurable operational and quality improvements in hospital outpatient care.

cases.source_description: Dementia care requires balancing safety with personal freedom, because residents may benefit physically and mentally from moving around, while care teams must manage risks linked to disorientation or wandering. The Smart Dementia project at Tante Louise uses eHealth technology to give people with Alzheimer’s disease more freedom inside and outside nursing-home settings. The operational objective is to support professional risk assessment: care teams decide how much freedom each resident can safely have, and the technology helps them monitor whereabouts when additional safeguards are needed. The implementation combines a wristwatch, mobile app, sensor technology and GPS-based location tracking, allowing nurses and authorised staff to locate a resident if necessary. At a conceptual level, the device collects location data, communicates it to relevant caregivers and supports a personalised care arrangement rather than imposing uniform restrictions. The expected impact is greater autonomy for residents, improved confidence for staff and families, and longer preservation of physical and mental activity. The project also demonstrates how personal health data can support more precise and individualised care, while raising obvious requirements around consent, proportionality and data protection. Its value lies in using technology as a supportive layer around professional judgement, not as a substitute for person-centred dementia care.

cases.source_description: Track AI addresses the difficulty of assessing visual function in children and other non-collaborative patients who may be unable to complete conventional ophthalmological examinations. Reliable early detection of visual impairment is essential for timely intervention, but clinical assessment can be challenging when patients cannot follow instructions or communicate clearly. The project, linked to Miguel Servet Hospital in Zaragoza, uses the DIVE medical device and aims to help physicians determine whether a patient has a visual impairment and, in some cases, estimate the probability of a specific pathology. The emerging technology implementation integrates artificial intelligence into the DIVE device through a dedicated app running on a Huawei P30 mobile phone. The app analyses data from visual explorations, especially patient gaze patterns, and compares them with a database generated from previous diagnoses, available both online and offline. At conceptual level, the system uses pattern comparison and probabilistic classification to support clinical interpretation of visual behaviour. Although focused on non-collaborative patients, it can also be used with collaborative patients. The expected impact is improved support for clinicians, faster and more accessible screening, and better identification of patients who may require further assessment or treatment. By combining portable technology with diagnostic-support capabilities, Track AI can strengthen paediatric and inclusive eye-care services.

cases.source_description: MasterMind in the Basque Country addressed the need to make high-quality treatment for depression more widely available to adults with mild and moderate depression. Access to psychological therapy can be constrained by limited professional capacity, distance, waiting times and the need for repeated face-to-face appointments. The project, involving Osakidetza within a broader European collaboration of 23 partners, aimed to use ICT to expand access while maintaining professional oversight. The emerging technology implementation consisted of Computerised Cognitive Behaviour Therapy delivered through the web application “Overcome your depression”, accessible by computer, tablet or smartphone. At conceptual level, the application provides therapy through six modules combining text, videos, images, graphs and interactive tasks. Patients complete tests within the platform, and these results communicate the evolution of their condition to health professionals. Clinicians periodically review the outputs and receive alerts when a patient’s results indicate possible concern. The expected impact is wider availability of depression treatment, fewer required face-to-face appointments and better continuity of monitoring between patients and professionals. By combining structured digital therapy with clinical supervision, MasterMind can improve service accessibility, support efficient use of healthcare resources and provide patients with a flexible treatment pathway that complements conventional mental-health services in the Basque health system.

By combining technical specification work with transparent IPR frameworks, MPAI can support innovation while reducing fragmentation in media and data-coding ecosystems. Its value lies in creating common reference points for industry and research actors developing or deploying advanced coding solutions.

cases.source_description: TreC+ brings together the digital health trials carried out in Trentino with citizens and health professionals, turning them into a single operational ecosystem for online health services. The service challenge is to guarantee citizens continuous, safe and integrated access to healthcare functions through one platform and one app, while maintaining the quality and reliability of care. The main stakeholders include the Autonomous Province of Trento, APSS, citizens, doctors, health professionals and the FBK research centre. The platform is designed around a constant exchange of data produced by patients and clinicians, with health information remaining under public control in APSS archives. Its implementation is based on open-source technologies and an open architectural model that allows proprietary tools and external solutions to be connected without moving health data away from the public system. The more advanced components, developed and experimented with FBK, explore virtual coaches, predictive models, chatbots and other intelligent applications. TreC+ can also integrate with existing healthcare-management systems, including booking services, electronic health records, payment systems and telemonitoring tools. The expected impact is broader access to digital health services, improved continuity of care, stronger data protection, and greater reusability in other regional, provincial, local health authority or hospital contexts. By combining public governance with modular integration, the ecosystem supports scalable digital healthcare while keeping citizens’ data central, protected and available.

These devices capture the passenger’s face and associate it with passport and ticket data, creating a temporary digital identity that is maintained for the duration of the passenger’s stay at the airport. Conceptually, the system combines biometric enrolment, document-data verification, facial matching, passenger-flow management and integration with airport access-control infrastructure. The expected impact is smoother passenger circulation, shorter queues, reduced manual document checks and more consistent identity verification across airport touchpoints. For airport operators, it can improve throughput and service quality, while supporting security objectives. However, because the system relies on biometric data, its use requires strict safeguards on consent, retention, accuracy, access control and proportionality.

cases.source_description: Facial images can be important investigative material when police need to compare a person shown in a photograph or video with people already recorded in law-enforcement databases. SARI, the Automatic Image Recognition System, was introduced in Italy for the Ministry of the Interior and the Central Anti-Crime Directorate of the State Police. The system is supplied by Parsec 3.26 S.r.l. and is structured around two components: SARI Enterprise and SARI Real-Time. SARI Enterprise supports retrospective identification by comparing a facial image already available to investigators with images in police databases of previously photo-recorded individuals. SARI Real-Time, by contrast, was designed to recognise people from a watch list through camera feeds. At a conceptual level, the technology combines biometric feature extraction, facial matching, image comparison and investigative review. Its operational value lies in helping officers narrow searches, identify possible matches and accelerate investigations where visual evidence is available. However, the two components raise different legal and ethical issues: retrospective matching for investigative purposes is different from real-time public-space recognition, which requires stronger safeguards because of its surveillance implications. The system should therefore be understood as an investigative-support tool whose outputs require human validation and legal control, not as an autonomous identification or enforcement mechanism. Current public material most clearly confirms knowledge of SARI Enterprise as the facial-recognition system used by Italian law enforcement for after-the-fact investigative identification.

cases.source_description: The EU-JAV vaccine conversation monitoring platform was developed to help public health actors understand how vaccination-related narratives circulate online across different countries and languages. The policy problem is that vaccine debates unfold rapidly through social media and web platforms, making it difficult for health authorities to detect emerging concerns, influential actors and misinformation dynamics in real time. Stakeholders include the Istituto Superiore di Sanità, EU-JAV partners, public health authorities, researchers, online communities and citizens exposed to vaccine information. In its initial phase, the platform operated in Italian, French and Spanish and was accessible via credentials. It monitored information flows from Twitter, Reddit, Wikipedia and Google Trends through a three-layer architecture: a Data layer, an Analysis layer and a Visualisation layer. The Data layer collected and cleaned raw information through platform APIs and keyword filters validated using recurrence and relevance criteria. The Analysis layer generated graphs, geolocated tweets and applied machine-learning processes for influencer analysis and early-signal detection, including the identification of active or influential users and emerging vaccine-related hashtags. The Visualisation layer presented results in an accessible way. The expected impact is stronger real-time monitoring of vaccine conversations, earlier detection of changing narratives, and better evidence for public communication strategies. By structuring online data into interpretable outputs, the platform supports more responsive vaccination policy and communication.

cases.source_description: Many advanced multimodal models have been primarily trained on English-language datasets, limiting their performance and applicability in languages with fewer annotated resources, such as Italian. This creates challenges for researchers, public administrations and digital service providers seeking to develop image–text retrieval, content moderation or assistive technologies tailored to Italian users. The project aims to bridge this gap by developing a multimodal model capable of understanding and linking Italian textual descriptions with visual content. The objective is to provide a robust foundation model that enables accurate alignment between images and Italian language inputs, supporting downstream applications in search, accessibility and digital services. The solution builds upon the Contrastive Language–Image Pre-training (CLIP) framework, combining a pre-trained Italian BERT language model (dbmdz) with a Vision Transformer architecture for image encoding. Using approximately 1.4 million paired image–text samples, the model is fine-tuned through contrastive learning techniques that optimise the similarity between matching image–text pairs while distinguishing non-matching pairs. The resulting architecture enables joint embedding of visual and textual data within a shared semantic space, accessible through an online demonstration environment. The Italian CLIP model improves multimodal understanding in a low-resource linguistic context, enhancing the accuracy of image–text retrieval and classification tasks in Italian. By reducing dependency on English-centric models, it strengthens digital sovereignty, supports innovation in language-specific applications and provides a scalable resource for further research and public and private sector use cases.

Expected results included reduced processing time per traveller, lower operational costs, improved mobility for border teams, and more reliable information flows between frontline officers and backend systems. cases.source_description: Neurological disorders are often difficult for patients to understand due to the complexity of medical imaging and the abstract nature of diagnostic explanations. Clinicians face challenges in communicating disease progression, anatomical alterations and treatment implications in a clear and accessible manner, particularly when relying on two-dimensional scans and technical terminology. NUMEL.AI addresses this communication gap by providing an interactive visualisation tool that enables doctors and patients to explore neurological conditions using the patient’s own medical imaging data. The objective is to enhance patient understanding, support shared decision-making and improve the quality of clinical consultations through immersive visual explanations grounded in real diagnostic data. The solution processes magnetic resonance (MR) images and other clinical imaging data imported directly from healthcare information systems to automatically generate personalised three-dimensional anatomical models. Computer vision techniques and body-tracking algorithms align these models with the patient’s body in real time using augmented reality rendering. Machine learning methods support image segmentation and the identification of relevant anatomical structures and disorder-related patterns. The system can operate locally or through a scalable, API-based cloud platform that allows secure data storage, retrieval and extensibility across healthcare environments. The tool improves the clarity and effectiveness of clinician–patient communication, enhances patient engagement and understanding of disease evolution, and supports more informed treatment discussions. Its scalable architecture facilitates integration with existing hospital systems, while automated model generation reduces preparation time for clinicians and increases the accessibility of advanced visualisation technologies in neurological care.

Researchers, legal experts, SMEs, industrial partners and academic institutions are therefore brought together to address both conceptual and computational barriers. Its expected impact is stronger legal technology research, improved foundations for compliance tools and future market-oriented services in legal reasoning.

cases.source_description: Public procurement oversight requires identifying high-risk tenders among very large numbers of procedures, a task that is difficult for experts and civil-society monitors to perform manually. DoZorro, linked to Ukraine’s ProZorro procurement ecosystem and Transparency International Ukraine, applies AI-supported risk analysis to help detect tenders that may involve corruption, collusion, unjustified disqualification or unfair selection of winners. The platform already enables suppliers, buyers, control authorities and citizens to provide feedback on procurement processes. The AI tool strengthens that function by prioritising tenders with suspicious patterns, allowing experts to focus on cases with the highest probability of irregularity. At a conceptual level, the system combines open procurement data, complaint data, risk indicators, machine-learning models and expert review. It does not replace legal investigation or procurement-control decisions; rather, it narrows the search space and supports human monitors by highlighting tenders that deserve closer analysis. Reported beta-test results included 26% more cases of unfounded winner selection, 37% more cases of groundless disqualification and 298% more cases of participant conspiracy being identified. The expected impact is better targeting of oversight resources, stronger anti-corruption monitoring, improved transparency and more efficient use of civil-society expertise. Recent open-contracting material describes DoZorro analytics platforms as continuing to interact with ProZorro’s central database.

cases.task: Kommers (KAI) semantics check tool
cases.context: Primona; Private sector; General services.; Sweden
cases.implementation: The tool leverages trained language models and domain-specific lexicons, combined with syntactic and semantic rule sets, to highlight problematic segments to the procurement author.
cases.outcome: UNKNOWN; 원천의 기대효과와 별도 관측 성과는 구분해야 합니다.
cases.source_description: Public procurement processes in both public and private sector organisations require clear, unambiguous tender documentation to ensure fair competition and avoid misinterpretation by potential bidders. However, procurement texts often contain complex legal and technical language, which can lead to misunderstandings, increased bidder risk, additional clarification rounds and, ultimately, delays in contract award and project execution. Stakeholders in this context include procurement officers, legal advisors, potential suppliers and contracting authorities, all of whom benefit from improved clarity and reduced ambiguity in procurement materials. The objective of this initiative is to enhance the quality and precision of procurement documentation by identifying semantic inconsistencies, ambiguous phrases and unclear requirements before tender publication. The solution integrates an AI assistant into Primona’s Kommers e-procurement platform, extending its existing modules with natural language processing (NLP) capabilities. The AI component performs semantic analysis on requirement statements, specifications and other textual elements within procurement documents to detect unclear wording, potential contradictions and language that might be misinterpreted by bidders. The tool leverages trained language models and domain-specific lexicons, combined with syntactic and semantic rule sets, to highlight problematic segments to the procurement author. It is embedded within the Kommers workflow, allowing users to run checks directly within their document preparation interface and receive actionable feedback in real time. By automating semantic validation, the tool reduces the risk of ambiguous or poorly phrased procurement documents reaching the market, improving clarity and fairness in competitive tendering. This leads to fewer clarification requests, faster procurement cycles, reduced administrative burden for contracting authorities and a lower risk of bid disputes. Enhanced document quality contributes to better supplier engagement, more accurate tender responses and ultimately more efficient public and private sector procurement outcomes.

cases.source_description: The Finnish State Treasury is responsible for overseeing and supporting financial management processes across central government entities, including the handling of a high volume of electronic invoices. Despite Finland’s advanced adoption of e-invoicing, invoice processing still requires manual verification of key data such as agreement numbers, amounts, supplier information and accounting references, creating inefficiencies and limiting full automation. A significant challenge identified by the State Treasury is the inconsistent structuring and placement of invoice data by suppliers and IT service providers, which hinders seamless machine processing. The objective of the initiative is to increase the level of end-to-end automation in public sector invoice handling, reduce manual workload and improve accuracy and processing speed across government financial operations. The planned solution combines artificial intelligence techniques and robotic process automation to analyse structured and semi-structured invoice data. Machine learning models are designed to automatically extract and validate relevant invoice fields, such as contract identifiers and payment amounts, while rule-based automation tools integrate with existing financial management systems to route, verify and post invoices. The system relies on standardised e-invoice formats and interoperability frameworks, and is embedded within the State Treasury’s digital financial infrastructure to enable scalable, centralised processing. The initiative aims to enable near real-time invoice validation, significantly reduce manual intervention, minimise processing errors and accelerate payment cycles. By improving data quality requirements and promoting standardisation among suppliers, the State Treasury strengthens the reliability and efficiency of public financial management, reduces administrative costs and enhances transparency and scalability in government accounting processes.

cases.implementation: Palkeet, the Finnish Government Shared Services Centre for Finance and HR, introduced robotic process automation to automate routine business processes across public administration support services. This approach allowed Palkeet to automate without immediately replacing all underlying legacy systems.
cases.outcome: UNKNOWN; 원천의 기대효과와 별도 관측 성과는 구분해야 합니다.
cases.source_description: Shared service centres handle large volumes of repetitive finance and HR tasks where accuracy, consistency and processing speed are essential. Palkeet, the Finnish Government Shared Services Centre for Finance and HR, introduced robotic process automation to automate routine business processes across public administration support services. The operational problem was that tasks such as purchase-invoice validation, supplier-register maintenance and other administrative checks required structured but repetitive work by staff. The implementation used UiPath software robots, alongside other tools where appropriate, to model and execute automated workflows. At a conceptual level, RPA bots log into existing systems, follow predefined process rules, validate data, move information between applications and flag exceptions for human review. This approach allowed Palkeet to automate without immediately replacing all underlying legacy systems. The expected impact is higher productivity, improved processing quality, fewer manual errors, faster throughput and better use of staff time for expert work. The project is recognised as one of the first major RPA implementations in the Finnish public sector and formed part of a wider government digitalisation agenda. UiPath’s case material states that Palkeet began considering RPA in spring 2015 and became one of the first Finnish organisations to foresee its benefits, while Palkeet remains an active shared-services provider in Finnish government.

cases.source_description: Public procurement reform requires digital systems that increase transparency, reduce administrative friction and create structured data across the full procurement cycle. Moldova’s Ministry of Finance developed mTender with support from the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development as an open-source electronic procurement system. The operational problem was to move from fragmented or paper-heavy procurement processes towards a transparent digital system connecting public buyers, private platforms and a central data layer. At a conceptual level, mTender digitises procurement planning, tender publication, bidding, data disclosure and contract-related monitoring. The reported use of robotic process automation for tracking contract execution reflects the wider goal of automating repetitive controls and improving visibility across the procurement lifecycle. The expected impact is more transparent public spending, greater competition, easier supplier participation, stronger data-driven monitoring and alignment with international open-contracting practice. The current MTender portal remains accessible and describes the system as supporting procurement from planning through payment, while recent Moldovan reporting indicates that a new e-Achiziții system has been approved as the next stage of modernisation.

cases.task: KRATID - Detecting traffic anomalies and incidents of the Estonian data exchange layer (X-Road)
cases.context: Information System Authority; Central-Government; General services.; Estonia
cases.implementation: KRATID uses machine learning to monitor traffic patterns in the Estonian data exchange layer and detect anomalies or possible incidents. The operational problem is that very large numbers of exchanges take place through X-Road, making it difficult for human administrators to identify unusual behaviour, technical faults or unexpected changes in service use manually.
cases.outcome: UNKNOWN; 원천의 기대효과와 별도 관측 성과는 구분해야 합니다.
cases.source_description: Digital government depends on reliable data exchange between public institutions, and Estonia’s X-Road is a critical infrastructure layer for secure communication between public and private-sector systems. KRATID uses machine learning to monitor traffic patterns in the Estonian data exchange layer and detect anomalies or possible incidents. The operational problem is that very large numbers of exchanges take place through X-Road, making it difficult for human administrators to identify unusual behaviour, technical faults or unexpected changes in service use manually. The implementation compares current data-exchange behaviour with previous periods and searches for differences that may indicate an error, abnormal usage or another event requiring attention. At a conceptual level, the system combines traffic monitoring, anomaly detection, historical pattern comparison and human review. If the system cannot determine whether an observed situation is erroneous or permitted, a user still decides how to interpret the signal. The expected impact is stronger operational awareness for the Information System Authority, faster detection of incidents, better guidance for X-Road users and more resilient digital public infrastructure. The use case should be separated from other Estonian AI examples sometimes listed in the same source, such as job matching, land-mowing detection or police traffic deployment; the core KRATID case concerns X-Road anomaly and incident detection.

In France, the Pasteur Institute, Greater Paris University Hospitals and the chatbot start-up Clevy released an open-source COVID-19 auto-diagnosis chatbot in March 2020. The objective was to provide a structured questionnaire through which users could report symptoms and receive an indication of their possible risk of contamination or need for further action. The implementation relied on a conversational questionnaire rather than a free-form diagnostic system: users answered predefined questions, and the bot mapped responses to risk-assessment guidance based on the available public-health knowledge at the time. At a conceptual level, the service translated triage logic into an accessible digital interface, supporting early self-assessment, orientation and public communication. The open-source character also allowed the tool to be reused or examined by other actors. The service should not be understood as a substitute for medical diagnosis; its role was to provide preliminary orientation during an emergency, when demand for health information was exceptionally high and official communication needed to scale quickly.

cases.problem: Managing scarce parking space in a dense city requires regular enforcement, reliable permit checks and a process that can cover large numbers of parked vehicles without excessive manual patrol effort.
cases.task: Automated parking control
cases.context: Amsterdam Parking Services; Local Government; Transport; Netherlands
cases.implementation: Amsterdam uses automated parking control to determine whether parked vehicles have the right to occupy paid parking spaces, either because a fee has been paid through a parking meter or app, or because the vehicle has a valid parking permit. The implementation uses scan cars equipped with cameras and automatic number-plate recognition to identify licence plates and check them against relevant payment and permit systems.
cases.outcome: UNKNOWN; 원천의 기대효과와 별도 관측 성과는 구분해야 합니다.
cases.source_description: Managing scarce parking space in a dense city requires regular enforcement, reliable permit checks and a process that can cover large numbers of parked vehicles without excessive manual patrol effort. Amsterdam uses automated parking control to determine whether parked vehicles have the right to occupy paid parking spaces, either because a fee has been paid through a parking meter or app, or because the vehicle has a valid parking permit. The implementation uses scan cars equipped with cameras and automatic number-plate recognition to identify licence plates and check them against relevant payment and permit systems. At a conceptual level, the scan car captures the plate, converts it into machine-readable data, checks the data against back-office records and flags cases where no valid parking right appears to exist. Human procedures can then verify and handle enforcement actions where needed. The expected impact is more efficient street-parking enforcement, better compliance with parking rules, reduced fraud and improved turnover of parking spaces. The system operates at large scale: Egis reports that Amsterdam’s on-street parking service uses ANPR to monitor more than six million vehicles per month.

The project aimed to give users a tool that could convert standard documents into personalised versions that are easier to understand. Its implementation used language technology to simplify text according to the needs of people with ASD. Conceptually, the system analysed source documents, identified linguistic features that may create comprehension barriers, and generated clearer alternatives through simplification, explanation, rephrasing or adaptation of wording. The expected impact was improved comprehension, greater autonomy, reduced reliance on intermediaries and better access to written information. For educators, carers, service providers and public bodies, such a tool could make communication more inclusive and reduce misunderstandings. By focusing on personalisation rather than one-size-fits-all simplification, FIRST recognised that accessibility depends on individual reading profiles and contexts. Its business and public value lie in making complex documents more usable for a group often underserved by mainstream text technologies.

The project therefore used a co-creation approach in which older people, public administrations, researchers and community actors worked together on services related to the production and use of open urban data. Its implementation combined mobile applications, open data, participatory design, local service scenarios and user-centred development. The project addressed themes including loneliness, social inclusion, safer and more accessible cities, data curation and personal health information. Conceptually, Mobile-Age linked civic data infrastructures with mobile interfaces and co-designed service models, ensuring that data-driven services responded to real needs in everyday urban life. The expected impact was improved accessibility of public services, stronger inclusion of older citizens in digital innovation, better reuse of open government data and more responsive local service delivery. By involving older people directly, the project strengthened both usability and democratic legitimacy.

Public bodies often manage high-volume tasks that require staff to copy, check or transfer information between digital systems, even when the rules are clear and human judgement is limited. In 2017, the Department of Public Expenditure and Reform coordinated a pilot in which four government departments selected suitable processes to test the potential of robotic process automation. The implementation used software robots to operate existing applications at user-interface level, automating labour-intensive, rules-based tasks without requiring wholesale replacement of legacy systems. Conceptually, RPA was applied as a non-invasive automation layer that could log into systems, follow predefined steps, transfer data, validate entries and generate outputs consistently. The expected impact was improved accuracy, fewer manual errors, faster processing and the release of staff time for higher-value work. The pilot also helped the Irish public service understand which process characteristics make automation feasible and what governance, procurement and implementation arrangements would be needed for wider adoption. A later government RPA framework indicates that the pilot contributed to a broader national approach to automation services.

Estonia’s Bürokratt initiative aims to create a network of public-sector virtual assistants that allow people to interact with the state in natural language. The operational problem is that even highly digital government systems can remain fragmented from the user’s perspective, especially when a request requires cooperation between different agencies. At a conceptual level, a citizen can ask a question or request a service through a conversational interface, while the system identifies the relevant institution, retrieves information and, where possible, supports service routing or administrative action. The longer-term vision is for personalised AI agents to cooperate across domains and help citizens solve problems without navigating complex portals or repeating information. GOV.UK faced a content-organisation problem because many pages were not tagged to the correct “sub-branches” of the site taxonomy, while manual classification at scale would have required substantial editorial effort. The Government Digital Service used natural language processing to make page text machine-readable and combined this with metadata such as publication date and department to learn patterns associated with existing content tags. At a conceptual level, the system transformed unstructured text into features, learned from already-tagged pages and predicted the most appropriate content categories for untagged pages. Predictions were then used selectively: where training examples were too few or categories too diverse, the team did not rely on model outputs. The expected impact was better content structure, improved user journeys, reduced manual tagging work and more consistent organisation across GOV.UK. GDS reported that machine learning helped tag 96% of untagged GOV.UK pages, corresponding to roughly 100,000 pages, while user researchers and content designers reviewed the outputs before wider rollout.

cases.task: Detection of mowing events on grasslands from Sentinel-data
cases.context: Estonian Agricultural Registers and Information Board (ARIB); Central-Government; Environmental protection n.e.c.; Estonia
cases.implementation: Estonia’s Agricultural Registers and Information Board applied satellite-data analysis to automate detection of mowing events on grasslands, supporting compliance checks for agricultural subsidies. The implementation uses time series from Sentinel-1 radar and Sentinel-2 optical imagery, allowing the system to observe vegetation changes over the growing season even under frequent cloud cover.
cases.outcome: UNKNOWN; 원천의 기대효과와 별도 관측 성과는 구분해야 합니다.
cases.source_description: Agricultural payment agencies must verify whether farmers comply with land-management requirements, but manual on-the-spot checks are costly, time-consuming and difficult to scale nationally. Estonia’s Agricultural Registers and Information Board applied satellite-data analysis to automate detection of mowing events on grasslands, supporting compliance checks for agricultural subsidies. The operational problem is that mowing is one of the conditions for receiving certain government grants, yet field inspections can only cover a limited sample of parcels. The implementation uses time series from Sentinel-1 radar and Sentinel-2 optical imagery, allowing the system to observe vegetation changes over the growing season even under frequent cloud cover. A deep-learning model with a reject option detects likely mowing events and can flag uncertain cases for further attention. At a conceptual level, the system converts satellite observations into a national monitoring layer for agricultural practice: changes in vegetation and surface characteristics indicate whether a field has probably been mown. The expected impact is fewer unnecessary field inspections, earlier reminders to applicants, better compliance monitoring and more efficient use of administrative resources. Public case records describe Estonia’s system as the first nationwide automated monitoring system for agricultural practices in the EU, operational from 2018, with reported mowing-detection accuracy of around 85%.

cases.task: London Police Facial Recognition System
cases.context: City of London Police; Local Government; Public order and safety n.e.c.; United Kingdom
cases.implementation: The system uses computer vision and deep learning models trained on large facial image datasets to extract biometric templates from live video feeds. These templates are compared against encrypted watch-list databases using pattern-matching algorithms.

cases.source_description: The Metropolitan Police Service in London seeks to enhance its capacity to identify individuals of interest in public spaces in order to prevent crime, safeguard vulnerable persons and support ongoing investigations. Traditional identification methods rely on post-event analysis or manual recognition, which can delay interventions and limit operational effectiveness. The deployment of live facial recognition aims to support frontline officers by automatically identifying individuals who appear on pre-defined police watch lists, such as wanted suspects or missing persons. Stakeholders include law enforcement officers, public authorities, oversight bodies and members of the public whose data may be processed in public settings. The objective is to enable rapid identification in real time while operating within the UK legal and regulatory framework. The system uses computer vision and deep learning models trained on large facial image datasets to extract biometric templates from live video feeds. These templates are compared against encrypted watch-list databases using pattern-matching algorithms. The solution is integrated with existing police camera infrastructure and operational command systems, generating alerts for officers when similarity thresholds are met. The technology supports high-speed processing of video streams in dynamic environments. The intended impact is improved response times, enhanced public safety and more efficient deployment of police resources. Operational benefits include automation of identity checks in crowded areas and support for targeted interventions, although the system also requires strict governance, oversight and accuracy monitoring to maintain reliability and public trust.

cases.problem: Loneliness and social isolation are persistent challenges in residential care homes, particularly among older adults with limited mobility or family contact. The pilot showed positive effects on resident engagement and mood, particularly for individuals with limited social contact.
cases.task: Robots to be used in UK care homes to help reduce loneliness
cases.context: University of Bedfordshire; Academic-Research; Old age.; United Kingdom
cases.implementation: Care staff reported that robots supplemented, rather than replaced, human interaction and could be deployed flexibly.

cases.source_description: Loneliness and social isolation are persistent challenges in residential care homes, particularly among older adults with limited mobility or family contact. A UK pilot explored whether social robots could complement care staff by providing companionship and daily interaction for residents. Stakeholders included care home residents, carers, management, families, and technology providers, with the objective of improving emotional well-being without replacing human care. Conducted between 2019 and 2020, the pilot introduced “Pepper” wheeled humanoid robots into selected care homes. The robots were pre-programmed and gradually adapted to residents’ preferences, enabling simple conversations, music playback, reminders, and interactive activities. Sensors and speech interfaces supported autonomous navigation and engagement, while learning components allowed the robots to personalise interactions over time. The systems operated locally within care facilities and were supervised by staff. The pilot showed positive effects on resident engagement and mood, particularly for individuals with limited social contact. Care staff reported that robots supplemented, rather than replaced, human interaction and could be deployed flexibly. While not a substitute for personal care, the solution demonstrated potential to scale as a supportive tool to reduce loneliness and enhance quality of life in long-term care settings.

The approach demonstrated strong scalability and laid the foundation for sustainable management of national audiovisual heritage.

cases.problem: Researchers in history, computer science, and the social sciences face significant challenges when analysing large collections of historical photographs, as manual examination is time-consuming and limits the scale of inquiry.
cases.task: Artificial intelligence dives into thousands of WWII photographs
cases.context: Aarhus University; Academic-Research; Cultural services.; Denmark
cases.implementation: This use case addresses these challenges through an interdisciplinary study that examines thousands of Second World War photographs, involving academic researchers and cultural heritage institutions, with the objective of uncovering latent patterns in visual content and advancing new methods for large-scale historical image analysis. The study is implemented using computer vision and pattern recognition techniques applied to extensive datasets of digitised wartime photographs, with models trained to extract visual features related to composition, subject matter, and contextual elements.

cases.source_description: Researchers in history, computer science, and the social sciences face significant challenges when analysing large collections of historical photographs, as manual examination is time-consuming and limits the scale of inquiry. Understanding patterns of authorship, perspective, and visual style in wartime imagery is important for historical interpretation, archival research, and cultural analysis. This use case addresses these challenges through an interdisciplinary study that examines thousands of Second World War photographs, involving academic researchers and cultural heritage institutions, with the objective of uncovering latent patterns in visual content and advancing new methods for large-scale historical image analysis. The study is implemented using computer vision and pattern recognition techniques applied to extensive datasets of digitised wartime photographs, with models trained to extract visual features related to composition, subject matter, and contextual elements. These models analyse similarities and recurring visual signatures across images, enabling the system to distinguish and attribute photographs to individual photographers based solely on image content, without relying on metadata. The results demonstrate that large-scale automated image analysis can reveal meaningful stylistic and contextual patterns in historical archives, including the ability to identify photographers with a high degree of accuracy. This approach significantly expands the analytical capacity of historical research, supports more systematic exploration of visual archives, and opens new opportunities for interdisciplinary collaboration and data-driven insights in the study of cultural heritage.

The ASTRiD project addresses this challenge by developing a digital tram depot capable of supporting autonomous vehicle movements within controlled environments. cases.source_description: City regions face increasing pressure to promote walking and cycling while ensuring that investments in active travel infrastructure are evidence-based. Transport for Greater Manchester (TfGM) planned a regional monitoring initiative to gain better insight into how pedestrians and cyclists use segregated routes, junctions, and priority corridors. Stakeholders included TfGM, local authorities, urban planners, and residents. The objective was to obtain continuous, anonymised data on active travel flows to support infrastructure planning, safety interventions, and evaluation of policy measures without relying on manual surveys. The planned solution involved the installation of around 100 roadside sensors supplied by Vivacity Labs. These sensors combine optical and signal-based detection to count pedestrians, cyclists, and vehicles in real time while processing data locally to avoid personal identification. Aggregated flow data would be transmitted to central dashboards and combined with contextual information such as time of day and location. According to public reporting, elements of the sensor deployment were initiated, but the programme was framed as an exploratory pilot rather than a fully institutionalised system. The initiative demonstrated the potential for scalable, low-intrusion monitoring of active travel, supporting more responsive transport planning and contributing to wider smart mobility strategies, even though full regional rollout was not confirmed at the time.

cases.context: University of Trento; Academic-Research; General services.; Italy

cases.source_description: The rapid spread of manipulated and deceptive images on social media has created significant challenges for journalists, platforms, institutions, and citizens seeking to assess the authenticity and provenance of digital content. Traditional verification methods struggle to keep pace with the volume and sophistication of falsified imagery, undermining trust in online information. This use case addresses these challenges by supporting the identification, classification, and long-term traceability of manipulated images, involving researchers, media professionals, and technology providers, with the objective of enabling reliable verification and increasing transparency in digital media ecosystems. The project combines image analysis techniques for recognising and classifying falsified or manipulated images with a distributed ledger system that records classification results in an immutable register. Each analysed image is processed to detect signs of manipulation and assigned a verification outcome, which is then permanently stored to preserve the history, provenance, and processing chain of the multimedia content. The register is made accessible for consultation, allowing users to verify whether an image has been assessed and to review its authenticity status. The approach strengthens the reliability of digital forensics by ensuring traceability and tamper resistance, improves confidence in media verification processes, and supports the development of trustworthy tools to combat misinformation, contributing to greater transparency and accountability in online content sharing.

cases.source_description: Public welfare systems face ongoing challenges in distributing financial support efficiently while preventing fraud, reducing administrative costs, and ensuring that vulnerable citizens can access benefits easily. In the United Kingdom, HM Treasury and the Department for Work and Pensions sought to explore new payment models that could modernise the delivery of government grants and welfare support. The objective of this use case is to improve the registration and payment of benefits, strengthen control over public expenditure, and support broader policy goals such as financial inclusion and poverty reduction. The proof of concept is implemented through a digital payment and registration framework based on distributed ledger technology, often referred to as GovCoin. The system records benefit entitlements and transactions in a shared, secure ledger, enabling automated checks, traceability of payments, and reduced reliance on intermediaries. Integration with existing government systems supports eligibility verification and compliance, while digital wallets enable recipients to receive and use funds more efficiently. The approach demonstrates potential to reduce losses from fraud and error, lower administrative overhead, and increase transparency in welfare payments. It also improves user experience for beneficiaries by supporting faster and more reliable access to support, while offering better value for money and a more sustainable footing for public expenditure.

The Royal Mint and CME Group sought to modernise gold markets by combining physical security with digital efficiency. The impact is a more flexible, resilient and innovation-ready settlement infrastructure that maintains systemic stability while supporting future technological evolution. This approach enhances scalability, ensures regulatory compliance and positions the UK payment system to adapt to industry developments.

cases.source_description: The Food Standards Agency (FSA), the UK’s food safety regulator, faces the ongoing challenge of ensuring transparency, traceability and regulatory oversight across complex meat supply chains, where fragmented records and limited data sharing can slow inspections and reduce trust. In the context of meat production and inspection, the FSA worked with an unnamed cattle slaughterhouse to address the need for consistent, verifiable and timely access to production and inspection data. Emerging Technology Implementation: The solution was implemented using a blockchain-based supply chain monitoring system, piloted through a proof of concept. Standardised data relating to meat inspection and production events were recorded on a shared distributed ledger accessible to both the FSA and the slaughterhouse. The approach focused on developing common data standards in collaboration with industry, enabling secure, tamper-evident data sharing and integration with existing operational systems at a conceptual level. Impact and Results: The trial demonstrated that the technology functions effectively within this segment of the food industry, delivering improved transparency and shared visibility across the supply chain. It validated the feasibility of real-time data access for regulators, strengthened trust between industry and government, and highlighted opportunities to scale the approach. The results showed clear potential for more efficient inspections, improved compliance assurance, and a collaborative model that can be expanded across the wider food sector.

The Government of Aragon implemented a pioneering hybrid blockchain solution combining Ethereum and Hyperledger Fabric technologies through the Alastria Consortium to automate and secure public tender evaluations. cases.outcome: UNKNOWN; 원천의 기대효과와 별도 관측 성과는 구분해야 합니다.
cases.source_description: The City of Antwerp, through its municipal IT agency Digipolis, explored ways to enhance public procurement processes by introducing greater transparency, reliability and trust in how requests for quotations and vendor offers are exchanged and recorded. Traditional procurement systems can be vulnerable to data tampering and lack robust, tamper-evident records of submissions, which may undermine confidence among procurers and bidders and lead to disputes or compliance challenges. The tool was developed in the context of public procurement stakeholders including municipal procurement officers, IT administrators, and suppliers, with the objective of testing whether distributed ledger technology could strengthen the integrity of procurement transactions while respecting existing procurement regulations. The solution developed combines blockchain-based and conventional components: procurers publish requests for quotations via a user interface linked to a customer relationship management system, and metadata from published requests and vendor submissions are recorded on a permissioned blockchain to provide immutable time-stamped attestations that documents have not been altered. The blockchain component, using a proof-of-authority configuration hosted by Digipolis and the Belgian Federal Government Procurement Organization (BOSA), underpins the process alongside smart contracts that log key events such as contract award outcomes. Integration with the CRM system ensures award notifications and non-award communications can be automated following on-chain events. The tool has been implemented as part of the BLING (Blockchain in Government) programme of proof-of-concept projects, and the early experience indicates the system is stable enough to support procurement workflows, offering enhanced transparency and tamper resistance compared to legacy systems while remaining compliant with public procurement law

cases.source_description: Estonia's comprehensive digital government services created an unprecedented national dependency on data infrastructure, raising concerns about continuity in the event of cyber attacks or physical disasters affecting domestic systems. The government established the world's first data embassy in Luxembourg, housing backup copies of critical national databases including land registry, population register, business register, and health records within a Tier 4 datacenter in Betzdorf. The facility operates under a bilateral agreement providing diplomatic immunity equivalent to a physical embassy, ensuring data sovereignty regardless of its physical location. Built with €2.2 million in funding (85% from EU ERDF), the infrastructure employs Guardtime's KSI Blockchain for data integrity verification alongside solutions from Cybernetica, Dell EMC, Ericsson, OpenNode, and Telia. The initiative has since inspired similar projects, with Monaco replicating the model in 2021.

cases.source_description: Academic and professional credential verification has traditionally relied on centralised institutions, creating administrative burdens for universities, graduates and employers who must repeatedly authenticate certificates and qualifications. To address inefficiencies in credential issuance and verification, the University of Nicosia pioneered the use of blockchain infrastructure to issue tamper-evident academic certificates that can be independently verified without requiring direct institutional confirmation. The initiative sought to modernise trust mechanisms in academic certification while supporting innovation in digital currency and blockchain education. Stakeholders include students, employers, academic institutions and accreditation bodies. The system records cryptographic hashes of academic certificates on the Bitcoin blockchain, enabling third parties to validate authenticity through decentralised verification processes. Secure digital signatures and blockchain time-stamping ensure document integrity while preserving personal data off-chain. The solution is integrated into the university’s academic administration systems and supports issuance for large-scale online programmes, including the Digital Currency MOOC and specialised MSc degrees. The pilot also included a deliberative process on the politics and economics of data and on how Barcelona could develop a democratic city data commons. The expected impact was stronger trust in digital participation, more privacy-respecting civic engagement and a practical demonstration of how public authorities can enable democratic processes without unnecessary personal-data exposure.

The Ministry of Education implemented an algorithmic system to automatically assign teachers to schools based on preferences, qualifications, and regional needs, processing massive datasets to generate placements within compressed timeframes. The case became a prominent example in debates about algorithmic accountability in public administration, highlighting tensions between efficiency gains and transparency requirements in automated government decision-making.

Nantes Métropole implemented an algorithmic system for solidarity transport pricing (Tarification Solidaire Transports) on its Naolib public transport network. The algorithm determines eligibility for free travel or discounts up to 50% on unlimited annual passes based on household income and family composition. All households with a family quotient of 900 or below qualify for solidarity pricing. Users apply at their local town hall, where agents collect supporting documents and enter information into Deltas, software developed by Nantes Métropole. Since May 2023, the eligibility threshold was raised from 600 to 900 family quotient, significantly expanding coverage. The solidarity pricing programme extends beyond metropolitan residents to include commuters from surrounding areas who travel within Nantes Métropole. This ensures transport affordability for the most vulnerable populations whilst supporting labour market access and social cohesion across the metropolitan region.

cases.source_description: Encouraging citizens to adopt sustainable behaviours such as recycling and low-emission mobility requires mechanisms that can reliably measure actions and translate them into tangible rewards. Municipalities often struggle to track these activities transparently and at scale, while citizens lack incentives that are trusted and easy to use. The Ecocoin pilot was created to address this gap by assigning concrete value to virtuous environmental actions within a local circular economy. Stakeholders include citizens, municipal waste collectors, local authorities and affiliated commercial partners. The objective is to promote sustainable behaviour while strengthening local economic circuits. The solution combines interconnected sensors used by waste collectors to measure recycling activities with a blockchain-based ledger that records verified actions immutably. Citizens create a digital profile with an associated wallet; when waste is delivered and measured, tokens are generated automatically and credited to the wallet. Initially deployed in the German state of Hesse and selected regions in Bavaria and North Rhine-Westphalia, the initiative involves public authorities, municipalities, and private sector partners. Its objective is to simplify online registration and authentication across domains such as e-government, mobility, and tourism, while strengthening data sovereignty and trust. The solution combines self-sovereign identity principles with existing identity infrastructures, building on OPTIMOS 2.0 and mobile identity wallets. Identity credentials are issued, stored, and shared under user control, with verification supported by decentralised trust mechanisms. The system integrates with public and private services without centralised identity databases. The project demonstrates reduced administrative burden, faster onboarding to digital services, and enhanced privacy protection. It provides a scalable and interoperable model for secure digital identities, supporting cross-sector use and reinforcing citizen-centric data governance.

cases.source_description: Italy's education system faced the annual challenge of assigning approximately 100,000 teachers to schools across diverse regions, a complex optimization problem that had historically relied on manual processes prone to errors and delays. The Ministry of Education implemented an algorithmic system to automatically assign teachers to schools based on preferences, qualifications, and regional needs, processing massive datasets to generate placements within compressed timeframes. The case became a prominent example in debates about algorithmic accountability in public administration, highlighting tensions between efficiency gains and transparency requirements in automated government decision-making.

Traditional audit methods cannot efficiently monitor the vast volume of internet commercial activity, creating opportunities for tax evasion through e-commerce platforms and social media. The system complements other AI initiatives in German tax administration including the Steuerchatbot virtual assistant (extended nationally and to English and French in 2024), nudging tools that adapt communication based on taxpayer risk profiles, and automated verification systems for processing tax returns. Public authorities and planners require accurate forecasts to support drinking water supply, agricultural irrigation, infrastructure protection, and land-use planning. The Federal Institute for Geosciences and Natural Resources and the Karlsruhe Institute of Technology address this need through a joint initiative focused on nationwide groundwater level prediction. Stakeholders include water authorities, municipalities, farmers, and infrastructure operators. The objective is to improve decision-making by providing timely and reliable groundwater forecasts that support risk assessment and adaptation strategies. The solution uses artificial neural network models trained on historical groundwater measurements, meteorological data, and hydrological variables. cases.source_description: Traditional satellite imagery captures only a limited portion of the electromagnetic spectrum, restricting scientists' ability to detect subtle environmental changes in vegetation health, water quality, soil composition, and mineral deposits essential for climate monitoring and resource management. EnMAP (Environmental Mapping and Analysis Program) is Germany's first hyperspectral satellite mission, launched in April 2022 aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9. The satellite carries a dual-spectrometer instrument capturing 230 spectral bands from 420 to 2450 nanometres at 30-metre ground resolution, enabling detection of biochemical and geochemical signatures invisible to conventional sensors. Operating in sun-synchronous orbit at 653 kilometres altitude, EnMAP records up to 5,000 kilometres of imagery daily with 4-day revisit capability. The German Research Centre for Geosciences (GFZ) leads scientific coordination whilst DLR manages operations. In 2024, the SpectralEarth dataset was released, comprising 538,974 image patches for training AI foundation models in hyperspectral analysis. EnMAP provides unprecedented environmental monitoring capability for agriculture, forestry, water management, and geology applications. The mission supports Copernicus services and contributes to climate protection initiatives by enabling precise characterisation of ecosystem changes. Data is freely available to the global scientific community through DLR's ground segment.

cases.source_description: International airport border control in Germany faced growing passenger volumes requiring faster processing whilst maintaining security standards and compliance with Schengen external border regulations. The Federal Police implemented EasyPASS, an automated border control system using biometric facial recognition developed by Bundesdruckerei, secunet, and Cognitec to verify travellers' identities against their e-passport chip photos. The system is deployed at Frankfurt, Munich, Hamburg, Hannover, Düsseldorf, Stuttgart, Berlin Brandenburg, and Cologne/Bonn airports, available to EU/EEA citizens aged 12+ and registered third-country nationals from the USA, Hong Kong, South Korea, Taiwan, and the UK. Travellers place their e-passport on the document reader, then proceed through gates where cameras capture facial images for 1:1 comparison against stored biometric data, with information also checked against Schengen databases. Data is stored for 48 hours (extendable to 30 days for police investigations), and the system strictly limits facial recognition to identity verification purposes under the Passport Act.

cases.source_description: Increasing urban traffic congestion leads to longer travel times, higher fuel consumption, and increased noise and air pollution. Optimising traffic signal systems is a critical lever for improving traffic flow in dense city environments, yet conventional control strategies struggle to adapt to dynamic traffic conditions. The KI4LSA project addresses this challenge by exploring adaptive control of traffic lights in inner-city areas. Stakeholders include transport authorities, municipalities, and road users seeking smoother traffic flow and reduced environmental impact. The objective is to optimise traffic signal behaviour in real time to minimise congestion and unnecessary stopping. The solution uses reinforcement learning, a data-driven control approach trained in detailed traffic simulations. Traffic signal controllers learn optimal strategies by observing traffic states and evaluating outcomes such as queue length and waiting time. After training, the learned control policies are evaluated against conventional approaches. The project demonstrates improved traffic flow, reduced stop-and-go behaviour, and lower emissions resulting from fewer accelerations and idling periods. The results highlight the potential of adaptive signal control to improve urban mobility efficiency and environmental performance, while providing a transferable framework for future smart traffic management systems.

cases.problem: Access to affordable water is a fundamental right, yet low-income households often struggle with utility costs.
cases.task: Nantes Social Water Pricing
cases.context: Nantes Métropole & Ville; Local Government; Social protection n.e.c.; France
cases.implementation: The algorithm calculates eligibility based on household income and family composition using data from the Caisse d'Allocations Familiales (CAF).
cases.outcome: UNKNOWN; 원천의 기대효과와 별도 관측 성과는 구분해야 합니다.
cases.source_description: Access to affordable water is a fundamental right, yet low-income households often struggle with utility costs. Traditional means-tested assistance programmes require complex application processes and frequently miss eligible beneficiaries who are unaware of available support. Nantes Métropole developed an open-source algorithm to determine eligibility for its social water tariff (Tarification Solidaire de l'Eau), guaranteeing that no household spends more than 3% of income on water for reasonable consumption of 30 cubic metres per person annually. The algorithm calculates eligibility based on household income and family composition using data from the Caisse d'Allocations Familiales (CAF). For CAF beneficiaries with family quotient below the threshold, assistance is granted automatically. Other residents can apply at their town hall, where agents enter information into Deltas software developed in-house by Nantes Métropole. The algorithm processes data in real time, providing immediate eligibility determination. The source code is published under the CeCILL-B open-source licence. In 2024, 5,866 households benefited from the social water tariff, receiving €407,153 in total assistance. Since January 2025, reformed Agence de l'Eau charges have been integrated into the pricing structure. The open-source approach supports transparency in public decision-making and enables other municipalities to adapt the algorithm for their own social pricing programmes.

cases.task: Nantes Solidarity Transport Pricing
cases.context: Nantes Métropole & Ville; Local Government; Social protection n.e.c.; France
cases.implementation: Nantes Métropole implemented an algorithmic system for solidarity transport pricing (Tarification Solidaire Transports) on its Naolib public transport network.
cases.outcome: UNKNOWN; 원천의 기대효과와 별도 관측 성과는 구분해야 합니다.
cases.source_description: Public transport affordability is crucial for social inclusion, yet fixed-price ticketing can exclude low-income residents from mobility services essential for employment, healthcare access, and social participation. Nantes Métropole implemented an algorithmic system for solidarity transport pricing (Tarification Solidaire Transports) on its Naolib public transport network. The algorithm determines eligibility for free travel or discounts up to 50% on unlimited annual passes based on household income and family composition. All households with a family quotient of 900 or below qualify for solidarity pricing. Users apply at their local town hall, where agents collect supporting documents and enter information into Deltas, software developed by Nantes Métropole. The algorithm processes data in real time, immediately notifying applicants of their entitlement level. Benefits apply to all household members regardless of age. Since May 2023, the eligibility threshold was raised from 600 to 900 family quotient, significantly expanding coverage. The solidarity pricing programme extends beyond metropolitan residents to include commuters from surrounding areas who travel within Nantes Métropole. This ensures transport affordability for the most vulnerable populations whilst supporting labour market access and social cohesion across the metropolitan region.

cases.context: City of Amsterdam and other dutch municipalities; Local Government; General services.; Netherlands
cases.implementation: It uses language-based classification models trained on historical report data, relying primarily on keyword recognition and probabilistic categorisation.

cases.source_description: Municipalities receive large volumes of reports from residents concerning issues in public space, such as waste, infrastructure damage or nuisance, which must be routed quickly to the correct department. Manual triage is time-consuming and can delay resolution. Signalen was developed as a shared, open-source system by and for Dutch municipalities to streamline the intake and handling of such reports. Stakeholders include local authorities, civil servants responsible for service delivery and residents submitting reports. The objective is to improve response times, reduce administrative workload and ensure consistent handling across municipalities. The system automatically categorises incoming reports based on their content and routes them to the appropriate municipal unit. It uses language-based classification models trained on historical report data, relying primarily on keyword recognition and probabilistic categorisation. The platform is API-driven and integrates with existing municipal case management systems. Personal data is optional and excluded from automated processing, ensuring privacy by design. Signalen is currently used by municipalities serving over two million residents and processes more than 600,000 reports annually. The system has improved operational efficiency, reduced misrouting, and increased transparency for citizens, while its open-source nature supports scalability, reuse and long-term sustainability across the Netherlands.

cases.implementation: LAIban operates as a conversational assistant deployed across all 80 public preschools in Helsingborg. It responds to common questions using structured content and language models trained on predefined educational and administrative data.
cases.outcome: UNKNOWN; 원천의 기대효과와 별도 관측 성과는 구분해야 합니다.
cases.source_description: Children in municipal preschools frequently ask practical questions about daily routines, activities and schedules, which can place additional demands on staff. The City of Helsingborg introduced LAIban to support children’s independence while complementing the role of educators. Stakeholders include children, preschool staff, municipal administrators and parents. The objective is to provide accessible, age-appropriate information while fostering children’s confidence and inclusion. LAIban operates as a conversational assistant deployed across all 80 public preschools in Helsingborg. It responds to common questions using structured content and language models trained on predefined educational and administrative data. The system supports multiple languages, reflecting the demographic diversity of its users, and adapts responses accordingly. Children were actively involved in the design and iterative improvement of the assistant, influencing both content and functionality. LAIban also explains its own role and limitations to children, supporting transparency and digital literacy. The solution remains in active use and has improved children’s autonomy, reduced repetitive questions for staff and enhanced inclusiveness through multilingual support. Its participatory design approach has strengthened trust and usability, while its controlled scope ensures reliability and age-appropriate interaction.

cases.source_description: Perceived safety is a critical factor influencing how citizens use and experience urban spaces, yet it is difficult to measure systematically over time. The AI Safety Perception Patterns project, developed by Senseable Stockholm Lab in collaboration with the City of Stockholm, addresses this challenge by creating a reproducible, data-driven approach to mapping perceived safety. Stakeholders include urban planners, architects, policymakers, and residents concerned with inclusive and secure public environments. The objective is to support long-term monitoring of perceived safety and evaluate the impact of urban interventions. The solution combines multiple data sources, including web-based surveys and urban data, to model safety perception across the city. Analytical methods identify patterns and generate spatial representations that are integrated into the city’s GIS platform. The approach is designed to be fully replicable, using the same code and methods year after year, enabling longitudinal analysis. The results provide planners with actionable insights into where and why safety perceptions vary, supporting evidence-based urban design. The project delivers a scalable framework for monitoring social sustainability and assessing the effectiveness of policy and design interventions over time.

In Tallinn, policymakers face complex choices around fleet caps, pricing, and incentives for shared mobility services, with limited visibility of their emissions outcomes. It supports more effective regulation of shared mobility, enhanced accountability of climate policies, and measurable reductions in transport-related emissions at city scale.

cases.source_description: Adolescents often face barriers to accessing mental health information and support, including stigma, lack of anonymity and limited service availability. Milli was developed in Finland to provide a confidential entry point for young people seeking information about mental health concerns. Stakeholders include adolescents, healthcare providers, psychologists and public health institutions. The objective is to improve early access to reliable information and guide users towards appropriate support when needed. Milli operates as a conversational assistant that responds to anonymous user queries and provides tailored information based on the user’s age group. It processes text inputs to identify themes and risk indicators, enabling differentiated responses and escalation in urgent situations. If signs of self-harm or crisis are detected, the system directs users to emergency services or trusted adults. Identifying information is automatically deleted, and users can request explanations about data use and system functioning. Milli currently handles between 500 and 1,200 queries per week. Reported impacts include improved accessibility to mental health information, reduced barriers to help-seeking and strengthened trust through transparency, privacy safeguards and user-centred design. Ongoing development focuses on fairness, accessibility and inclusive language.
