cases.task: Predicting Image Quality Degradation in Digital Radiology
cases.context: Azienda Provinciale per i Servizi Sanitari di Trento (APSS); Local Government; R&D health.; Italy
cases.implementation: The objectives of the project are two-fold: automating processing of radiological image, conducting images analysis using in-house software macros and bash script and discovering trends on an ongoing basis with the aim of detecting and fixing DR system performance problems before clinical operations are affected. The second step was developing a predictive model for assessing the degradation state of DR system using the automatically images-processed database.
cases.outcome: UNKNOWN; 원천의 기대효과와 별도 관측 성과는 구분해야 합니다.
cases.source_description: Optimal design of medical x-ray imaging systems is essential for delivering maximum image quality while minimizing radiation risk to patients. The performances of imaging devices could degrade over time. For this reason, quality control (QC) programs are in place in the health systems to verify that the clinical image quality remains acceptable over the years guaranteeing the diagnostic capability. The Medical Physicists (MP) is the responsible for the QC program, ensuring high standards in medical diagnostics and maintaining the reliability and safety of medical imaging. Currently MPs perform constancy quality checks on Digital Radiography (DR) system, acquiring radiological images on phantoms and extracting specific information (e.g., non-uniformity). The results are then compared to baseline values and any deviation is evaluated. In such scenario the QC tests only provide a “snapshot” of the system performance at a specific moment over time, until the next inspection or service event not allowing to anticipate malfunctions. The objectives of the project are two-fold: automating processing of radiological image, conducting images analysis using in-house software macros and bash script and discovering trends on an ongoing basis with the aim of detecting and fixing DR system performance problems before clinical operations are affected. Performance characteristics of 19 DR systems from 5 manufacturers have been analyzed over 10 years of monthly and annually QC test. Study has been focused on non-uniformity test, based on 4 image parameters and their tolerances: Local signal non-uniformity, Global Signal non-uniformity, Local Signal to Noise Ratio non-uniformity, Global Signal to Noise Ratio non-uniformity. 1825 images were analyzed running the in-house software macros and bash script on each image to calculate the 4 baseline metrics. The second step was developing a predictive model for assessing the degradation state of DR system using the automatically images-processed database. The model has to predict the pass/no-pass label for each image. The building process involves leveraging the combined strengths of Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and Long Short-Term Memory Networks (LSTMs) to analyze sequential radiological images from a images-processed database, grouping images into sequences for effective analysis akin to video sampling. By analyzing the sequential radiological images, this model aims to preemptively identify trends in equipment degradation. This capability is crucial for maintaining high standards in medical diagnostics, ensuring reliability and safety in medical imaging and patient care. The CNN architecture, based on ResNet-18, efficiently extracted spatial features, while the LSTM component, incorporating temporal data, was crucial in detecting patterns of degradation over time. Training and validation of the model were conducted on cloud based machine-learning platform, providing the necessary computational resources and scalability. Data augmentation strategies were implemented to balance the dataset, particularly addressing the scarcity of no-pass labels, thereby enhancing the model’s predictive capability. The model demonstrated a consistent training loss, indicating effective learning, and achieved a validation accuracy of 88.2% after 100 epochs, showcasing its ability to accurately classify the condition of DR systems. This level of accuracy reflects the model’s strong performance and its potential to generalize well to new data. In summary, in this project we proposed a new approach to QC test, starting from the availability of images and data stored through 10 years of activity. A predictive tool, based on AI-model was developed for non-uniformity QC test, with the result of decreasing the interval to detection of substandard performance. This type of approach, in which the primary goal is to preemptively identify trends in equipment degradation, can change the QC scenario.

MODUL-F addresses this challenge by enabling administrations at federal, state, and local levels to digitise internal specialist procedures quickly and consistently. As a result, administrations can digitise processes faster, lower development and maintenance costs, and improve consistency across jurisdictions. MODUL-F increases scalability, empowers non-technical staff, and accelerates digital transformation, delivering measurable efficiency gains and supporting sustainable modernisation of public administration.

cases.task: AI4Justice, Intelligent assistant to support judges in drafting sentences by locating texts of previous judgments and jurisprudence
cases.context: Centre de Telecomunicacions i Tecnologies de la Informació de la Generalitat de Catalunya (CTTI); Regional Government; Law courts; Spain
cases.outcome: UNKNOWN; 원천의 기대효과와 별도 관측 성과는 구분해야 합니다.
cases.source_description: The time dedicated by judges to search for precedents and legal foundations to write a sentence is high and an impediment to being more agile in the drafting of sentences, causing a high response time and a sense of slow justice. Currently, the location of paragraphs of interest of legal or procedural references, of any documentary information or the entirety of the magistrates' own judgments or resolutions previously issued, which may be applicable or reusable in the drafting of new judgments or resolutions, becomes a manual and costly process that causes magistrates to spend a lot of time locating, remembering, and reviewing previous judgments, relying on their memory, both for their content and the date they were issued. In Catalonia, the judge usually performs a manual search in the procedural management application for justice (eJusticia.cat), in the archive of the magistrate's own judgments, or through the Judicial Documentation Center (CENDOJ), depending on the General Council of the Judiciary (CGPJ), as well as other repositories or jurisprudential databases. The search is more or less effective depending on what the magistrate remembers at that time from similar cases or parts of an old judgment that may be applicable to the current one. The unmet need is to locate reusable information within judicial documents, such as sentences issued in any instance and jurisdiction, in order to speed up and facilitate the drafting of new sentences by judges. Currently, the location of paragraphs of interest (headings, legal foundations, dispositive part or judgment), legal or procedural references or the entirety of the judges' previous sentences, that are applicable or reusable in the drafting of new sentences, becomes a manual and costly process that causes judges to spend a lot of time locating, remembering and reviewing previous judgments, based on memory, both of their content and of the date they were issued. The solution proposed is an assistant to judges and magistrates that, by entering an open text or prompt, can quickly, accurately, and relatedly obtain all applicable historical information for the sentence being drafted. In the same way, the assistant must provide the applicable legal foundations and sentence draft for a better management of mass litigation cases with hundreds of very similar claims accumulate that has also similar resolutions. It is important that the judicial powers have the necessary resources to ensure agile and efficient justice, such as having digital tools that facilitate the location of reusable information from previous sentences and jurisprudence to draft new sentences.

cases.source_description: The Spanish Ministry of the Presidency, Justice and Parliamentary Relations launched the Virtual Desktop of Digital Immediation (EVID) in 2020 to facilitate remote judicial hearings while ensuring full legal guarantees. Courts needed a secure digital mechanism to conduct proceedings remotely without compromising procedural integrity, identity verification or evidentiary reliability. EVID provides a virtual environment enabling remote participation of judges, lawyers and citizens, integrating secure videoconferencing, document exchange and procedural management tools. To ensure non-repudiation, non-manipulation and non-impersonation, the system anchors key procedural events on a blockchain infrastructure. Cryptographic hashing and timestamping mechanisms record actions, documents and consents in an immutable distributed ledger, guaranteeing traceability and integrity throughout each hearing. Encrypted identity verification components support reliable participant authentication. By combining secure digital workflows with tamper-evident audit trails, EVID enhances accessibility, reduces travel and administrative burdens and supports environmentally sustainable justice services while maintaining procedural security and evidential robustness.

cases.source_description: Legal texts are essential to public life, yet their technical language often makes them difficult for citizens to understand, limiting access to rights, obligations, and public information. In Catalonia, the Entitat Autònoma del Diari Oficial i de Publicacions and the Legal Portal of Catalonia address this issue by making plain-language summaries of legal rules available to the public, with the aim of improving comprehension, accessibility, and transparency in the dissemination of current law. The objective is to reduce the barrier created by specialist legal drafting and to help citizens navigate Catalan legislation more confidently, while making clear that the official legal text remains the only authoritative source. The implementation uses generative AI to produce unofficial summaries of Catalan legal rules in plain language for publication on the Legal Portal. The initial rollout covered 44 rules in Catalan and 44 in Spanish, with the Generalitat stating that the approach would extend to the more than 14,000 legal provisions then in force; later reporting indicated that more than 16,000 summaries had been made available. The summaries are expressly presented as informational, not as legal advice. The impact includes easier public access to legal information, faster large-scale production of citizen-friendly summaries, and improved transparency and inclusiveness in legal communication, while supporting a more scalable model for making complex public information understandable.

cases.source_description: Accurate land registration is a longstanding challenge in Portugal, particularly for rural and mixed-use properties where ownership information may be incomplete, fragmented, or difficult to access. The BUPi initiative was created to modernise property management by improving the identification, georeferencing, and registration of land parcels, while also reducing regional disparities in access to information and supporting better territory management. The objective is to make property data more accessible and reliable, increase transparency, and provide a stronger evidence base for land governance, public planning, and sustainable development. The implementation combines the BUPi digital platform with machine-learning techniques that support property identification, anomaly detection, land-use classification, and faster processing of geospatial and registry-related information. At a conceptual level, the system links administrative property records with georeferenced parcel data and analytical tools so that land can be identified more precisely and processed more efficiently. Public reporting on the programme notes the scale of the task, with more than eight million land records still requiring georeferencing during the expansion phase, and highlights the use of advanced technologies to accelerate knowledge about the territory. The impact includes improved data quality, quicker land-registration processes, stronger transparency, and better support for strategic decision-making, creating a more scalable and accurate basis for understanding and managing Portuguese territory.

cases.source_description: Flood risk management requires rapid and accurate assessment of potential river overflows, yet traditional hydraulic models can be computationally intensive and slow to update. This initiative explores the feasibility of using advanced predictive algorithms to simulate flood risks more efficiently by combining flow measurements with geospatial datasets. The proof of concept initially focused on the Tordera river basin, integrating hydrological data, terrain models and environmental indicators into a unified analytical framework. The system aims to complement conventional modelling approaches by providing faster decision-support outputs during emergency planning. Early results indicate improved computational efficiency and enhanced situational awareness. The approach supports agile emergency response, better resource allocation and scalable application to additional river basins, strengthening resilience to extreme weather events.

cases.source_description: Timely transport of biological samples between healthcare facilities is critical for diagnostic accuracy and patient care, yet conventional road transport can be slow and subject to variability. This pilot project in the Girona health region evaluated a drone-based logistics route connecting the Hospital of Olot and the Vall d’en Bas primary care centre. The system conducted recurrent flights transporting blood and urine samples to the hospital and delivering medical equipment in return. Flight operations were assessed for cost, reliability and sample integrity compared with road transport. Results showed a reduction in transport time from 20 minutes by road to 7 minutes by drone, with improved sample quality due to reduced agitation and shorter exposure duration. The solution also demonstrated increased scheduling flexibility and responsiveness for urgent deliveries. The pilot highlights the potential of unmanned aerial logistics to enhance efficiency, reliability and quality in regional healthcare supply chains.

In Barcelona, the Service of the Official Provincial Gazette and Official Documentation and Publications sought to improve the efficiency and transparency of this process by automating the drafting of short summaries for official notices published in the provincial gazette. The objective is to reduce manual effort for both submitters and staff, speed up publication processing, and improve the accessibility of official information for users of the gazette and related public-information services. The impact includes faster summary production, lower workload, improved consistency, and better scalability as publication volumes grow. It also supports transparency by making official content easier to understand and reuse within public-information services.

ALT-EDIC addresses this challenge by creating a common European infrastructure for language technologies, with a particular focus on strengthening the foundations for large language models while preserving linguistic diversity and cultural richness. The objective is to improve Europe’s competitiveness, expand the availability of European language data, and support interoperable language-technology capacity across participating states. The implementation uses the European Digital Infrastructure Consortium model, allowing member states to pool funding and resources in a coordinated structure. Official ALT-EDIC and related language-data-space materials describe activities including linguistic-data production and curation, evaluation and normalisation support, adaptation of models to user needs, and advice to the wider ecosystem. The impact includes stronger shared infrastructure, more reusable multilingual resources, and better conditions for developing European language technologies at scale. It also creates long-term strategic value by supporting common standards, reducing fragmentation, and reinforcing Europe’s capacity to develop language AI aligned with its regulatory, linguistic, and public-interest goals.

The LDT CitiVERSE EDIC initiative was created to link existing local digital twins and form the foundation of a broader European CitiVERSE, enabling more coordinated development of data-driven and simulation-based tools for urban policy and citizen interaction. The objective is to strengthen cooperation between participating countries, improve the use of digital twins in smart-city policy, and support new forms of simulation and engagement around issues such as traffic, congestion, air quality, and decarbonisation. The impact lies in stronger interoperability between local digital twins, greater capacity for collaborative urban innovation, and more scalable smart-city services across Europe, creating both public-sector efficiency gains and better-informed citizen participation.

In Sweden, the Svea initiative was created as a joint effort between authorities, municipalities, regions, and industry, coordinated by AI Sweden, to develop shared capability rather than fragmented local solutions. The objective is to support public employees in routine text tasks, free time for more interpersonal and creative work, and establish the conditions for national cooperation on shared AI solutions in the public sector. The implementation is organised in phases, beginning with data generation, change management, use-case identification, and prototype development, and continuing with large-scale testing and evaluation. Svea itself is a web-based chat assistant built on open-source, model-agnostic architecture running on Swedish infrastructure; it can already answer organisation-specific questions, summarise documents, extract information, and rewrite text in easy-to-read Swedish. AI Sweden states that participating organisations collectively spent 2,500 hours annotating training data for the assistant. The impact includes stronger reuse of data and effort across institutions, improved scalability of AI adoption, and better productivity in text-heavy public work, while helping organisations prepare for labour shortages and rising service demand.

Because they have the potential to create highly realistic content, they can also pose a threat to democracies through the creation and circulation of deepfakes, which spread false information and undermine trust. cases.source_description: TrustLLM is a Horizon Europe project designed to develop open, trustworthy and sustainable large language models for European languages, with an initial focus on Germanic languages and underrepresented linguistic communities. The strategic problem is that Europe needs language-model infrastructure that is transparent, reliable, energy-conscious and less dependent on closed non-European systems. The implementation will develop large language models trained on substantial multilingual European text resources, while addressing reliability, bias, hallucination, sustainability and accessibility. TrustLLM is explicitly positioned as a response to the need for reliable generative models and mitigation of risks such as hallucinations and bias.

The project won the “Supporting the preparation of initiative acts” area in a call promoted by the Italian Chamber of Deputies, which selected three winning projects from 28 proposals. Its three prototypes are designed to help users explore regulatory sources, simplify and summarise amendments, and measure the alignment between bills and the policies they intend to pursue. The implementation combines generative AI, legal informatics, regulatory-source analysis, summarisation and legislative-support functions. The consortium is coordinated by Alma Mater Studiorum – University of Bologna / ALMA-AI and includes CNR-Igsg with Aptus.AI, Luiss Guido Carli University with Asimov AI, the University of Turin and the University of Verona. The expected impact is more efficient legislative preparation, improved access to regulatory context, clearer amendment analysis and stronger evidence on whether proposed bills match policy goals. Its value depends on careful human oversight and constitutional safeguards in parliamentary processes.

cases.source_description: The ALEIA digital assistant responds to the difficulty citizens face when trying to identify the regional aid schemes for which they may be eligible. Île-de-France has around 350 aid schemes, and this breadth of provision can make access confusing for residents, associations or other potential beneficiaries. The Regional Council therefore sought a tool that could guide users through the available support landscape and provide clear answers based on the region’s own documentation. Developed by the start-up Aleia, the solution combines a search engine and a conversational agent. It uses the French Mistral language model to formulate responses grounded in the region’s corpus of documents, while data are hosted in France and answers are continuously improved. The system is also designed to recognise when a user asks about support that falls outside the region’s responsibilities and to respond negatively rather than providing irrelevant guidance. Conceptually, the assistant combines document retrieval, generative language modelling, conversational interaction, controlled knowledge sources and French-hosted data infrastructure. The expected impact is simpler access to regional support, reduced user confusion, more efficient routing towards relevant schemes and less pressure on administrative staff handling repetitive eligibility questions. By linking conversational access with an official documentary corpus, the system can improve transparency and make regional aid more navigable.

The research challenge is that developing new materials for energy storage, industry, food and plastics can be slow, costly and experimentally intensive, while sustainability transitions require faster discovery of safer and lower-impact alternatives. By applying generative methods to molecules rather than text, the initiative can support innovation in sectors where material performance and environmental impact are central.

The expected impact is stronger technological coverage for Finnish, improved resources for researchers and developers, and reduced dependence on multilingual systems that may underperform for smaller language communities. By combining university expertise, national library resources and EU funding, the project contributes to Europe’s capacity for language-specific AI development.

cases.source_description: DepuChat proposes a public chatbot to make information on the Italian Chamber of Deputies more accessible, usable and transparent for citizens. The democratic problem is that parliamentary information is often technically complex, dispersed across institutional documents and difficult for non-specialist users to interpret. The project, developed by the IDEAS Research Centre at Roma Tre University in collaboration with the Department of Legal Sciences at the University of Florence, aims to bring citizens closer to institutions by allowing them to query information on the Chamber, its bodies and procedures, individual MPs, and political positions expressed by MPs and the Government. The implementation uses generative AI to create a conversational and potentially graphical interface over parliamentary data. Conceptually, the system combines institutional data retrieval, natural-language interaction, summarisation and visual presentation to help users explore parliamentary activity more easily. The expected impact is improved transparency, broader civic access to legislative information and stronger democratic engagement. The project was announced in July 2024 as a winner of the Chamber of Deputies’ call for ideas, so its current form appears to be a selected proposal or prototype rather than a fully operational public service.

cases.source_description: France’s experiment on generative artificial intelligence in public services was launched to assess how such tools could support civil servants in responding to users more efficiently. The administrative problem is that public agents handle large numbers of online opinions, comments and procedural interactions, many of which require clear written replies but can be repetitive and time-consuming. The initiative involved 1,000 volunteer agents equipped with a tool to help draft responses to users during online procedures, while preserving a human-in-the-loop model: agents supervise, modify and approve responses before they are sent. The experiment is led by the Interministerial Directorate for Public Transformation and the Interministerial Digital Directorate, with a solution provided by Allobrain. The system uses generative language technology to propose draft responses based on anonymised data, meaning confidentiality is intended to be preserved. The model supports response writing rather than replacing the public official, and the approach is framed as a way to save time on specific tasks while strengthening human contact between public services and citizens. The planned extension to France services counters would broaden the support to agents assisting users face to face. The expected impact is faster response preparation, reduced administrative burden, improved consistency in written replies and more time for personalised support where human judgement is most valuable.

cases.source_description: Legislab is designed to support analysis of the Italian legislative system and assist parliamentary offices in monitoring legal quality. The institutional problem is that new legislative proposals must be assessed against a large and continuously evolving corpus of laws, from the Constitution onwards, making it difficult to identify relevant precedents, overlaps, inconsistencies or references. The project, developed by the Politecnico di Milano and the Istituto Einaudi, is intended for the offices of the Chamber of Deputies and combines a database of Italian laws with analytical and generative functions. Its implementation allows users to input a topic or draft title and receive relevant articles and laws that may need to be considered. The system is deliberately constrained to reduce hallucination risks: it relies on existing legal data, objective information and linguistic metrics from scientific literature rather than generating free-form legal text. The expected impact is stronger legislative quality monitoring, faster identification of relevant legal sources and better support for expert legislative drafting, while preserving the role of legal professionals and parliamentarians in writing the law.

The model was introduced by researchers at the Sant’Anna School of Advanced Studies to improve performance on downstream legal NLP tasks where generic Italian BERT models lose accuracy. cases.context: https://predictice.com/; Private sector; R&D public order and safety.; France
cases.implementation: Predictice uses generative language technology to make legal research more efficient by producing automatic summaries of court decisions. The implementation applies GPT-3 and ChatGPT-style language-model capabilities to the task of document synthesis.

cases.source_description: Predictice uses generative language technology to make legal research more efficient by producing automatic summaries of court decisions. The practical challenge for legal professionals is that judicial documents can be long, technical and time-consuming to read, while some decisions may prove irrelevant only after several minutes of review. Predictice provides access to a large legal corpus of around 26 million documents, including court decisions, and aims to help users assess relevance more quickly. The implementation applies GPT-3 and ChatGPT-style language-model capabilities to the task of document synthesis. Rather than asking the model to produce legal advice, the tool focuses on summarising existing decisions, a use case considered more reliable by the Predictice team than generating autonomous legal answers. Conceptually, the system combines large-scale legal-document retrieval, generative summarisation, natural language processing and user-facing legal search functions. The expected impact is faster review of case law, reduced time spent on irrelevant documents, improved productivity for lawyers and legal researchers, and easier navigation of large legal databases. By providing concise summaries of lengthy decisions, Predictice can support legal professionals in prioritising which documents deserve closer reading. However, because legal interpretation remains sensitive, summaries should be treated as decision-support outputs and checked against the original court text.

cases.source_description: Henchman supports legal professionals in drafting and improving contract clauses by extending the range of available drafting options during contract preparation. The practical challenge in legal work is that lawyers frequently need to adapt existing clauses to specific transactional contexts, client preferences or drafting conventions, while maintaining consistency, precision and speed. The platform is therefore relevant to law firms, in-house legal teams, contract managers and clients relying on efficient document production. Its objective is to make contract drafting more agile by helping users refine language, adjust wording and introduce clause-level variations without starting from scratch. The implementation uses GPT-3.5 to assist with targeted drafting operations, such as changing a clause from singular to plural or adding a new element to an existing provision. Conceptually, the system combines large language model functionality with contract-drafting workflows, allowing users to generate or modify text within a controlled legal-document environment. The expected impact is faster clause adaptation, reduced repetitive editing, improved consistency across contract drafts and greater productivity for legal teams. By supporting incremental drafting rather than replacing legal judgement, the tool can help professionals focus on negotiation strategy, legal risk and client-specific tailoring. Its value depends on appropriate human review, since AI-generated legal text must be checked for accuracy, enforceability and alignment with the intended contractual position.

cases.source_description: Sofia faces persistent air pollution and traffic congestion, particularly in rapidly developing neighbourhoods with limited public transport coverage. The INNOAIR project aimed to improve urban mobility and air quality by piloting greener, on-demand public transport services in the districts of Manastirski Livadi and Buxton. Coordinated by the Municipality of Sofia and managed by the Sofia Development Association, the initiative tested five electric minibuses with a capacity of 20 passengers each during a one-year trial starting in 2023. Advanced routing algorithms were used to determine optimal service routes based on municipal datasets, including registered vehicles, public facilities and demographic information, complemented by data gathered through community engagement and urban walks. While routes remained fixed once defined, departure times operated on a demand-responsive basis. The pilot provided residents with alternatives to private car use, contributing to reduced traffic volumes and lower emissions. The project demonstrated improved accessibility, enhanced user satisfaction and measurable environmental benefits, supporting scalable deployment of intelligent, low-emission mobility services.

The impact includes improved visibility of street health, more informed prioritisation of maintenance activity, and stronger evidence for infrastructure decisions. It also demonstrates a scalable model for combining citizen participation with digital monitoring to improve local public services.

cases.source_description: For blind and visually impaired people, digital images often remain difficult to access in a meaningful way, because standard image analysis tools are typically designed around the assumptions and preferences of sighted users. This creates a gap between what current systems can technically describe and what users actually need in order to form an accurate and useful mental representation of visual content. The objective of this use case is to improve accessibility by developing image interpretation tools tailored to the needs, expectations, and sensory strategies of blind and visually impaired users, with these users involved directly as co-designers and evaluators. The system concept therefore links multimodal models with tactile interfaces and user-centred evaluation methods. The anticipated results include more relevant and nuanced image descriptions, improved usability and trust, and a more inclusive digital experience. More broadly, the project supports accessible design innovation, stronger user adoption, and better alignment between emerging image technologies and real user needs.

The expected impact includes stronger interdisciplinary capability, improved methods for safer transport systems, and a more scalable pipeline of expertise. It also creates long-term value through knowledge transfer, international collaboration, and more reliable foundations for future road safety innovation.

cases.source_description: Civil servants work with large volumes of briefings, letters, speeches, meeting minutes, and other documents, and much of their time can be absorbed by locating key information, summarising content, and drafting routine material. Redbox was created inside the UK government to address this administrative burden by giving officials a secure generative AI tool for document interaction and general workplace tasks. The objective was to improve productivity, reduce time spent on repetitive document handling, and help staff engage more efficiently with complex written material so they could focus more on higher-value work. The implementation, developed by the Incubator for AI, provided a chat-based and document-oriented assistant that could summarise files, answer questions about their contents, and support drafting and exploration of official material, including at OFFICIAL-SENSITIVE level. Public information from i.AI states that Redbox was rolled out to more than 6,000 users and used across over 150,000 chats and 1.3 million messages. At a conceptual level, the tool combined secure access to large language models with document-processing workflows tailored to government use. The impact included faster information handling, lower administrative effort, and valuable learning for future public-sector AI deployment, even though the project was later sunset as comparable enterprise tools became more widely available in government.

cases.source_description: Social and fiscal rules are often complex, difficult to compare, and hard for both citizens and administrations to apply consistently without digital support. OpenFisca addresses this by turning legal and policy rules into executable code that can be reused to simulate entitlements, compare scenarios, and power public-facing services such as benefit calculators. The objective is to create a common, computable representation of rules so that governments, researchers, developers, and civil society can debate, test, and deliver social and fiscal policy more transparently. The implementation uses the open-source OpenFisca framework, which models taxes and benefits through formal variables, entities, and rule logic that can be exposed through APIs and reused in services such as Mes Aides and Aides Jeunes. The current youth-oriented simulator publicly states that it can estimate eligibility for more than 1,060 aids in a few clicks, while beta.gouv.fr describes OpenFisca as a leading practical implementation of the Rules as Code movement used in multiple countries. At a conceptual level, the solution combines legal modelling, microsimulation, and software engineering to produce machine-executable policy logic. The impact includes faster and more transparent eligibility estimation, easier reuse across public services, and a scalable foundation for policy simulation, digital entitlement tools, and evidence-based reform analysis.

General-purpose language models often struggle in this context because they are not sufficiently exposed to specialised legal corpora or evaluated against tasks that reflect genuine legal knowledge. The aim of this use case is to strengthen the development and assessment of legal language models by providing resources that better capture the linguistic and conceptual demands of legal work in a multinational setting. At a conceptual level, the project examines how pre-training objectives, model size, and training data influence performance, comparing newly trained and existing models on legal language understanding tasks. The approach supports domain-specific model development grounded in structured evaluation rather than generic performance measures alone. The results show that performance depends strongly on both the data used for pre-training and the scale of the model, highlighting the value of specialised legal resources. The broader impact lies in enabling more reliable legal text processing, improving the quality of downstream legal applications, and supporting more robust, scalable development of language technologies for multilingual legal environments.

Eastnets’ SafeWatch Screening ChainFeed aims to improve how watchlists are distributed and updated so that banks can rely on consistent, verifiable, near-real-time data feeds. Conceptually, it replaces or augments batch-based processes with a ledger-backed “chain feed” where authorised participants can verify that they are operating on the latest approved version, and where update events can be cryptographically validated end-to-end. Integration focuses on connecting the ledger layer to existing screening systems via APIs and automated workflows so institutions receive updates without manual intervention. Expected impacts include reduced operational workload, fewer update errors, stronger resilience against tampering, improved audit readiness, and faster compliance response—supported by participation in the European Blockchain Sandbox to address regulatory expectations for critical compliance infrastructure.

cases.source_description: GPT@JRC was developed inside the European Commission’s Joint Research Centre to give staff a secure environment for experimenting with large language models in science-for-policy work. The operational challenge is that JRC staff routinely handle complex knowledge tasks, including summarising evidence, translating material, drafting briefings, proofreading, classification, sentiment analysis and preparing analytical inputs for policy processes. Using external generative tools can create confidentiality and compliance risks, particularly where internal documents or sensitive policy material are involved. GPT@JRC therefore provides controlled access to language-model capabilities within a secure platform. The implementation allows JRC staff to use LLMs for day-to-day productivity tasks and to test how generative functions can be embedded into existing tools and workflows through automated access and processing. Conceptually, the platform combines secure model access, experimentation facilities, internal governance, prompt-based interaction and potential integration with other JRC systems. The expected impact is improved productivity, faster document handling, enhanced quality of drafts and summaries, and better understanding of how generative AI can support science-for-policy work. It also served as an important precursor to broader Commission-level tools, helping the institution test safe adoption patterns before wider deployment.

cases.source_description: AI4POL is a Horizon Europe project designed to support regulators and policymakers in governing artificial intelligence and digital services more effectively. A central focus is consumer protection, particularly whether people understand online-contract information or simply accept long and technical texts without meaningful comprehension. The project aims to generate evidence on how regulatory measures are perceived, how companies and policymakers can receive useful feedback, and how the impact of rules in areas such as digital services and AI can be improved. Its implementation combines AI tools, policy research, human-centred analysis and stakeholder engagement. AI systems may help summarise complex legal or contractual information in simpler language, while the broader project develops tools, insights and frameworks aligned with European values, human rights and citizens’ needs. The consortium is led by Tilburg University and includes TUM and other research partners, with an advisory board involving regulators, policymakers, consumer-protection bodies, civil-society organisations and AI firms. The expected impact is stronger evidence for regulation, better consumer understanding and more effective oversight of AI and digital markets.

cases.problem: Researchers, policymakers and citizens often face difficulties navigating millions of multilingual legislative documents and parliamentary records.
cases.task: EU Parliament archive access with Claude.AI
cases.context: European Parliament; European Institution/Agency; General public services n.e.c.; European Union
cases.implementation: Archibot, built using Claude via Amazon Bedrock, provides a conversational interface enabling users to search, retrieve and interpret archival material rapidly.
cases.outcome: UNKNOWN; 원천의 기대효과와 별도 관측 성과는 구분해야 합니다.
cases.source_description: The European Parliament introduced “Ask the EP Archives”, known as Archibot, to improve access to its extensive historical archives. Researchers, policymakers and citizens often face difficulties navigating millions of multilingual legislative documents and parliamentary records. Archibot, built using Claude via Amazon Bedrock, provides a conversational interface enabling users to search, retrieve and interpret archival material rapidly. The system processes natural language queries, matches them to indexed archive content and generates contextualised responses, drawing from over 2.1 million official documents. Advanced language models support multilingual understanding and summarisation of complex legislative texts. The deployment has reduced document search time by approximately 80 per cent, increased customer satisfaction by around 60 per cent and expanded monthly query capacity tenfold. By streamlining discovery and interpretation of archival content, Archibot enhances transparency, public engagement and institutional knowledge management within the European Parliament.

cases.source_description: Gladsaxe Municipality launched GladGPT to provide municipal employees with an internal text and information assistant for everyday administrative work. The organisational challenge was to help staff navigate municipal information more quickly, draft texts more efficiently and access relevant internal knowledge without relying on dispersed intranet searches or repeated enquiries. The main stakeholders include Gladsaxe Municipality, municipal employees, IT and governance teams, and residents who may indirectly benefit from faster administrative work. Introduced in 2023, the chatbot is based on OpenAI ChatGPT-4 technology and operates in a closed environment. It is trained on all content from Gladsaxe’s intranet and selected parts of the municipality’s website, allowing employees to ask questions, locate information and generate draft texts within a municipal context. Conceptually, the system combines a large language model, internal knowledge retrieval, secure deployment arrangements and a conversational interface adapted to public-sector use. The expected impact is improved employee productivity, faster access to organisational information, more efficient drafting of routine texts and reduced time spent searching internal resources. By using a closed environment, the municipality seeks to benefit from generative AI while limiting exposure of internal data. The tool’s value remains linked to appropriate staff guidance, quality control and human review of generated content, particularly where outputs relate to citizens or administrative decisions.

cases.task: LATXA: a Basque language LLM
cases.context: HiTZ; Academic-Research; General services.; Spain
cases.implementation: The LATXA family consists of base transformer-based LLMs trained on curated Basque corpora using large-scale self-supervised learning.
cases.outcome: UNKNOWN; 원천의 기대효과와 별도 관측 성과는 구분해야 합니다.
cases.source_description: The Basque language, as a low-resource European language, faces structural disadvantages in the development of advanced natural language processing tools, limiting digital inclusion and the availability of high-quality language technologies for public services, education and industry. Existing large language models are predominantly trained on high-resource languages, constraining their effectiveness in Basque and reducing linguistic sovereignty. Stakeholders include language technology researchers, public institutions, educational bodies and technology developers working in the Basque ecosystem. The objective of the LATXA project is to develop foundational large language models specifically pre-trained for Basque, providing a robust technical base for downstream applications rather than a direct-to-consumer chatbot. The LATXA family consists of base transformer-based LLMs trained on curated Basque corpora using large-scale self-supervised learning. Model development was conducted on in-house GPU infrastructure, with final large-scale training executed on the Leonardo supercomputer at CINECA under the EuroHPC Joint Undertaking. These open models are released for expert users who can integrate or fine-tune them for task-specific applications. Expected impacts include strengthened digital presence of Basque, enhanced research capacity, support for public-sector language tools and a scalable foundation for future instruction-tuned and domain-adapted systems.

cases.problem: Digital services in Web3 and decentralised finance require trustworthy user authentication mechanisms, yet many current approaches struggle to balance privacy, regulatory compliance, and usability.
cases.task: Decentralised and Secure Approach to User Authentication
cases.context: European Commission; European Institution/Agency; R&D general public services.; Germany
cases.implementation: The purpose of this use case is to provide a secure identity solution that enables verified participation in decentralised ecosystems while preserving privacy and supporting compliance requirements. At a conceptual level, the system combines automated and human-assisted identity verification with decentralised token issuance, storing the resulting credential in the user’s wallet for use in on-chain interactions.
cases.outcome: UNKNOWN; 원천의 기대효과와 별도 관측 성과는 구분해야 합니다.
cases.source_description: Digital services in Web3 and decentralised finance require trustworthy user authentication mechanisms, yet many current approaches struggle to balance privacy, regulatory compliance, and usability. Service providers need ways to verify that users are legitimate without exposing unnecessary personal data, while regulators and enforcement authorities require appropriate safeguards for accountability in cases of fraud or illicit activity. The purpose of this use case is to provide a secure identity solution that enables verified participation in decentralised ecosystems while preserving privacy and supporting compliance requirements. The implementation is based on a Web3 identification solution developed by a consortium including the IOTA Foundation and other partners, and tested within the European Blockchain Sandbox. At a conceptual level, the system combines automated and human-assisted identity verification with decentralised token issuance, storing the resulting credential in the user’s wallet for use in on-chain interactions. The token allows applications to distinguish verified from unverified users without routinely revealing personal information, while maintaining controlled mechanisms for revocation or authorised disclosure. The impact includes stronger trust in Web3 transactions, reduced onboarding friction for compliant services, and improved privacy compared with conventional identification methods. It also supports scalability for regulated decentralised applications, lowers compliance risk, and creates value by enabling more secure and interoperable digital identity management.

cases.problem: Traditional disbursement mechanisms can make it difficult to control how money is spent, whether it reaches the intended recipients, and whether it produces the desired economic or social effect. The impact includes lower administrative burden, reduced fraud and misuse, and improved traceability of public or organisational spending.
cases.task: Purpose Bound Money
cases.context: European Commission; European Institution/Agency; R&D economic affairs; Netherlands
cases.implementation: The objective of this use case is to provide a more secure and efficient way to distribute earmarked funds so that money is spent only for approved purposes, by approved recipients, within defined limits and timeframes. The implementation is based on a blockchain-enabled model known as Purpose Bound Money, developed and deployed through the MultiKnip project and examined within the European Blockchain Sandbox.
cases.outcome: UNKNOWN; 원천의 기대효과와 별도 관측 성과는 구분해야 합니다.
cases.source_description: Public authorities and organisations distributing subsidies, grants, and allocated budgets often face operational problems linked to fraud, misuse, unused funds, and heavy administrative processes. Traditional disbursement mechanisms can make it difficult to control how money is spent, whether it reaches the intended recipients, and whether it produces the desired economic or social effect. The objective of this use case is to provide a more secure and efficient way to distribute earmarked funds so that money is spent only for approved purposes, by approved recipients, within defined limits and timeframes. The implementation is based on a blockchain-enabled model known as Purpose Bound Money, developed and deployed through the MultiKnip project and examined within the European Blockchain Sandbox. At a conceptual level, the system allows the issuer to define rules governing who receives funds, how much can be spent, where they may be used, for what purpose, and until when. Payments are then settled only for actual use at approved retailers, linking programmable controls with accountable fund distribution. The impact includes lower administrative burden, reduced fraud and misuse, and improved traceability of public or organisational spending. Additional value comes from more efficient subsidy delivery, better control over outcomes, and positive local economic effects through targeted spending within approved ecosystems.

cases.task: Groningen Werkt Slim
cases.context: Municipality of Groningen and the Province of Groningen; Local Government; Environmental protection n.e.c.; Netherlands
cases.implementation: The objective of this use case is therefore to make targeted sustainability support easier to distribute, easier to use, and easier to control, while encouraging uptake of energy-saving measures and allowing future expansion into other green initiatives. The implementation uses MultiKnip, a blockchain-based wallet for purpose-bound tokens built on IOTA technology, through which Groningen issues €300 in digital funds to eligible SMEs via the Groningen Werkt Slim app.
cases.outcome: UNKNOWN; 원천의 기대효과와 별도 관측 성과는 구분해야 합니다.
cases.source_description: In Groningen, small and medium-sized enterprises often face practical barriers when trying to invest in energy-efficiency improvements, particularly where modest subsidy schemes must be distributed quickly, spent only on approved purposes, and linked to local suppliers. The challenge is to ensure that public support reaches the intended businesses, is used for eligible products and services, and creates measurable local value without adding excessive administrative effort for the municipality, retailers, or beneficiaries. The objective of this use case is therefore to make targeted sustainability support easier to distribute, easier to use, and easier to control, while encouraging uptake of energy-saving measures and allowing future expansion into other green initiatives. The implementation uses MultiKnip, a blockchain-based wallet for purpose-bound tokens built on IOTA technology, through which Groningen issues €300 in digital funds to eligible SMEs via the Groningen Werkt Slim app. These tokens can be spent only on approved energy-saving products and services, such as purchases at regional hardware stores and work carried out by “energy-fixers”, with QR-code-based transactions linking users, retailers, and municipal reimbursement flows. The impact includes lower administrative burden, reduced misuse, faster and more traceable subsidy distribution, and stronger local economic participation. It also creates a scalable foundation for extending controlled funding to further measures such as green roofs and electric vehicle charging infrastructure.

cases.task: Electronic voting systems by employing decentralized identities
cases.context: European Commission; European Institution/Agency; R&D general public services.; Greece
cases.implementation: The objective of this use case is to create a citizen-centred e-voting framework that increases trust, protects privacy, and broadens participation in public consultations and governance processes. cases.source_description: Electronic voting continues to face unresolved challenges around voter anonymity, ballot secrecy, trusted counting, and verifiability, all of which are essential if digital participation is to be accepted in public decision-making. At the same time, public bodies need voting systems that are accessible, compliant with digital identity and data-protection rules, and inclusive for citizens who may struggle with traditional in-person processes. The objective of this use case is to create a citizen-centred e-voting framework that increases trust, protects privacy, and broadens participation in public consultations and governance processes. The implementation is represented by TREVO, which combines decentralised identifiers, verifiable credentials, and zero-knowledge proofs to authenticate and authorise voters while preserving anonymity and secrecy. A mobile wallet acts as the core interface, enabling interoperable authentication based on trusted public-sector anchors and supporting real use cases in the Greek municipality of Trikala. The solution is designed around end-user co-creation, linking identity credentials, privacy-preserving cryptographic methods, and voting workflows in a conceptually integrated system aligned with EU guidance on digital identity and data protection. The expected results include stronger voter trust, more secure and auditable digital ballots, and improved accessibility for elderly, disabled, and remote users. It also offers lower process costs, reduced paperwork and travel, and better scalability for future digital participation services.

cases.source_description: Public-service media organisations need trustworthy, rights-aware ways to engage with generative AI, especially where questions of data use, attribution, verification, and audience trust directly affect their core mission. Within the Trusted European Media Data Space, the GenerativeAI @ TEMS activity addresses this by creating a framework for discussion and collaboration around the use of AI in media-data environments, with the EBU treating AI as a strategic priority. The objective is to help media actors adopt generative AI responsibly, protect rights and provenance, and ensure that high-quality media data can support trustworthy AI systems. The implementation is not a single chatbot or model, but a coordinated initiative involving publications, stakeholder engagement, data-space development, and collaboration with companies such as Mistral. Recent TEMS and EBU materials show that the topic remains active in 2025, including discussion of AI governance priorities and the role of TEMS as an enabler of trusted, rights-cleared media content for AI-related use cases. The impact lies in shaping governance, data access, and collaboration conditions for future AI deployment in public-service media, creating strategic value through standards, interoperability, and trusted data practices rather than through one direct end-user service.

cases.problem: Freelance work is often coordinated through fragmented platforms, informal governance, or conventional management structures that can increase transaction costs, create ambiguity over rules and payments, and weaken trust between contributors.
cases.task: Decentralised Autonomous Organisation for freelance work
cases.context: European Commission; European Institution/Agency; General economic, commercial and labour affair; Spain
cases.implementation: The purpose of this use case is to provide a more efficient and trust-based operating model for freelance collaboration in Web3 settings, where work, reputation, and funding can be coordinated through programmable rules. The implementation is embodied in MINOS, a platform that operates as a decentralised autonomous organisation and uses blockchain-based code to define and enforce organisational rules.

cases.source_description: Freelance work is often coordinated through fragmented platforms, informal governance, or conventional management structures that can increase transaction costs, create ambiguity over rules and payments, and weaken trust between contributors. In decentralised digital work environments, there is a need for new organisational models that allow teams to manage resources, responsibilities, and incentives transparently without relying on a fixed management hierarchy. The purpose of this use case is to provide a more efficient and trust-based operating model for freelance collaboration in Web3 settings, where work, reputation, and funding can be coordinated through programmable rules. The implementation is embodied in MINOS, a platform that operates as a decentralised autonomous organisation and uses blockchain-based code to define and enforce organisational rules. Its architecture is structured around domains and permissions, allowing teams, projects, or departments to organise work and control access to functions, while funding pots and expenditure units manage token-based payments. In parallel, a domain-specific reputation mechanism records the value of contributions over time, supports merit-based decision-making, and aligns reward distribution with recent participation. The impact includes lower coordination costs, stronger transparency in resource allocation, and more reliable collaboration across distributed freelance networks. It also improves organisational flexibility, supports scalable governance, and enables a more structured and incentive-compatible approach to digital work.

cases.source_description: Across Europe, smaller bond and equity issuances, especially those linked to SMEs and renewable-energy projects, often struggle to attract a broad investor base because traditional securities processes are costly, fragmented, and difficult to scale. A key challenge is to create an infrastructure that connects issuance, registration, custody, trading, and settlement more efficiently while remaining compatible with regulatory requirements and existing market structures. The objective of this use case is to reduce friction in capital formation and help address funding gaps by making tokenised securities easier to issue, manage, and trade. The implementation is delivered through NYALA’s Digital Asset Platform, built on the public Polygon PoS chain, which supports the minting, distribution, registration, and custody of tokenised securities while linking on-chain and off-chain ownership information. The platform functions conceptually as a back-end engine connecting investment platforms into a broader trading ecosystem under the DLT Pilot Regime, with off-chain trading through an existing multilateral trading facility and on-chain settlement infrastructure. It also integrates an e-money token for delivery-versus-payment and automated dividend distribution. The impact includes improved efficiency and transparency across the securities value chain, broader investor access to previously sub-scale instruments, and stronger scalability for digital capital markets. It also offers lower operational friction, faster settlement, and greater potential to mobilise financing for growth-oriented and sustainability-linked projects.

cases.task: Verifiable Web for AI
cases.context: European Commission; European Institution/Agency; R&D economic affairs; Slovenia
cases.implementation: The goal of this use case is to create a more trustworthy foundation for AI by making source information discoverable, verifiable, and attributable across decentralised environments. The technology is intended for a wide spectrum of uses, including industry, infrastructure, science, and misinformation-related applications, and conceptually integrates decentralised data publishing, knowledge graph structuring, and AI retrieval workflows.

cases.source_description: Many AI systems rely on external information sources that may be inaccurate, manipulated, or impossible to verify, creating risks around hallucinations, bias, provenance, and misuse of data. For public bodies, infrastructure operators, and large organisations, this weakens trust in generated outputs and limits the safe deployment of AI in knowledge-intensive environments where factual grounding and ownership of information matter. The goal of this use case is to create a more trustworthy foundation for AI by making source information discoverable, verifiable, and attributable across decentralised environments. The implementation is based on OriginTrail’s Decentralized Knowledge Graph, a permissionless network operating above a blockchain layer and designed to provide a trusted knowledge foundation for AI applications. Within this architecture, decentralised retrieval-augmented generation extends conventional RAG by organising external knowledge in a structured graph and associating it with provenance and ownership signals, thereby supporting neuro-symbolic decentralised AI. The technology is intended for a wide spectrum of uses, including industry, infrastructure, science, and misinformation-related applications, and conceptually integrates decentralised data publishing, knowledge graph structuring, and AI retrieval workflows. The impact includes more reliable generated content, stronger resistance to manipulation, and improved transparency about where information comes from. It also supports scalable knowledge sharing, incentivises data ownership, and increases the business value of AI systems that depend on auditable, high-integrity information.

cases.task: Trrue Chain
cases.context: European Commission; European Institution/Agency; R&D economic affairs; Italy
cases.implementation: The purpose of this use case is to optimise fundraising for impact-focused projects by combining distributed-ledger technology with governance mechanisms that support ethical standards and regulatory compliance.

cases.source_description: Impact investment and ESG-linked fundraising frequently suffer from high transaction friction, fragmented compliance processes, and persistent concerns about the credibility of sustainability claims. Investors, project sponsors, and regulators all need mechanisms that improve trust, reduce cost, and maintain legal certainty without losing the benefits of digital infrastructure. The purpose of this use case is to optimise fundraising for impact-focused projects by combining distributed-ledger technology with governance mechanisms that support ethical standards and regulatory compliance. The implementation is centred on Trrue Chain, a blockchain infrastructure designed to verify on-chain data through a network of trusted participants while preserving legal relationships required for regulated financial activity. Built with Polkadot Substrate and Cumulus, the system enables interoperability across blockchains and is intended to connect traditional financial markets with Web3 environments. At a conceptual level, it combines governance protocols, verification layers, and interoperable digital-asset tooling to support compliant fundraising and help address greenwashing risks in financial services. The expected impact includes faster and more secure fundraising processes, lower operational cost than traditional systems, and improved confidence in the quality and integrity of impact investment data. It also supports scalability for responsible investment ecosystems and creates business value by making ESG-positive projects easier to finance within a more transparent and regulation-aware framework.

cases.problem: Access to high-value assets such as commercial property and other real-world assets has historically been limited to institutional investors and wealthy individuals, largely because of high entry thresholds, illiquidity, and complex transaction structures.
cases.task: Tokenization and fractional ownership of real estate and RWAs
cases.context: European Commission; European Institution/Agency; R&D economic affairs; Ireland
cases.implementation: The objective of this use case is to widen access to asset-backed investment opportunities by enabling fractional ownership and more liquid participation in real estate and other tokenised real-world assets.
cases.outcome: UNKNOWN; 원천의 기대효과와 별도 관측 성과는 구분해야 합니다.
cases.source_description: Access to high-value assets such as commercial property and other real-world assets has historically been limited to institutional investors and wealthy individuals, largely because of high entry thresholds, illiquidity, and complex transaction structures. This restricts participation, narrows sources of capital, and reduces the flexibility with which assets can be financed or traded. The objective of this use case is to widen access to asset-backed investment opportunities by enabling fractional ownership and more liquid participation in real estate and other tokenised real-world assets. The implementation is provided through REClosure’s financial technology platform, which tokenises underlying assets and divides ownership into digital units that can be offered to a broader investor base, including retail participants. At a conceptual level, the platform links asset tokenisation, ownership representation, and marketplace trading functions so that value derived from rental returns or asset appreciation can be associated with fractional digital holdings. The example presented for the sandbox describes a €20 million office property split into 500 units of €20,000, illustrating how tokenisation can lower barriers to entry while preserving tradability. The impact includes broader investor inclusion, improved liquidity for traditionally illiquid assets, and greater flexibility in capital raising. It also supports more scalable market participation, expands access to diversified investments, and increases the efficiency with which real-world assets can be financed and exchanged.

cases.task: Certificate Management System for the Global Trade dominium
cases.context: European Commission; European Institution/Agency; Agriculture, forestry, fishing and hunting; Italy
cases.implementation: The purpose of this use case is to create a more trustworthy, efficient, and scalable way for businesses, authorities, and supply-chain partners to exchange, sign, verify, and track certificates and related trade documents while reducing operational friction and improving compliance.

cases.source_description: Global trade still depends heavily on fragmented document flows, repeated data entry, manual validation, and paper-based certificates, creating delays, fraud risks, and weak visibility across logistics, mobility, and supply-chain operations, particularly in sensitive sectors such as food and agriculture. The purpose of this use case is to create a more trustworthy, efficient, and scalable way for businesses, authorities, and supply-chain partners to exchange, sign, verify, and track certificates and related trade documents while reducing operational friction and improving compliance. The implementation is based on a fully automated certificate management system developed by ReLOG3P and Morpheus.Network. At a conceptual level, it combines a cloud-based self-service portal, an integrated document-handling database, digitisation tools such as OCR and uploaders, and digital sign-off capabilities, with blockchain back ends on Ethereum and Hyperledger plus IPFS-based immutable trails. Each uploaded document receives a decentralised unique identifier and a timestamped provenance record containing creation, access, signature, and revision data, while APIs allow integration with authorities and ERP systems. The impact includes faster shipment execution, improved supplier management, proactive alerts for non-compliant or expiring certificates, reduced delays and rework, and stronger traceability. It also increases trust in document authenticity, supports food and goods safety, lowers operating costs, and provides a scalable foundation for more transparent and compliant global trade processes.

cases.problem: As digital identity, verifiable credentials, and Web3 services expand, public bodies, businesses, and regulators face a growing challenge in determining who can be trusted to issue, verify, and rely on digital attestations across different technical environments.
cases.task: Universal trust registry
cases.context: European Commission; European Institution/Agency; R&D economic affairs; Lithuania
cases.implementation: The objective of this use case is to create a more flexible and portable model for managing trusted accreditation structures across distributed environments, so that institutions can operate trusted lists and trust chains without being locked into a single ledger. At a conceptual level, the solution uses a ledger-agnostic architecture for trust registries and sequential, traversable lists of verifiable accreditations built on distributed-ledger infrastructure, drawing on DID Core and DID URL practices and extending the EBSI trust-chain model into a broader universal trust registry approach.
cases.outcome: UNKNOWN; 원천의 기대효과와 별도 관측 성과는 구분해야 합니다.
cases.source_description: As digital identity, verifiable credentials, and Web3 services expand, public bodies, businesses, and regulators face a growing challenge in determining who can be trusted to issue, verify, and rely on digital attestations across different technical environments. Existing trust frameworks are often tied to specific ledgers or ecosystems, which limits interoperability and makes it harder to prepare for regulatory frameworks such as eIDAS 2.0, the European Digital Identity ecosystem, and related digital-market requirements. The objective of this use case is to create a more flexible and portable model for managing trusted accreditation structures across distributed environments, so that institutions can operate trusted lists and trust chains without being locked into a single ledger. The implementation is being developed by a consortium led by Soverio with cheqd, Danube Tech, and Netis. At a conceptual level, the solution uses a ledger-agnostic architecture for trust registries and sequential, traversable lists of verifiable accreditations built on distributed-ledger infrastructure, drawing on DID Core and DID URL practices and extending the EBSI trust-chain model into a broader universal trust registry approach. The expected impact includes stronger interoperability across identity ecosystems, improved readiness for future regulatory compliance, and easier cross-platform trust management. It also offers greater scalability for digital credential ecosystems, lower integration friction, and more robust foundations for trusted digital services in both public and commercial settings.

cases.source_description: Organisations using tokenisation for everyday services such as event tickets, museum access, proof-of-attendance records, or fan engagement often face a regulatory problem: although their tokens are not financial instruments or crypto-assets under MiCAR, the hosted wallets embedded in their applications may still technically receive, hold, or transfer crypto-assets, including for transaction fees. This creates uncertainty, potential compliance burdens, and a risk that firms using distributed-ledger technology could face significantly higher operational costs than competitors delivering similar services through non-blockchain technologies. The aim of this use case is to clarify how such wallet services can be provided on a level playing field while preserving innovation in non-financial token use. The implementation is being explored by the 2Tokens consortium with partners including Amdax, Custodiex, Celebratix, Metaseum, TDE, and CMS. Conceptually, the solution examines hosted or white-label wallet models for non-financial tokens, alongside the possibility of lighter regulatory treatment or exemptions, while still accommodating the technical reality that wallets may need to process network fees or hold transferable digital assets. The impact could include lower compliance friction, reduced cost barriers for service providers, and more viable adoption of token-based services in mainstream cultural and consumer applications. It also supports regulatory clarity, fairer competition, and greater scalability for digital-token services whose primary purpose lies outside financial markets.

In Portugal, suspicion arose after an appeal-court ruling reportedly contained odd phrasing and citations that lawyers argued might have been produced with the help of an AI system, prompting scrutiny of whether judges had relied on such tools in preparing a decision. The issue matters because courts depend on trust, legal accuracy, and human responsibility, and any use of AI in judicial reasoning or drafting can affect confidence in the integrity of judgments. The reported implementation, insofar as it can be described as one, would have involved a judge or judges using a general-purpose generative AI assistant to help produce legal text rather than a formally authorised court system integrated into judicial workflow. Public reporting indicates that the judges disputed the allegations and that the matter led to official discussion and inquiry rather than confirmation of an endorsed technology solution. The impact of the episode lies in highlighting governance risks: it intensified debate about standards for AI use in courts, the need for human oversight, and the importance of clear rules on whether and how judges may use generative tools.

More broadly, the pilot is intended to improve efficiency, security, and resilience in capital markets, support innovation in digital financial infrastructure, and create a scalable foundation for future forms of digitally issued public debt.

For municipalities and waste-management operators, this creates both a financial and an environmental burden, especially where available operational data is underused and vehicle routing is not dynamically aligned with real needs. The aim of this use case is to improve the efficiency and sustainability of urban waste collection by ensuring that collections take place only when needed and with the most suitable routing and vehicle allocation. This improves operational performance, lowers congestion and heavy-vehicle presence on local streets, and creates stronger long-term value through more data-driven and scalable waste-management practices.

cases.source_description: Many urban locations, such as pedestrian crossings, cycle lanes and narrow pavements near traffic, become especially hazardous at night when poor visibility increases the risk of accidents for vulnerable road users. Municipalities often struggle to identify these lighting-related risks systematically, and conventional inspection methods may not be frequent or detailed enough to support timely maintenance decisions. SAFELIGHT addresses this challenge by helping cities detect high-risk locations and improve illumination where it matters most for safety. The stakeholders include host cities, road-maintenance teams, mobility planners and vulnerable users such as pedestrians and cyclists, with the objective of reducing night-time accident risk through better-targeted lighting interventions that can be integrated into ordinary maintenance operations. The solution is implemented through the Autonomous Urban Inspector for Lighting, which analyses road and street visibility using data collected in the urban environment and automatically identifies locations where conditions are unsafe. At a conceptual level, the system combines automated inspection, risk assessment and recommendation functions, after which Flash Lighting proposes the most suitable technical responses for each site. A second inspection is then carried out once lighting changes are implemented in order to validate the improvement in visibility. The expected impact is more precise identification of dangerous locations, more efficient maintenance planning and better evidence for safety interventions. More broadly, SAFELIGHT creates value by providing a scalable, operationally usable method for improving urban lighting and helping reduce accidents involving vulnerable road users.

The expected impact is reduced energy use, better maintenance insight, improved environmental monitoring and a foundation for broader Smart City services using existing infrastructure.
