The impact includes faster and more accurate production of digital replicas, improved visitor engagement and broader accessibility to collections through interactive formats. More broadly, the initiative creates value by opening commercial opportunities, strengthening local capability and demonstrating how cultural institutions can combine preservation, education and innovation in a scalable and socially meaningful way.

cases.source_description: Warwickshire County Council developed the “Access to Food” project to better understand how residents, particularly those living in deprived areas, access healthy and affordable food options. The operational challenge was that identifying and classifying local food-related businesses and services manually required significant staff effort and limited the speed with which the council could generate useful insights for policy and service design. The stakeholders included council analysts, service planners and communities facing barriers to food access, with the objective of improving the evidence base for local decision-making while exploring whether new tools could reduce manual workload and support future analysis. The solution was implemented through an in-house experiment using the open-source Llama 2 model to classify local businesses, allowing the council to retain full data sovereignty. At a conceptual level, the project tested large language model capabilities against more conventional data-science methods in a controlled environment, examining performance, infrastructure needs, governance implications and operational fit. Although traditional analytical methods proved more accurate in this case, the pilot showed that language-model tools may still have value for automating parts of labour-intensive classification tasks. The impact lies less in immediate performance gains and more in strategic learning: the project generated valuable insight on hardware, security and governance requirements, while highlighting where future time savings and productivity improvements might be realised through carefully controlled adoption in local government settings.

cases.source_description: Access to British Sign Language interpreters is essential for Deaf BSL users to participate fully in work, healthcare, public services and social life, yet existing booking systems are often fragmented, inefficient and unable to match users with available interpreters reliably. This creates a practical barrier even where interpreter capacity exists, because the process of finding the right person at the right time can be slow and opaque. SignPort was developed to address this access problem, with Deaf Action and Burrotech focusing on choice, control and equity for Deaf BSL users rather than simple administrative efficiency alone. The stakeholders include Deaf BSL users, interpreters, public-service organisations and booking agencies such as the NHS, with the objective of improving interpreter access and making the process more user-centred and scalable. The solution is implemented as a mobile app that matches users to interpreters according to need, availability and timing. At a conceptual level, the platform combines booking logic, user preferences and service coordination into a digital matching workflow that reduces fragmentation and improves responsiveness. The team is also extending the service through additional features, including a fully integrated web version, to make it more attractive for interpreters and easier for agencies to adopt. The expected impact is faster and more reliable access to interpreters, improved user autonomy and a more efficient matching process, with broader value in accessibility, inclusion and service scalability.

cases.source_description: When Bath and North East Somerset Council consulted on proposed parking-charge changes in 2024, it received more than 4,300 responses and over 18,000 free-text comments. Processing such a large volume of qualitative feedback manually would normally require weeks of officer time, slowing decision-making and making it harder to provide clear, consistent and accountable reporting on what residents had said. The council therefore needed a way to accelerate analysis without losing visibility of the issues raised. The stakeholders included council officers, decision-makers and residents participating in the consultation, with the objective of improving the speed, clarity and reliability of consultation analysis. The solution was implemented through ConsultAI, deployed in partnership with The Future Fox. At a conceptual level, the platform processes large volumes of consultation responses, identifies themes, analyses longer comments and produces editable reports in Excel and Word format, enabling officers to review and refine outputs within familiar working tools. The system completed the full analysis within three days, compared with an estimated six weeks of manual effort. The impact was therefore both substantial and measurable: major time savings, quicker decision support and more consistent reporting. More broadly, the use case creates value by improving transparency and accountability in public consultation, while giving councils a scalable way to handle large volumes of citizen feedback more efficiently.

cases.source_description: In 2020 and 2021, the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government commissioned a large-scale digital consultation across the Oxford-Cambridge Arc, a region spanning five counties and 3.3 million residents, to inform the development of a long-term Spatial Framework. The project achieved a 28% conversion rate, significantly higher than traditional surveys, and successfully engaged groups often underrepresented in consultation, including people under 35 and ethnic minorities. The impact was a more inclusive, data-rich and strategically useful consultation process, demonstrating the value of digital engagement and analytical tools in large-scale spatial planning.

cases.source_description: Pittsburgh needed a more effective way to manage congestion caused by a difficult urban road network shaped by hills, bridges and irregular street layouts. Traditional pre-programmed traffic signals were poorly suited to these changing conditions and contributed to delays, excess idling and inefficient traffic flow. The use case therefore focused on improving mobility through smarter signal control, with the objective of reducing travel time, cutting emissions and creating a more responsive traffic-management system. The stakeholders include city authorities, transport planners, drivers, pedestrians and researchers at Carnegie Mellon University, who developed the SURTRAC system to support a more adaptive model of urban traffic control. The solution is implemented through a decentralised signal-management platform that uses sensors and cameras to detect traffic in real time, predict short-term flows and adjust signal timings dynamically. At a conceptual level, intersections communicate with one another while still making local decisions, creating a coordinated network without relying on a single central controller. First deployed in 2012 across nine intersections in East Liberty, the system quickly demonstrated strong results: travel times fell by about 25%, idling by more than 40%, braking by 30% and emissions by roughly 21%. The project was later expanded to dozens of intersections and spun off into Rapid Flow Technologies for wider deployment. More broadly, the case shows how adaptive traffic control can improve mobility, reduce environmental impact and offer a scalable model for smarter urban infrastructure.

cases.source_description: The Royal United Hospital in Bath needed a more effective way to gather patient feedback without overloading staff or relying on low-response manual survey processes. In urgent care and orthopaedic outpatient settings, traditional feedback collection created administrative burden for nurses and produced very limited response volumes, making it difficult for the hospital to gain representative insight into patient experience. The use case therefore focused on improving both engagement and operational efficiency through a more accessible and automated feedback mechanism. The stakeholders include patients, nurses, departmental managers and hospital administrators, with the objective of raising response rates, reducing staff workload and generating more useful evidence for service improvement. The solution is implemented through Hello Lamp Post’s interactive chat platform, structured around the Friends and Family Test and deployed directly in the relevant hospital wards. At a conceptual level, the system automates survey delivery through conversational interaction, allowing patients to respond more easily while the hospital receives structured and analysable feedback without depending on manual administration. The results were substantial: completion rates rose from just 2% to 70%, and each department saved around 300 staff-hours annually, representing staffing-cost savings calculated at GBP 11 per hour. The hospital also obtained richer insight into care quality, with 58% of orthopaedic patients rating their care as good and 5% identifying areas for improvement. More broadly, the project creates value by transforming patient engagement, improving operational efficiency and strengthening service improvement through better-quality feedback.

cases.source_description: Public administrations are increasingly interested in using advanced analytical systems to improve policy design and service delivery, yet this raises difficult questions around transparency, bias, discrimination, legality and public trust. AI4Gov addresses this governance challenge by helping policymakers and public institutions develop tools and frameworks that support automated, evidence-based decision-making while protecting democratic values and fundamental rights. The stakeholders include public authorities, policymakers, researchers and citizens, with the objective of making technological adoption in government more trustworthy, interpretable and aligned with frameworks such as GDPR and the EU AI Act. The solution is implemented through a European programme that develops governance models, practical tools and pilot use cases to improve transparency, explainability and ethical oversight in public-sector applications. At a conceptual level, the project combines technical methods for trustworthy systems with policy-oriented design and user-friendly interfaces, enabling public bodies to test how advanced automation can be introduced without sacrificing accountability or fairness. This also supports greater citizen understanding and confidence in the use of digital systems in governance. The expected impact is better-quality public decision support, reduced risk of harmful bias and improved institutional readiness for responsible adoption. More broadly, AI4Gov creates value by strengthening democratic legitimacy, supporting more transparent public innovation and helping governments modernise in a way that is both effective and rights-conscious.

The provincial council oversees 63 drinking-water treatment plants serving 137,910 residents, alongside wastewater responsibilities, and needs better ways to detect leaks, losses, malfunctioning equipment and avoidable energy use. This pilot addresses that problem by helping technicians and policymakers use existing operational data more effectively in day-to-day management and long-term planning. The solution is implemented by building intelligent tools on top of existing water-management systems and datasets. At a conceptual level, the pilot uses analytical models to identify non-obvious inefficiencies, abnormal patterns and possible system malfunctions, translating these findings into operational insights for maintenance and service optimisation. The same evidence base can also inform budget allocation and infrastructure planning decisions. The expected impact is earlier detection of leaks and losses, more efficient energy use and better-informed technical interventions. More broadly, the pilot creates value by improving reliability in public water services, supporting sustainable infrastructure management and showing how existing municipal data can be turned into practical governance and operational benefits.

The JSI SDG Observatory pilot addresses this challenge by creating a clearer and more usable evidence base for tracking sustainability progress. The stakeholders include researchers, policymakers and institutions working on SDG implementation, with the objective of making indicators easier to gather, visualise and interpret so that they can inform strategy, monitoring and public decision-making more effectively. The solution is implemented as a web-based toolkit that aggregates and displays SDG-related indicators in a structured and accessible format. At a conceptual level, the observatory combines data collection, harmonisation and visual analytics so that users can explore trends, compare indicators and identify areas requiring policy attention. This turns fragmented sustainability information into a more coherent monitoring environment and supports more timely use of evidence in governance. The expected impact is better visibility of SDG progress, improved usability of indicator data and stronger support for evidence-based policy discussions. More broadly, the pilot creates value by enhancing transparency in sustainability monitoring, reducing friction in the use of complex datasets and giving policymakers and researchers a more practical tool for understanding where action is succeeding and where additional intervention may be needed.

cases.source_description: National strategies on advanced digital technologies are now widespread, but understanding how these policy documents address issues such as bias, fairness and responsible governance remains a complex analytical task. The OECD AI policy-analysis pilot addresses this challenge by helping institutions examine national strategies in a more systematic way, with particular attention to how bias is treated in policy frameworks. The stakeholders include policymakers, governance researchers and organisations interested in responsible digital regulation, with the objective of improving understanding of policy quality, highlighting best practices and supporting more informed development of future governance approaches. The solution is implemented through analytical and visual tools that examine national policy documents and generate comparative summaries of how bias-related questions are addressed. At a conceptual level, the pilot combines policy-text analysis, thematic categorisation and visual presentation methods to reconcile large numbers of documents and make differences in emphasis, completeness and good practice easier to identify. These outputs can then support reflection and policy learning rather than replacing expert interpretation. The expected impact is clearer visibility of policy strengths and gaps, better benchmarking across national strategies and stronger support for more ethical policy development. More broadly, the pilot creates value by improving the transparency and usability of policy analysis, helping decision-makers move from broad strategy statements towards more concrete, informed and responsible approaches to governance.

cases.task: Machine Learning towards a greener grid
cases.context: Turing Institute; Academic-Research; Fuel and energy; United Kingdom
cases.implementation: The implementation developed improved solar and wind forecasting approaches using data science methods created with researchers from the Alan Turing Institute. The use case is significant because it applies AI to a critical infrastructure function where forecast accuracy has direct operational, environmental and economic consequences.
cases.outcome: UNKNOWN; 원천의 기대효과와 별도 관측 성과는 구분해야 합니다.
cases.source_description: Electricity systems with high shares of wind and solar generation require more accurate forecasting because renewable output changes with weather and time of day. The “Towards a Greener Grid” project applied machine-learning and statistical forecasting to help National Grid Electricity System Operator balance the British electricity system more efficiently. The operational problem is that inaccurate renewable forecasts can force the system operator to procure more reserve or rely on backup generation, increasing costs and emissions. The implementation developed improved solar and wind forecasting approaches using data science methods created with researchers from the Alan Turing Institute. At a conceptual level, the models learn from historical generation, weather and system data to predict renewable output more accurately, especially for day-ahead operational planning. The expected impact is better balancing of supply and demand, reduced reliance on fossil-fuel backup, lower consumer costs and increased ability to integrate renewable energy into the grid. The use case is significant because it applies AI to a critical infrastructure function where forecast accuracy has direct operational, environmental and economic consequences. It demonstrates how machine learning can support decarbonisation not by producing energy directly, but by helping the grid absorb cleaner generation more reliably.

cases.task: TrackIT Blockchain - The value chain for the traceability of Made in Italy
cases.context: Italian Trade Agency; Central-Government; Economic affairs n.e.c; Italy
cases.outcome: UNKNOWN; 원천의 기대효과와 별도 관측 성과는 구분해야 합니다.
cases.source_description: Exporting companies often need to prove origin, quality, sustainability and production history to international buyers, while the “Made in Italy” brand is exposed to counterfeiting and misleading imitation. TrackIT Blockchain, promoted by the Italian Trade Agency, supports selected Italian exporters by providing blockchain-based supply-chain traceability connected to consumer-facing product information. The objective is to help companies, especially SMEs, communicate the authenticity and value of their products in sectors such as agri-food, fashion, cosmetics, furniture and design. The implementation records key production and provenance data on a blockchain and links that information to goods through QR codes or smart tags. At a conceptual level, the platform connects supply-chain events, company narratives, certification information and immutable distributed-ledger records, allowing consumers or business partners to scan a product and view its verified story. The expected impact is stronger consumer trust, better protection of the Made in Italy brand, improved export promotion and more transparent communication of quality and sustainability characteristics. Official ICE material presents TrackIT as a service that registers production data in blockchain and allows consumers to visualise the history of the product and company by scanning a smart tag. ICE also states that the project makes a standard traceability service available to 500 companies, with current participation deadlines extended into 2026.

cases.source_description: Construction-material supply chains involve multiple actors, technical certifications, environmental requirements and lifecycle information that can be difficult to trace reliably from raw materials to final use or disposal. BLOCH4MAT applies blockchain technology to strategic construction-material sectors in Emilia-Romagna, including ceramic tiles, bricks and composite materials. The project’s objective is to analyse where blockchain can bring effective advantages to producers and stakeholders, then develop a prototype platform able to make product information traceable, secure, unambiguous and non-falsifiable across the lifecycle. The implementation is coordinated by Centro Ceramico and involves scientific partners such as TEKNEHUB, CIRI-EC and Consorzio Futuro in Ricerca, together with companies including InnovationCHAIN and other industry actors. At a conceptual level, the platform records supply-chain information on materials, production steps, processing, certification and possibly end-of-life phases, while also exploring integration with BIM and other digital construction tools. The expected impact is greater transparency, anti-counterfeiting protection, process optimisation, improved coordination among construction actors and better availability of verified material data for digital building workflows. Public project material states that the central activity is the creation of a prototype blockchain platform for ceramic slabs, brick products and fibrous composite materials.

IT4LIA is Italy’s AI Factory initiative, designed to provide national and European users with AI-optimised supercomputing capacity, data-processing tools and related services. The operational problem is that AI adoption in strategic sectors depends on access to high-performance infrastructure and expert support, not only on algorithms. The implementation centres on the CINECA data centre in Bologna, where a new AI-optimised supercomputer is being integrated with existing high-performance computing and cloud systems. At a conceptual level, the factory provides a shared infrastructure layer for developing, training, testing and deploying AI applications in sectors such as agritech, cybersecurity, manufacturing, climate, earth sciences and public administration. The expected impact is stronger Italian and European AI competitiveness, wider access to advanced computing, accelerated innovation by SMEs and start-ups, and better translation of research into operational AI services. The initiative is significant because it treats AI capacity as public strategic infrastructure, linked to EuroHPC and national industrial-policy objectives.

cases.source_description: Remote rural areas and islands often face weaker connectivity, making it harder to provide modern healthcare, education and civil-protection services. 5G-TERRA addresses this digital divide by deploying 5G infrastructure in sparsely populated areas of central Greece and Greek islands. The operational problem is that communities with limited broadband access may struggle to benefit from telemedicine, remote monitoring, immersive learning or real-time emergency-alert systems. The implementation combines new 5G radio access equipment, upgraded backhaul links, cloud and edge resources, and a transition from non-standalone to standalone 5G architecture. At a conceptual level, the network becomes an enabling layer for three public-interest domains: digital healthcare, smart and green schools, and public protection. In healthcare, it supports wearable monitoring, video links for paramedics, remote medical support, electronic records and clinical decision support. In education, it enables connectivity, environmental monitoring and AR/VR learning. In civil protection, it supports wildfire and flood detection through IoT, AI, cameras, drones and risk-prediction tools. The expected impact is more equal access to essential services, better emergency preparedness, improved educational quality and stronger social inclusion for communities that would otherwise remain digitally underserved.

The operational challenge is that many high-value applications require contextual awareness rather than isolated signal processing: simultaneous translation in a noisy environment requires knowing who is speaking; cardiology applications may require linking imaging data with physiological patterns; disaster-management tools may need to combine satellite, drone and environmental signals.
cases.task: DVPS ('Diversibus Viis Plurima Solvo') - creating a new generation of artificial intelligence models
cases.context: Translated; Consortium; R&D economic affairs; Italy
cases.outcome: UNKNOWN; 원천의 기대효과와 별도 관측 성과는 구분해야 합니다.
cases.source_description: Current artificial-intelligence systems remain strong at processing digital representations such as text, images and video, but they are still limited when they need to understand real-world context across several sensory channels at once. DVPS, or “Diversibus Viis Plurima Solvo”, addresses this limitation by developing multimodal foundation models that combine linguistic, visual, auditory and sensory inputs to build more grounded representations of the physical world. The operational challenge is that many high-value applications require contextual awareness rather than isolated signal processing: simultaneous translation in a noisy environment requires knowing who is speaking; cardiology applications may require linking imaging data with physiological patterns; disaster-management tools may need to combine satellite, drone and environmental signals. DVPS therefore focuses on models that can learn across modalities, transfer knowledge between domains and adapt more efficiently when labelled data are limited. The project will develop AutoDVPS, an open-source toolkit for multimodal foundation-model design, pre-training, fine-tuning and modality expansion, as well as DVPSBench, a benchmarking suite for assessing performance, robustness and ethical implications. The expected impact is to strengthen Europe’s capacity in next-generation AI by producing reusable methods, open assets and demonstrators in language communication, cardiology and geo-intelligence. The case is relevant because it goes beyond language-model deployment and targets foundational AI capabilities for real-world interaction. Translated announced the initiative with EUR 29 million in backing and 20 partners across nine countries, while CORDIS lists the Horizon Europe grant agreement as running from 1 July 2025 to 30 June 2029.

cases.task: A chatbot to protect the identities of those reporting school bullying

cases.implementation: The case is relevant because it applies AI not to surveillance or discipline, but to safer reporting and privacy-preserving child protection.

cases.source_description: School bullying is often under-reported because victims and witnesses fear reprisals, social exposure or being identified indirectly through the details of their report. The Petscraft project led by Inria addresses this problem by exploring an AI-based chatbot capable of receiving reports while protecting the identity of the person submitting them. The operational challenge is subtle: anonymity is not achieved simply by removing a name, because free-text reports can contain clues about a pupil’s class, schedule, relationship network, writing style, location or personal circumstances. A large language model might also infer personal traits or identity markers from apparently harmless text. The project therefore focuses on privacy-enhancing technologies that can filter, rewrite or transform the report so that the school receives useful information about the incident while reducing the risk that the reporter can be identified. The approach is first tested on public datasets before being applied to sensitive bullying-reporting material, which is important given the vulnerability of minors and the seriousness of the information involved. At a conceptual level, the chatbot acts as an anonymisation layer between the reporter and the institution: it encourages disclosure, protects the person raising the alert and helps schools detect and respond to bullying more effectively. The case is relevant because it applies AI not to surveillance or discipline, but to safer reporting and privacy-preserving child protection. Petscraft itself is an Inria project team created with INSA Centre Val de Loire and the University of Orléans, focused on privacy-enhancing technologies.

By applying AI to recognise and classify handwritten text, the initiative can convert unstructured citizen input into structured data more quickly and consistently. At a conceptual level, the system supports administrative accountability by improving the data pipeline behind complaints management: it does not replace the citizen’s right to complain or the authority’s duty to respond, but helps process and evaluate submissions more efficiently. The expected impact is shorter processing times, improved evaluation standards, more consistent support for users and better analytical insight into recurring service problems. The case is relevant because it applies AI to a foundational accountability mechanism in public administration.

cases.implementation: AIAP-N2O addresses this challenge by using sensor data, AI, data analysis and process knowledge to understand and reduce N₂O formation in wastewater treatment. cases.source_description: Wastewater treatment plants can emit nitrous oxide, a greenhouse gas with a high climate impact, but emissions are difficult to manage because they depend on complex biological and operational conditions inside process tanks. AIAP-N2O addresses this challenge by using sensor data, AI, data analysis and process knowledge to understand and reduce N₂O formation in wastewater treatment. The operational problem is that treatment plants need practical control strategies that can be implemented across different hardware and software environments, rather than solutions that work only in one specific plant or vendor system. The project will collect data from three wastewater treatment plants over one to one and a half years, including measurements from two types of N₂O sensor technologies. These data will be used to develop an open and detailed description of how process-tank control can avoid or reduce nitrous oxide formation. At a conceptual level, the project converts plant-level measurements into generalisable process knowledge: AI helps identify the conditions and parameters that drive emissions, while the resulting guidance can be used by treatment plants or third-party control providers to build their own control strategies. The expected impact is lower greenhouse-gas emissions, better environmental performance in water and wastewater management, and easier adoption of N₂O reduction practices across the sector. The case is relevant because it uses AI not simply to optimise efficiency, but to make climate mitigation operational in public environmental infrastructure. The project is led by Duotec A/S with the Danish Technological Institute, DTU Sustain and several wastewater utilities.

cases.problem: The operational challenge is that conventional de-icing methods often rely on indirect external indicators, such as temperature and humidity, which may trigger de-icing even when ice formation is not actually present.
cases.task: Energy-efficient de-icing with camera detection and artificial intelligence
cases.context: Danish Ministry of Climate, Energy, and Utilities; Central-Government; Fuel and energy; Denmark
cases.implementation: This leads to unnecessary energy use and higher operating costs. AICID uses camera detection together with humidity and temperature sensors to identify real ice formation more accurately and control de-icing cycles only when needed.
cases.outcome: UNKNOWN; 원천의 기대효과와 별도 관측 성과는 구분해야 합니다.
cases.source_description: Ventilation systems are critical for energy-efficient buildings because heat exchangers can recover a large share of the heat from exhaust air, reducing the need for additional heating. However, ice formation on heat exchangers can reduce efficiency, increase energy consumption and damage the system if not managed correctly. The Danish AICID project addresses this problem by developing an AI-based control algorithm for more precise de-icing in ventilation systems. The operational challenge is that conventional de-icing methods often rely on indirect external indicators, such as temperature and humidity, which may trigger de-icing even when ice formation is not actually present. This leads to unnecessary energy use and higher operating costs. AICID uses camera detection together with humidity and temperature sensors to identify real ice formation more accurately and control de-icing cycles only when needed. The project includes analysis of camera and sensor technologies, testing, development and implementation of the algorithm on EXHAUSTO ventilation systems, demonstration in homes managed by Haderslev Boligselskab and lifecycle assessment to confirm environmental benefits. The expected results are substantial: the project aims to reduce heat loss in ventilation systems by at least 40%, reduce de-icing periods from around 40% to between 5% and 0.5% annually, and lower the temperature threshold for de-icing from 5°C to between -5°C and -10°C. The wider expected impact is improved building energy efficiency, lower operational costs, longer equipment lifetime and significant national energy-saving potential.

cases.source_description: Renovation and maintenance decisions in residential buildings have a major influence on resource use, emissions and the long-term sustainability of the construction sector. HabitAi addresses this challenge by exploring how dynamic and contextual building data can be collected, structured and made usable for homeowners and construction-sector actors. The operational problem is that many decisions about single-family homes are still taken on the basis of fragmented, static or siloed data. Information about building characteristics, condition, maintenance needs, climate impact and renovation options may exist across different registries or professional assessments, but it is not necessarily available in a form that supports practical decision-making by the homeowner. The HabitAi preliminary project examined whether it is technically possible to carry out cross-cutting data collection and digitalisation of currently locked or fragmented building data for Danish single-family houses. The intended outcome is a digital toolbox that can help homeowners and the building sector decide when maintenance, renovation or preservation is preferable to demolition, and how to achieve the greatest environmental benefit within the homeowner’s financial constraints. At a conceptual level, the project is about converting building data into decision support: rather than treating each renovation as an isolated case, data can help identify sustainable pathways for preserving resources, extending building lifetimes and reducing climate impact. The case is relevant because it focuses on the residential building stock, where individual decisions collectively have large environmental consequences. However, the official source describes HabitAi as a preliminary project and does not confirm a fully operational AI product; it should therefore be presented as a feasibility and data-structuring initiative.

cases.source_description: Renovation, repair and deconstruction of masonry buildings are labour-intensive activities that can expose workers to repetitive strain, dust, noise and physically demanding manual work. The Danish project on robotic removal of masonry joints addresses this problem by developing and testing robotic technologies that can remove mortar joints in masonry more precisely and efficiently. The operational challenge is that brick buildings often have long potential lifetimes, but repairing or selectively dismantling them requires careful removal of joints without damaging reusable materials. Conventional manual methods can be slow and physically demanding, while demolition may lead to unnecessary material loss and reduce the possibility of circular reuse. The project therefore focuses on full-scale development, testing, dissemination and implementation of robotic technologies for the construction sector, with specific attention to extending building lifetime and enabling more effective deconstruction. At a conceptual level, the solution combines robotics, sensing and control methods to identify and remove joints accurately, supporting both selective repair and recovery of building materials. The expected impact is improved productivity in construction and renovation, reduced wear and tear on craft workers, better occupational safety, longer building lifetimes and increased reuse of masonry materials in the circular economy. The case is relevant because it shows how automation can support the green transition in construction not only through new materials, but also by making repair and deconstruction more practical. The official project page describes the initiative as an environmental-technology development, testing and demonstration project within the MUDP programme.

cases.source_description: Education systems need digital tools that support students, parents and teachers without adding new administrative burdens or fragmenting learning information across incompatible platforms. Ukraine’s Mriia is a state educational ecosystem designed to help pupils learn, parents follow progress and educators manage teaching processes more efficiently. The operational problem is particularly acute in Ukraine’s wartime education context, where schools may operate remotely, in shelters or under disrupted conditions, and where families need reliable digital access to schedules, assignments, grades and communication. Mriia provides a web portal and mobile application that connect schools, students, parents and teachers through a common educational environment. The official platform presents functions including homework, schedules, learning plans, progress tracking, educational content, secure chats based on Signal, support at all stages and a digital education document called Mriia ID. cases.source_description: Rapid diagnosis of brain injuries and neurological conditions is critical because delays can directly affect survival, treatment options and long-term patient outcomes. The expected impact is faster diagnosis, fewer medical errors, more timely treatment decisions and stronger access to specialist-style diagnostic support in locations under pressure. The case is significant because it links AI diagnostics with telemedicine and emergency care in a high-stakes wartime health context.

cases.source_description: Chronic diseases such as diabetes can lead to severe complications when early signs are not detected, and diabetic retinopathy is a major preventable cause of vision loss. CheckEye addresses this problem through an AI-based platform for large-scale screening of diabetic retinopathy and, more broadly, chronic-disease complications. The operational problem is that many patients do not receive regular specialist eye examinations, particularly under wartime conditions where access to healthcare facilities is disrupted. CheckEye enables screening through retinal image analysis, using AI to identify signs of diabetic retinopathy and prioritise patients who require ophthalmological follow-up. At a conceptual level, the platform shifts screening from a scarce specialist-service model towards a scalable preventive-health model: images can be collected through distributed screening points, analysed by AI and used to identify patients needing further care. In Ukraine, CheckEye reports implementation across six regions, including Chernivtsi, Zakarpattia, Vinnytsia and Kyiv regions, in cooperation with the Ukrainian Diabetes Federation under the “Seeing a Colourful World-2” project. The reported results suggest that around 30% of screened patients had diabetic retinopathy without knowing it, while the platform reports 95% sensitivity and 90% specificity. The expected impact is earlier detection, prevention of avoidable vision loss, more efficient use of ophthalmologist capacity and stronger resilience of screening services during crisis. cases.source_description: Urban mobility around major transport hubs is difficult to manage because cars, trams, buses, bicycles, electric scooters, pedestrians and ferry passengers interact dynamically, particularly during peak arrival and departure periods. Helsinki’s drone- and AI-supported traffic-monitoring initiative addresses this problem by collecting high-resolution mobility data around the West Harbour, one of Europe’s busiest ferry-port areas. The operational challenge is that transport planners need to understand not only aggregate traffic volumes, but also how passengers move between ferries, trams, metro lines, trains, taxis, scooters, bicycles and walking routes. Since 2023, drones have been used above the harbour area to collect bird’s-eye-view video of multimodal traffic. AI systems process the footage to detect and classify vehicles and track movement patterns, including speed, direction and interaction between transport modes. These outputs are then converted into anonymised trajectory data and integrated into AI-powered digital twins, allowing city regulators and engineers to test traffic-management strategies virtually before implementing them in the real world. At a conceptual level, the initiative turns temporary aerial observations into simulation-ready data for urban planning. It also raises important governance questions, since even GDPR-compliant drone monitoring can create public concerns about surveillance, transparency and cybersecurity. The project aims to test soft measures such as route recommendations and incentives to travel at off-peak times, and to trial an app suggesting alternative routes or modes. The wider expected impact is reduced peak congestion, smoother intermodal connections, better planning evidence and support for sustainable urban mobility

cases.source_description: Tourism pressure in environmentally sensitive coastal areas creates a difficult management problem for local authorities and protected-area managers: high visitor numbers can damage fragile habitats, reduce visitor experience and make it harder to plan cleaning, enforcement, traffic management and conservation measures. The TOURISMO pilot at Golden Bay, also known as Ir-Ramla tal-Mixquqa, responds to this challenge by introducing a beach-monitoring system designed to provide evidence on visitor flows and behaviour. The site is one of the Mediterranean pilot areas of the TOURISMO project, which focuses on innovative and sustainable management of tourism flows. The operational problem is that overcrowding at Golden Bay affects both the natural environment and the quality of the tourism experience, but without systematic data it is difficult to know when, where and how visitor pressure is developing. The implementation uses GDPR-compliant people-counting CCTV and deep-learning algorithms to monitor pedestrian and vehicular traffic, producing insights on visitor density and movement during peak tourist seasons. At a conceptual level, the system turns the beach into a monitored management environment where real-time or near-real-time data can support decisions on conservation, services and visitor-flow control. The expected impact is better protection of the area’s dune ecosystems and flora and fauna, improved NATURA 2000 management planning, more informed local stakeholder coordination and a stronger basis for balancing tourism with environmental preservation. The case is significant because it applies AI-enabled monitoring to sustainable tourism governance rather than to promotion or visitor marketing.

cases.task: Open Rights Data Exchange - A Common European data space for copyright
cases.context: European Commission; European Institution/Agency; Broadcasting and publishing services.; European Union
cases.implementation: The case is significant because it applies blockchain to the governance of digital creative assets, where reliable metadata and identity binding are essential for fair remuneration and lawful reuse.

cases.source_description: Copyright markets depend on reliable information about who created a work, who owns or administers rights, what licences apply, and how royalties should be allocated. The Open Rights Data Exchange addresses the persistent problem that rights data are often fragmented, inconsistent, difficult to verify and poorly interoperable across platforms, distributors and collecting systems. This creates friction for creators, rights holders, publishers, online services and licensing intermediaries, increasing transaction costs and weakening monetisation opportunities. ORDE proposes a common European rights-data infrastructure built on the European Blockchain Services Infrastructure. The operational model allows creators and rights holders to register a digital work by linking a content fingerprint with a verified identity and rights metadata. This binding can then be timestamped and stored immutably on the ledger, creating a verifiable reference point for authorship, ownership and licensing information. At a conceptual level, ORDE functions as a trusted rights-data exchange layer: it does not replace copyright law or licensing contracts, but makes rights information more discoverable, machine-readable and verifiable. Platforms, distributors and users could query this information to understand whether a work can be used, under what conditions and who should be compensated. The expected impact is faster licensing, reduced disputes, more transparent royalty allocation, lower administrative burden and stronger interoperability in European cultural and creative markets. The case is significant because it applies blockchain to the governance of digital creative assets, where reliable metadata and identity binding are essential for fair remuneration and lawful reuse.

The Digital Ferry Onboarding Experience addresses this problem by using EBSI-based digital identity wallets and verifiable credentials to simplify the journey from ticket booking to embarkation. The operational challenge is that passengers may need to manage different paper and digital documents, while ferry companies must verify identity and discount eligibility reliably and prevent misuse of boarding passes. Cyclades Fast Ferries, the University of the Aegean and the European Digital Identity Wallet Consortium are working on a model in which students can store educational identity credentials in a personal digital wallet. The boarding pass can then be issued as a verifiable credential and stored in the same wallet. At embarkation, the passenger presents the boarding pass from the wallet and the ferry officer verifies it directly. At a conceptual level, the project demonstrates how digital identity infrastructure can streamline cross-border mobility services by replacing manual document checks with trusted, standardised and privacy-preserving verification. cases.source_description: Large sporting events require complex infrastructure works to be delivered under strict deadlines, intense public scrutiny and high expectations for safety, legacy and accountability. The Milan-Cortina 2026 digital-twin use case applies dynamic virtual modelling to Olympic construction sites so that infrastructure works can be monitored, communicated and experienced in a more transparent way. The operational problem is that Olympic construction projects involve multiple sites, contractors, design inputs, schedules and safety requirements, while citizens and stakeholders may have limited visibility of progress before the venues and infrastructure are completed. The implementation described by the Italian Ministry of Infrastructure and Transport integrates design data, sensors and 3D models into a digital twin of the infrastructure, creating an interactive representation that can be updated in real time. At a conceptual level, the digital twin acts both as a construction-management tool and as a public-transparency interface: technical teams can follow the evolution of works, while the public can access immersive experiences that allow them to “enter” the construction sites virtually. The expected impact is more efficient monitoring of works, improved oversight of construction progress, stronger safety and risk-management capacity, and a clearer public narrative about the Olympic infrastructure legacy. The case is relevant because it connects digital-twin technology not only with engineering control, but also with civic transparency around major public investment.

The operational problem is that planning decisions often require several types of information that are not naturally visible together: a proposed surface-level intervention may conflict with underground utilities, while green-space choices may need to respond to heat-island patterns or neighbourhood-level climate evidence. cases.source_description: Railway stations are complex public environments where passenger flows, energy performance, building systems, safety, maintenance and emergency planning need to be managed together. The Monte-Carlo Station digital twin applies AI, simulation and sensor integration to support smarter operation of transport infrastructure. The operational problem is that station managers need to understand how people, heat, airflow, equipment and building systems interact in real time, but traditional facility-management systems often treat these elements separately. SNCF Gares & Connexions partnered with Akila and NVIDIA to deploy a real-time AI and simulation platform at Monte-Carlo train station, using Akila’s digital-twin platform and NVIDIA Omniverse technologies. At a conceptual level, the system merges several computational layers: a 3D digital twin for simulation, AI training based on historical and real-time data, and AI agents that can generate operational insights from cross-system analytics. The platform ingests data such as crowd movement, solar heating, airflow and IoT sensor feeds, allowing operators to visualise and interact with station conditions. The expected impact is better energy management, preventive maintenance, reduced intervention times, lower downtime, improved emergency simulation and new safety, security and crowd-control capabilities. The case is significant because it presents the station as a “physical AI” environment where built infrastructure can be continuously simulated, analysed and optimised rather than managed only through static building information.

cases.source_description: Ocean governance requires the ability to understand how climate change, pollution, coastal erosion, biodiversity loss and human activity may affect marine systems over different timescales. The European Digital Twin of the Ocean provides an AI-powered platform for exploring “what-if” scenarios and translating complex marine data into actionable intelligence. The operational problem is that policymakers, environmental agencies, researchers and communities need to anticipate future ocean conditions, but relevant information is spread across satellite observations, in-situ measurements, numerical models and specialised marine services. The EU DTO integrates data from the Copernicus Marine Service, EMODnet and other sources, combining them with artificial intelligence and advanced GPU computing. At a conceptual level, the platform creates a dynamic virtual representation of marine systems that can simulate scenarios such as Sargassum drift, turtle movements and fishing-risk exposure, coastal erosion protection, plastic-pollution drift and local coastal-risk projections. AI models can accelerate forecasting, producing results in seconds rather than hours and improving ocean-current prediction accuracy. The expected impact is more informed marine policy, better coastal and biodiversity planning, stronger pollution response, increased transparency and wider access to ocean intelligence as a public good. The case is significant because it treats digital twins as decision infrastructure for planetary-scale environmental governance, linking scientific modelling with practical policy and community use.

cases.source_description: Democratic backsliding is difficult to analyse because it develops through complex interactions between institutions, political actors, citizens, media systems, legal frameworks and informal norms. TWIN4DEM addresses this challenge by using digital twin technology and computational social science to prototype dynamic representations of democratic systems in Czechia, France, Hungary and the Netherlands. The operational problem is that traditional democracy-monitoring tools can identify institutional deterioration, but they often struggle to simulate how different drivers of democratic erosion interact over time or how specific policy interventions might strengthen resilience. TWIN4DEM therefore brings together political scientists, computational social scientists, humanities scholars, technologists and democracy stakeholders to model the pathways leading to executive aggrandisement and threats to rule-of-law institutions. At a conceptual level, the project treats democratic systems as complex adaptive systems that can be represented through data aggregation, natural-language processing, agent-based modelling and dynamic simulation. These digital twins are intended to help researchers and stakeholders test hypotheses, simulate policy scenarios and anticipate democratic risks before they become entrenched. The project also emphasises GDPR-compliant, open and FAIR tools, participatory engagement with policymakers and civil society, and the creation of an open-source community around democracy research. The expected impact is stronger analytical capacity for identifying early warning signs of democratic decline, more evidence-based policy responses, and improved democratic resilience across Europe. The case is significant because it extends digital twin methods beyond physical infrastructure into institutional and political systems.

cases.source_description: Wildfires are becoming more frequent and severe in Mediterranean regions, creating urgent pressure for better early warning, prevention and operational response. Dryads addresses this challenge by developing an AI-powered environmental-monitoring platform for forest resilience and wildfire-risk management in Greece. The operational problem is that fire risk is shaped by many interacting factors, including weather, microclimate, vegetation, human activity, terrain, sensor signals and real-time visual information. Traditional monitoring approaches may not combine these data sources quickly enough to detect danger, assess vulnerability or predict how a fire could evolve. Dryads is a cooperation project between the SCAN Laboratory of the National and Kapodistrian University of Athens and the Greek Ministry of Environment and Energy, funded by ICLEI with support from Google.org. The platform uses multimodal sensing and AI to extract microclimate profiles, identify anthropogenic risk factors, monitor fire outbreaks and predict fire evolution. At a conceptual level, the system combines IoT sensors, satellite imagery, weather data, real-time video streams and geospatial modelling into an AI-enabled forest-management environment. The expected impact is earlier wildfire detection, more accurate risk assessment, improved prevention planning, stronger protection for communities and better climate-adaptation capacity for forests. The case is significant because it moves wildfire governance from reactive response towards continuous sensing and predictive forest-resilience management.

cases.source_description: Extreme rainfall and flash floods create urgent information needs for emergency services, especially when roads, infrastructure and affected communities are difficult or dangerous to access. The Valencia case concerns the use of drones, scientific expertise and high-resolution geospatial information after the DANA event that struck the province on 29 October 2024. The operational problem was that emergency responders needed to assess damage rapidly, locate debris and vehicles, identify pollution and infrastructure impacts, and support decision-making in areas where ground access was constrained. CSIC activated its Disaster and Emergency Advisory Group on 30 October 2024, mobilising around 200 professionals from multiple research centres and deploying drones in the Barranco del Poyo and nearby municipalities such as Paiporta, Picanya, Catarroja and Massanassa. The implementation used low-altitude drone flights to collect high-resolution images, which were then used to detect dragged vehicles, contaminating waste and infrastructure damage, as well as to support three-dimensional modelling of affected areas. At a conceptual level, the case illustrates how integrated geospatial systems can turn emergency data into operational intelligence, giving responders and planners a rapid spatial understanding of disaster impacts. The expected impact is faster situational assessment, better prioritisation of emergency action, stronger scientific support for civil protection and improved preparation for future climate-related disasters. The case should be framed as emergency-response geospatial intelligence rather than as a fully institutionalised city digital twin unless stronger municipal evidence is added.

cases.source_description: Urban regeneration requires planners, developers, elected officials and residents to understand how proposed projects will affect the physical city before construction begins. Nottingham City Council’s digital-twin work uses 3D geospatial modelling to support planning, redevelopment and public engagement. The operational problem is that traditional two-dimensional drawings and isolated planning documents can make it difficult to assess the visual, spatial and cumulative effects of new development, particularly across a city centre undergoing major renewal. Nottingham’s approach combines a 3D object model, real-world scans of buildings and location-specific planning data, using ArcGIS Urban and related GIS technology. At a conceptual level, the digital twin acts as a shared planning environment: it allows planners to visualise existing conditions, test development proposals, discuss schemes more interactively with developers and communicate future scenarios in a way that is easier for non-specialists to understand. The expected impact is a faster planning process, better-quality discussions with applicants, improved transparency, stronger investor confidence and more accessible public consultation. The case is relevant because it shows how a city-wide 3D model can become a practical planning tool rather than a purely visual showcase. It also demonstrates that AI-empowered or digitally enabled cities often depend first on high-quality geospatial data infrastructure, into which more advanced analytics and simulation functions can later be integrated.

The European Commission’s Digital Twin for the Reconstruction of Ukraine is being developed to support Ukrainian authorities across the full reconstruction cycle. The first phase will focus on residential buildings, with potential later extension to infrastructure such as rail, roads, bridges and energy substations. The case is significant because it applies AI-enabled digital twins to post-war reconstruction, where speed, accuracy, public trust and financial accountability are essential.

cases.task: TRACE4EU - Building the foundation of traceable seafood supply-chain infrastructure
cases.context: European Commission; European Institution/Agency; Fishing and hunting; European Union
cases.implementation: TRACE4EU Seafood Tracing uses the European Blockchain Services Infrastructure to build a traceability model for seafood products, with a focus on Norwegian king crab and related supply-chain actors. TRACE4EU uses verifiable credentials, QR codes and blockchain timestamping to create an auditable chain of events for seafood products.
cases.outcome: UNKNOWN; 원천의 기대효과와 별도 관측 성과는 구분해야 합니다.
cases.source_description: Seafood supply chains require reliable traceability because illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing, mislabelling and weak documentation can undermine food safety, sustainability and consumer trust. TRACE4EU Seafood Tracing uses the European Blockchain Services Infrastructure to build a traceability model for seafood products, with a focus on Norwegian king crab and related supply-chain actors. The operational problem is that information about catch origin, fisher identity, product handling, customs clearance, packaging, transport and final sale may be stored in separate systems or exchanged through documents that are hard to verify. TRACE4EU uses verifiable credentials, QR codes and blockchain timestamping to create an auditable chain of events for seafood products. At a conceptual level, each step in the product journey can be recorded and linked: a fisher receives an identity credential, catch information is registered, product and sales-order credentials are issued, packaging and customs credentials are added, and downstream buyers or consumers can verify provenance against the ledger. This creates a digital traceability layer that supports authorities, intermediaries, retailers and end customers. The expected impact is stronger detection of illegal fishing, improved confidence in catch certificates, better food-safety oversight, more transparent supply-chain documentation and support for future Digital Product Passport capabilities. The case is relevant because it applies EBSI to supply-chain integrity in a sector where public regulation, market trust and environmental sustainability are closely connected. It should be treated as an EBSI pilot infrastructure case rather than a fully scaled operational system.

cases.source_description: Food manufacturers need reliable methods to determine shelf life, prevent spoilage, ensure regulatory compliance and maintain consumer trust across complex supply chains. Traditional shelf-life management often relies on empirical estimates, laboratory testing at limited points in time and conservative date-marking assumptions that may not fully reflect real production and distribution conditions. Shelfex AI, developed by the Belgian food safety technology company Handary, addresses this problem by combining biotechnology, analytical science and artificial intelligence into a predictive framework for food integrity. The operational problem is that spoilage and microbial risk are dynamic: they depend on ingredient quality, processing parameters, packaging, storage conditions and distribution environments. Shelfex AI integrates laboratory data and production parameters to authenticate ingredients, predict spoilage before it occurs and support compliance with date-marking requirements. It is complemented by Microfier smart labels, which provide real-time microbial signals directly on packaging, and Hékôn intelligent micro-perforated membranes, which regulate gas balance and monitor storage conditions during distribution. At a conceptual level, the system turns shelf-life management from a retrospective or judgement-based process into a data-driven predictive control system. The expected impact is improved food safety, reduced waste, more accurate date marking, stronger supply-chain transparency and greater trust between manufacturers, regulators and consumers. The case is relevant because it shows how AI can support food safety and sustainability through predictive monitoring of product integrity, although it is primarily a private-sector technology rather than a public-administration deployment.

cases.source_description: Illegal timber trade creates environmental, regulatory and geopolitical risks, particularly where sanctioned wood products may enter European supply chains through indirect routes or falsified documentation. The Lithuanian blockchain-for-trade case addresses this problem by proposing a blockchain-based traceability system for timber, with specific relevance to Russian and Belarusian wood entering EU markets. The operational problem is that conventional certification and paperwork can be manipulated, and authorities or buyers may struggle to verify whether timber was harvested legally, transported through legitimate channels and processed according to sustainability rules. Researchers from Kaunas University of Technology and Vytautas Magnus University developed a model that assigns each log a unique identifier and records its journey on a blockchain, from permits through transport and sale. Smart contracts are used to validate each action, including blocking attempts to harvest without permits or introduce fictitious suppliers. At a conceptual level, the system creates a tamper-resistant audit trail for timber, combining product-level identification, sustainability scoring and automated rule enforcement. The source reports that simulation tests processed up to 550 transactions per second and that participants with higher sustainability scores achieved up to 95% successful trades. The expected impact is stronger enforcement against illegal timber, better supply-chain transparency, improved buyer confidence and more effective implementation of sanctions and deforestation-related due diligence

cases.source_description: On-chain exchange-traded funds and index products require the underlying asset basket to remain aligned with the fund’s intended composition when new shares are issued or existing shares are redeemed. In traditional fund operations, this process can involve intermediaries, manual reconciliation and delayed portfolio adjustment. 31Third’s issuance- and redemption-triggered rebalancing use case applies blockchain automation to this specific operational problem. The system is designed for on-chain ETFs and similar portfolio products where subscription and redemption events automatically trigger rebalancing of the underlying assets. At a conceptual level, the platform connects fund-share issuance, redemption logic and smart-contract-powered portfolio execution: when fund shares are created or redeemed, the system adjusts the underlying asset basket so that allocations continue to reflect the fund’s target composition without requiring separate manual intervention. This creates a more direct link between investor activity and asset management. Smart order routing can optimise execution across decentralised exchanges, market makers and liquidity pools, while compliance features are intended to support institutional-grade operation. The expected impact is more efficient fund administration, lower execution friction, better transparency for investors and stronger scalability for on-chain index products. The case is particularly relevant because it illustrates how blockchain can be used not merely to represent assets digitally, but to automate specific financial-market operations that are traditionally handled through administrative and intermediary-heavy workflows. As with the related 31Third portfolio-rebalancing use case, it should be treated as a sandboxed financial-innovation case rather than a public-service deployment.

Blocksquare’s notarised real-estate tokenisation framework addresses this problem by combining blockchain tokens with legally grounded property claims, notarised loan agreements and registered mortgages. cases.context: CHARONIUM GmbH; Private sector; Executive and legislative organs, financial and fiscal affairs, external affairs.; European Union

cases.source_description: Digital assets such as cryptocurrencies, NFTs and tokenised real estate create practical and legal challenges for inheritance, because heirs, notaries, lawyers and financial institutions may not know what assets exist, how to verify ownership or how to transfer them securely after death. CHARONIUM Legacy addresses this problem by providing a blockchain-powered platform for digital estate discovery, verification and transfer. The operational problem is that traditional probate and inheritance procedures were designed for bank accounts, physical property and registered financial assets, while decentralised digital assets may be held across wallets, exchanges and tokenised platforms. CHARONIUM Legacy is designed for legal professionals, notaries and financial institutions, offering automated asset verification across blockchains such as Bitcoin and Ethereum, centralised exchanges and tokenised platforms. At a conceptual level, the platform converts digital inheritance into a structured workflow: assets can be discovered, tokenised into proofs of ownership, registered in tamper-proof records and transferred through smart-contract-based processes under legal conditions. The system also supports beneficiary and investor management, automated notifications, probate processing, cross-border compatibility, AML alignment and GDPR compliance. The expected impact is reduced legal uncertainty, lower administrative burden, fewer disputes, improved fraud resistance and clearer procedures for the inheritance of digital assets. The case is significant because digital estate management is becoming increasingly important as crypto-assets and tokenised property enter mainstream wealth portfolios. For public-sector cataloguing, it should be presented as a regulated blockchain innovation case involving legal-sector processes, not as a government-run inheritance platform.

cases.context: Traced Systems; Private sector; Waste management.; European Union
cases.implementation: The operational challenge is that batteries move through production, use, collection, recycling and secondary markets, but critical data may not follow the physical product in a secure, standardised and privacy-preserving way. The project developed and deployed a Digital Product Passport application over six months, with Instagrid providing manufacturing data, Batteriretur contributing collection and recycling logistics, Cling Systems supporting secondary battery transactions and Traced Systems deploying the Chromia blockchain for decentralised data management.

cases.source_description: Battery value chains involve manufacturers, users, collectors, recyclers, marketplaces and regulators, each of whom needs reliable information about product origin, chemistry, condition, ownership, usage and end-of-life handling. The blockchain-powered Digital Product Passport pilot involving Traced Systems, Instagrid, Batteriretur and Cling Systems addresses this information problem in the downstream phase of the battery lifecycle. The operational challenge is that batteries move through production, use, collection, recycling and secondary markets, but critical data may not follow the physical product in a secure, standardised and privacy-preserving way. The project developed and deployed a Digital Product Passport application over six months, with Instagrid providing manufacturing data, Batteriretur contributing collection and recycling logistics, Cling Systems supporting secondary battery transactions and Traced Systems deploying the Chromia blockchain for decentralised data management. At a conceptual level, the Digital Product Passport acts as a controlled data layer for the battery: different actors receive role-based access to relevant information, while blockchain supports traceability, provenance and integrity. Manufacturers can gain downstream insight into battery use, collectors can access chemistry and lifecycle information to improve sorting and recycling, and secondary-market participants can verify battery health and provenance. The expected impact is improved circularity, better recycling efficiency, stronger regulatory alignment, greater confidence in second-life markets and more transparent sustainability reporting. The case is relevant because it demonstrates how blockchain can support practical industrial data exchange under emerging European product-passport and circular-economy requirements.

cases.context: Multi; Private sector; General economic, commercial and labour affair; European Union
cases.implementation: Multi, developed by Kunveno Teknologos, uses distributed ledger technology to create a community-driven financial ecosystem governed through on-chain proposal voting.
cases.outcome: UNKNOWN; 원천의 기대효과와 별도 관측 성과는 구분해야 합니다.
cases.source_description: Decentralised finance aims to reduce reliance on centralised institutions, but many systems still face governance, transparency, liquidity and manipulation risks. Multi, developed by Kunveno Teknologos, uses distributed ledger technology to create a community-driven financial ecosystem governed through on-chain proposal voting. The operational problem is that digital-asset reserves and basket tokens need credible mechanisms for asset selection, governance and liquidity provision if they are to operate transparently and sustainably. Multi’s design includes two core tokens: a governance token for the decentralised autonomous organisation, and a fully collateralised basket token backed by a dynamic reserve of crypto assets. Participants propose asset allocations, while the reserve structure is determined through a meritocratic, game-theoretic competition mechanism. At a conceptual level, the system transforms portfolio governance into a decentralised process: participants compete to improve reserve allocation, the DAO defines the rules of the competition, and rewards are distributed through staking mechanisms. The platform also functions as a decentralised exchange through an automated multi-party trade algorithm, issuing fully collateralised tokens according to liquidity needs and dynamically adjusting supply to maintain market balance. The expected impact is greater transparency, more resilient decentralised governance, reduced dependence on intermediaries and a new model for community-managed financial infrastructure. The case should be framed as a blockchain sandbox and decentralised-finance innovation case, because it concerns private-sector financial infrastructure rather than a public-service tool.

cases.source_description: Smart contracts can execute financial and operational logic automatically, but bugs or vulnerabilities in their code can lead to irreversible losses, exploitation or loss of trust in blockchain systems. DOWSERS addresses this problem by applying formal verification methods to smart contracts before or after deployment. The operational problem is that testing can identify known bugs, but it cannot prove the absence of entire classes of vulnerabilities across all possible execution states. This is particularly important in decentralised finance and token ecosystems, where a small error can expose developers, investors and institutions to major financial risk. DOWSERS provides a suite of software tools and algorithms that analyse source code from repositories and bytecode already deployed on blockchain networks. At a conceptual level, the platform applies mathematical reasoning to prove or disprove whether a smart contract satisfies specified properties, drawing on formal-verification techniques used in safety-critical sectors such as aerospace, nuclear systems, rail and automated transport. It can identify vulnerabilities including reentrancy attacks, race conditions, authorisation errors, buffer overflows and unsafe external calls, while also detecting ambiguities, inconsistencies and poor security practices. The expected impact is stronger trust in blockchain applications, better developer guidance, more informed investment decisions and reduced cybersecurity risk across decentralised systems. The case is relevant to public-sector and regulatory discussions because smart-contract assurance is a prerequisite for safe adoption of blockchain in finance, public registries, digital credentials and other high-trust domains.

cases.source_description: Electricity systems are becoming harder to balance as renewable generation, heat pumps, electric vehicles and distributed energy resources create more variable patterns of supply and demand. Enoda ENSEMBLE™ addresses this challenge by using distributed ledger technology to coordinate decentralised energy assets so that they can provide frequency and ancillary services to the grid. The operational problem is that grid stability has historically depended on large centralised plants, including fossil-fuelled peaker plants, which can respond to frequency deviations but are expensive, carbon-intensive and poorly aligned with decarbonisation objectives. At a conceptual level, the platform creates a trusted coordination layer between grid operators, aggregators and distributed assets, allowing performance data, transactions and balancing contributions to be recorded transparently. The expected impact is lower transaction costs, reduced barriers for renewable and distributed assets, greater grid flexibility and less reliance on conventional balancing generation. The case is relevant because it applies blockchain to a concrete energy-transition bottleneck: how to integrate decentralised clean-energy resources into operational grid services without losing trust, compliance or system stability. cases.source_description: Cloud-service certification depends on evidence that must remain trustworthy over time, but evidence-management processes can be complex, manual and vulnerable to doubts about integrity. EMERALD addresses this problem through a blockchain-based trustworthiness system that supports cybersecurity certification and auditing of cloud services. The operational problem is that cloud service providers, certification bodies and auditors need to collect, store and verify evidence demonstrating security controls, while also preserving privacy and protecting sensitive technical information. EMERALD provides a framework in which evidence collectors can automatically generate proofs of integrity, while the wider system can automatically check whether stored evidence has been tampered with. Authorised users, including internal or external auditors, can also perform manual verification through a graphical interface. At a conceptual level, the blockchain layer does not need to expose all evidence publicly; rather, it records integrity proofs and supports long-term verifiability, traceability and resistance to modification. This allows certification evidence to remain auditable without compromising confidentiality. The expected impact is more efficient cybersecurity certification, stronger trust in cloud-service evidence, reduced administrative burden for auditors and providers, and improved capacity to demonstrate compliance over time. The case is relevant because it applies blockchain to assurance and certification, where trust depends on evidence integrity rather than on tokenisation or financial exchange. For catalogue purposes, it should be presented as a sandbox-stage cybersecurity assurance use case.

At a conceptual level, the system separates eligibility verification from identity disclosure, reducing data exposure while maintaining regulatory accountability.
