cases.source_description: The Ministry of Labour and Social Policies (MLPS) supervises pension and social security institutions, including private-law entities established under D.Lgs No. 509/1994 and No. 103/1996. Its responsibilities cover both legal-administrative and financial oversight, including the approval of resolutions on contributions, benefits, governance, and appointments; the review of budgets, financial statements, actuarial reports, and investment plans; the assessment of financial sustainability and regulatory compliance in cooperation with other authorities, including MEF and COVIP. These activities generate large volumes of documentation and complex procedures, while being managed by a limited number of officials. The resulting administrative burden has increased processing times and highlighted the need for advanced digital tools to improve efficiency, consistency, knowledge sharing, and decision-making. The platform represents the first integrated digital environment specifically designed to enhance, streamline, and accelerate the supervisory and monitoring activities carried out by the MLPS overseeing private pension schemes. The platform has been conceived to support the supervision of 20 private pension funds currently operating in Italy, providing a comprehensive digital environment for the analysis, management, and assessment of both financial and governance-related information. The system is structured around two integrated modules. 1. Document Management, Analysis, and Knowledge Discovery Module The first module is dedicated to the collection, storage, processing, indexing, and intelligent analysis of all documents periodically submitted by pension funds to their supervisory authority. Through a centralized and highly searchable repository, supervisory staff can rapidly retrieve relevant information, navigate large volumes of documentation, and perform cross-document analyses that would otherwise require significant manual effort. The platform manages a wide range of documents, including annual budgets, financial statements, actuarial balance sheets, investment plans, board resolutions, minutes, reports issued by the Board of Statutory Auditors, and other regulatory filings. Advanced indexing and semantic-search capabilities enable users to identify specific information within seconds, compare data across multiple reporting periods, and conduct in-depth analyses of financial, governance, and operational trends. The system also includes sophisticated analytical tools that allow supervisors to generate reports, perform data aggregations, visualize historical developments through comparative tables and time-series analyses, and monitor key indicators over extended periods. These functionalities significantly improve the efficiency and consistency of supervisory activities while reducing the operational burden on staff. A particularly valuable feature concerns the assessment of board resolutions submitted for approval. In addition to the resolutions themselves, the platform incorporates a comprehensive and constantly updated repository of applicable legislation, regulatory provisions, pension-fund statutes, internal regulations, and governance rules adopted by each scheme. By combining this legal and regulatory framework with the economic, financial, and actuarial information extracted from the funds' reports, the platform leverages advanced Artificial Intelligence algorithms to support supervisory decision-making. Users can interact with the AI engine either through predefined prompts tailored to specific supervisory tasks or through a free-form conversational interface. The system can identify relevant regulatory references, highlighting potential inconsistencies or compliance issues, assessing the coherence of proposed decisions with applicable rules, and providing reasoned analyses to support the approval or rejection of board resolutions. Furthermore, it assists supervisory personnel in drafting technical opinions, advisory reports, and formal assessments, substantially reducing preparation time while improving the quality, consistency, and traceability of regulatory evaluations. 2. Appointment Management and Eligibility Assessment Module The second module issues invitations to complete application forms for appointments to the audit bodies of 20 pension schemes, the 36 administrative committees responsible for managing INPS (National Institute of Pension Schemes) funds, and four private complementary pension funds. Applications are transmitted to and verified by the Supervisory Authority’s staff. The module manages the full initial submission workflow, from the invitation sent to the candidate through the transmission of the completed application and supporting documents to the competent supervisory staff. This also supports efficient handling of each individual appointment procedure. Through a certified authentication system, selected individuals can complete an online form, upload a CV and an ID document and, after confirming the accuracy of the information entered, automatically generate the documents that the Administration must publish on its transparency portal. After applicants review and verify the submitted information, the platform performs a preliminary formal review using an artificial intelligence algorithm. It provides feedback indicating, for example, whether a document is expired, a file has the wrong format, a file submitted as a CV is not a curriculum vitae, the CV contains a name different from the applicant’s, or the CV lacks the declarations required for self-certifications and sworn statements. When formal errors are detected, the platform alerts applicants, enabling them to correct the issues and upload the appropriate documentation. This initial phase reduces completion errors and processing times. Consequently, applications reach the competent authority complete and formally compliant, allowing its staff to focus on substantive rather than formal checks. Immediately after submission, an officer of the Supervisory Authority can review the documentation and initiate automated checks to verify its completeness and formal correctness and, within the information available on the platform, identify potential risks concerning conflicts of interest, incompatibility, or ineligibility for appointment. For example, the platform examines candidates’ CVs and the positions they declare they currently hold or have held during the previous two years, to identify companies affiliated with or controlled by the pension institution concerned. This assessment is conducted by analysing the notes to the institution’s financial statements. If an officer needs to clarify additional issues, an AI-powered free-text chat function is available. It enables the officer to query all documentation stored on the platform, including declarations and supporting documents, conduct further analysis, and investigate matters requiring additional scrutiny. *** A core innovation of the platform is the transformation of previously siloed information into a shared institutional knowledge base. Historically, supervisory processes were managed by different offices, resulting in fragmented information, duplicated activities, and limited knowledge transfer. The platform overcomes these constraints by integrating documents, data, regulatory sources, and procedural information within a single digital environment. This substantially reduces the effort required to store, analyze, and retrieve relevant information, while enhancing collaboration, preserving institutional knowledge, and improving the overall effectiveness and efficiency of supervisory activities

cases.task: INPS ISAC – Generative Artificial Intelligence applied to social security contribution compliance.
cases.context: INPS - National Social Security Institute; Central-Government; Social protection n.e.c.; Italy
cases.outcome: UNKNOWN; 원천의 기대효과와 별도 관측 성과는 구분해야 합니다.
cases.source_description: INPS, in agreement with the Ministry of Labour and Social Policies, the Ministry of Economy and Finance (MEF) and the National Labour Inspectorate (INL), has developed the Statistical Indicators of Contribution Reliability (Indicatori Statistici di Affidabilità Contributiva, known as ISAC) in order to promote preventive contribution compliance and to identify cases of under-declaration of employment, by means of indicators that compare tax and social security contribution data. The process provides for compliance letters to be sent to companies, setting out any deviations in the indicators, as determined by the Institute. Once the compliance letters have been sent, companies may justify and explain the deviations, including by attaching appropriate documentation, by submitting specific communications through the INPS channels. The generative AI component operates in the analysis of the communications submitted by companies: it analyses and assesses the replies and any attachments in line with the deviations determined by the Institute; it extracts the evidence provided by the company; it assigns the companies’ replies to specific clusters; it proposes an explainable justification of the analysis carried out and also prepares a draft reply to the company itself. INPS staff govern the entire process: they examine, modify, supplement and/or validate the output produced by the AI system, that is, they retain responsibility for the final decision in providing feedback to the company. The outcomes feed into monitoring, enabling continuous improvement of the system. The first application concerns the “Wholesale food trade” sector and the “Hotel and non-hotel accommodation facilities” sector, for a total of 35,491 companies analysed and 20,038 compliance letters sent. The solution improves consistency, timeliness and traceability and will be extended to six further production sectors, namely: - Bar, ice-cream parlour, pastry shop and confectionery production activities, for a total of 91,048 businesses; - Retail sale of medical and orthopaedic goods, for a total of 2,551 businesses; - Installation of electrical, plumbing and other building installations, for a total of 113,063 businesses; - Bespoke and mass production of clothing, accessories and household linen, and related processing, for a total of 17,543 businesses; - Hairdressing services, for a total of 38,794 businesses; - “Maintenance and repair of motor vehicles, motorcycles and mopeds”, for a total of 49,035 businesses. The legal entities affected will total 312,034, while approximately 176,000 letters will be sent. The proposed solution has been designed with features of flexibility and modularity that also allow it to be extended to further processes, promoting the standardisation of activities and the optimisation of the resources employed.

cases.source_description: Evidence on artificial intelligence and work evolves rapidly and remains fragmented across public institutions, research bodies, firms, workers and social partners. SIO (Sistema Intelligente dell’Osservatorio, the Intelligent System of the Observatory) is the AI-enabled evidence infrastructure of Italy’s Observatory on Artificial Intelligence and Labour, established within the Ministry of Labour and Social Policies. It combines a curated, source-linked knowledge base, a public conversational interface and an adaptive consultation environment for the Observatory’s bodies. Its governed architecture separates orchestration from generation, applies differentiated access and keeps validation and institutional responsibility with the Ministry and the Observatory. SIO supports a more structured, comparable and traceable evidence-to-policy cycle and provides a transferable model for public institutions addressing fast-moving technological change.

cases.source_description: SyRCI-IA is Madrid City Council’s human-supervised artificial intelligence capability for classifying and routing suggestions, complaints and compliments to the competent municipal unit. Embedded in SYRCI, the corporate case-management system, it combines deterministic rules with three BERT-based classifiers. Municipal staff retain responsibility: receiving units validate or return routings, and corrections inform rules and retraining. In production since 4 November 2024, by 9 May 2026 it had supported 38,221 routings; 30,225 were validated as correct (79.08%). Within the measured scope, rules and AI automate 97.46% of routings; AI accounts for 47.06% of automated routings. A dashboard refreshed daily covers 84 units and 523 users; two full retraining cycles and a formal risk assessment support safe, accountable operation. Published on the Interoperable Europe Portal with a bilingual reuse and implementation guide, it offers public administrations a documented route to replication.

cases.task: Privacy-safe synthetic test data: AI-generated replicas of statistical microdata for software development and testing at Statistics Netherlands
cases.context: Statistics Netherlands (CBS); Private sector; General public services n.e.c.; Netherlands
cases.implementation: Together with technology partner BlueGen, CBS generated a synthetic replica of a large, complex relational dataset using generative AI (a diffusion transformer) trained entirely inside CBS's secure, air-gapped environment.
cases.outcome: UNKNOWN; 원천의 기대효과와 별도 관측 성과는 구분해야 합니다.
cases.source_description: Statistics Netherlands (CBS) builds and maintains the software pipelines that produce official statistics. New software is developed in an environment that is less strictly secured than production, so real microdata about citizens and businesses may not be used there. Dummy or rule-based test data cannot capture the complexity of the real data. Together with technology partner BlueGen, CBS generated a synthetic replica of a large, complex relational dataset using generative AI (a diffusion transformer) trained entirely inside CBS's secure, air-gapped environment. The synthetic data mirrors the structure, statistical patterns and business rules of the real microdata while containing no real records. It enabled a new statistical pipeline to be developed and tested on realistic data, surfaced real defects before production, and removed the risk of a data leak from the development environment. Resemblance and utility scores exceeded 85%; measured privacy risk was zero

cases.task: ISIA Intelligenza artificiale generativa come nuovo modello di servizio pubblico alle imprese
cases.context: Camera di Commercio Irpinia Sannio; Local Government; General economic, commercial and labour affair; Italy
cases.implementation: What distinguishes the case, however, is not the technology adopted, which is widely available, but the decision to use it to adapt the administration to the user rather than requiring the user to adapt to the administration. Finally, it concerns channels: no function can be accessed through only one route, ensuring that users who are unable to use one channel are not excluded from the service.
cases.outcome: UNKNOWN; 원천의 기대효과와 별도 관측 성과는 구분해야 합니다.
cases.source_description: The Irpinia Sannio Chamber of Commerce carries out its functions in a territory that clearly illustrates a challenge common to much of Europe. Almost ninety thousand businesses, predominantly micro and small enterprises, are distributed across two provinces characterised by a high proportion of inland areas and served by only two Chamber of Commerce offices. For many of these businesses, access to a public service has never been a question of whether the service is available, but rather of compatibility: between office opening hours and working hours, between the institutional office and the distance separating it from the municipality where the business is located, and between the language of administrative procedures and that of those who must navigate them without qualified intermediaries. The proposed solution addresses this gap. ISIA is the organisation’s virtual assistant, operational since 29 May 2025 and migrated to a generative artificial intelligence-based architecture in May 2026, representing the first such case within the Italian Chamber of Commerce system. It queries the institutional knowledge base to provide contextualised answers, guides users through access to the eight active Online Services, and enables appointments to be booked directly: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pbVtQO1rWyA. What distinguishes the case, however, is not the technology adopted, which is widely available, but the decision to use it to adapt the administration to the user rather than requiring the user to adapt to the administration. First and foremost, this concerns language: following the migration to generative AI, requests asking users to rephrase their questions fell from 4.0% to 0.3% of messages, providing a measure of how significantly the terminology barrier has been reduced. It also concerns time: more than half of interactions take place outside public opening hours, and during evening and night-time hours the assistant is not merely an alternative channel but the only one available. Finally, it concerns channels: no function can be accessed through only one route, ensuring that users who are unable to use one channel are not excluded from the service. Human support has not been removed, but rather repositioned towards higher-value activities. Artificial intelligence is placed at the entry point of a four-level service pathway that always ultimately leads to a person: from independent access to information to assisted conversation, from online transactions to an interview with an operator, either in person or via video call, including document exchange and payments. Content remains under the responsibility of the competent offices; the system provides information and guidance without adopting administrative decisions, while responsibility for the administrative procedure remains with a natural person. By diverting from the service desk those requests that can be resolved upstream, automation has made operators more available for cases that genuinely require human expertise, while also making them accessible without requiring users to travel. The institutionally decisive step took place on 27 July 2026: through an administrative order issued by the Secretary-General, access to the five services involving the highest level of direct interaction was made subject to appointment booking, which can be completed either through the website or directly through a conversation with the virtual assistant, complemented by a remote service desk via videoconference. The virtual assistant does not simply operate alongside the service desk: it orchestrates access to the different service channels while ensuring that human support remains available at all times: https://www.irpiniasannio.camcom.it/notizie/nuova-modalita-accesso-agli-sportelli-prenotazione. The project forms part of “Le Camere del Futuro” (“The Chambers of the Future”), a national programme promoted by Unioncamere for the digital transformation of the Chamber of Commerce system. Irpinia Sannio is the first Chamber to integrate generative artificial intelligence into this framework: what has been implemented is therefore not an isolated experiment, but a prototype embedded within an architecture already shared by all Italian Chambers of Commerce. Alongside this transformation, the organisation has implemented a structured capacity-building programme targeting both its own staff and businesses operating in the territory, based on the principle that public technology that nobody knows how to use cannot generate public value. The solution was designed in accordance with the European and national accessibility framework: Directive (EU) 2016/2102 on the accessibility of the websites and mobile applications of public sector bodies; the harmonised EN 301 549 standard incorporating WCAG 2.1 Level AA criteria; and the relevant Italian implementing legislation (Law No 4/2004, as amended by Legislative Decree No 106/2018), together with the AgID Guidelines on the Accessibility of ICT Tools. The new institutional website, launched as part of the project, is built on the reference model for Italian public administration websites, which incorporates accessibility requirements into its navigation structure, colour contrasts and markup semantics. The organisation publishes its accessibility statement in accordance with the AgID model and maintains an active feedback mechanism through which users can report accessibility difficulties. Accessibility, however, has been interpreted more broadly than technical compliance alone, because the divide affecting businesses in this territory is not solely related to sensory accessibility. **Channel redundancy.** No function is accessible through only one route. An appointment can be booked through the website, in conversation with the virtual assistant, or at the reception desk, which schedules the first available appointment for anyone arriving without a prior booking. Information about an administrative requirement is available as a structured information sheet that can be browsed by category or keyword, as a conversational response, or through a discussion with an operator. Users who are unable to use one channel are therefore not excluded from the service. **Cognitive and linguistic accessibility.** The assistant responds in natural language to questions formulated in natural language, without requiring users to know administrative terminology. The reduction in requests for users to rephrase their questions from 4.0% to 0.3% of messages, measured following the technological upgrade, indicates the extent to which this barrier has been lowered: it is the administration that adapts to the user’s language, rather than the other way around. **Physical and temporal accessibility.** The remote service desk via videoconference, including document exchange and online payments, enables users to access Chamber of Commerce services without travelling. This is particularly relevant for people with reduced mobility and for businesses located in inland municipalities far from the two physical offices. More than half of interactions with the assistant take place outside public opening hours: service availability is therefore no longer dependent on compatibility between office opening hours and entrepreneurs’ working schedules. **Economic accessibility.** All components — the virtual assistant, specialist support, online services and the training programme — are provided to users free of charge. Accessibility is also one of the topics covered by the training programme offered to businesses, through a dedicated corporate case study. Accessibility is therefore not only a requirement applied to the service itself, but also knowledge transferred to the local business community. The solution was not acquired through a procurement procedure to which the EU standard contractual clauses would have been applicable. By means of a managerial decision dated 7 February 2025, the Irpinia Sannio Chamber of Commerce joined “Le Camere del Futuro”, the national programme promoted by Unioncamere for the digital transformation of the Italian Chamber of Commerce system. The solution is developed and operated by InfoCamere, an in-house company owned by the Chambers of Commerce, within the service relationship connecting the infrastructure operator with the entire Chamber system. Consequently, there was no competitive procurement procedure for acquiring an artificial intelligence system from an external supplier; rather, the Chamber joined a system configuration that had already been designed and made available to participating Chambers. Nevertheless, the safeguards that the model contractual clauses are intended to ensure are addressed through other mechanisms. The operator is a publicly owned entity controlled by the contracting administrations and subject to their equivalent control: data, infrastructure and service continuity therefore remain within the public-sector perimeter. Ownership of and responsibility for information content remain with the competent Chamber offices. Traceability of system use is ensured through structured reporting covering the entire period of operation, which is available for audit and internal control purposes. The quality of responses is subject to systematic assessment, with documented results. The system performs an information and guidance function and does not adopt administrative decisions: responsibility for the administrative procedure remains with a natural person, as required by Italian rules governing the use of artificial intelligence within public administration. The organisation nevertheless considers the EU standard contractual clauses to be a useful reference and intends to examine them in connection with future developments of the solution, including as a framework for verifying the safeguards already in place within its relationship with the infrastructure operator. **Technology Partner:** InfoCamere S.C.p.A., the in-house company of the Italian Chamber of Commerce system. **Scientific Partners:** Societing Lab — an action-research programme of the University of Naples Federico II; Giustino Fortunato Telematic University (e-learning platform and issuance of Open Badges).

cases.source_description: Bid rigging in public procurement is difficult to detect through conventional investigation, because collusive tenders are designed to appear competitive. The Danish Competition and Consumer Authority (KFST) developed Bid Viewer in-house to screen large volumes of tender data for signals of horizontal agreements between bidders. The tool computes a set of statistical indicators of non-competitive bidding behaviour — covering the number and pattern of tenders, the variance and distribution of bid prices, bid rotation and incumbency patterns — and feeds these indicators into machine learning screens that combine them into a single model. The models are trained and evaluated on tender data containing known cartel cases, and assign each tender a probability score reflecting its likelihood of collusion, allowing case handlers to prioritise the tenders most worth investigating. Artificial neural networks are used alongside the statistical screens to improve classification performance. Bid Viewer is used operationally by the Authority to support a range of investigations, specifically the identification of bid rigging. The tool has been developed in cooperation with the Spanish and Swedish competition authorities and has been transferred to counterpart authorities in other European countries, including the Estonian Competition Authority and the United Kingdom, making it a reference case for cross-border reuse of an anti-collusion analytics solution. Its public value lies in stronger enforcement capability, better allocation of scarce investigative resources, and protection of public spending against cartel overcharges.

cases.source_description: North Rhine-Westphalia has established the first statewide digital standard for tender preparation in a large German federal state. The Ministry for Home Affairs, Local Government, Building and Digitalisation (MHKBD) concluded a framework contract with the Munich-based GovTech company GovRadar GmbH, opening access in April 2025 to all 427 municipalities and extending it in July 2025 to all state authorities, agencies, higher education institutions and state-owned undertakings. The cloud-based solution focuses on the content preparation phase of procurement rather than process administration. It supports the drafting of legally compliant technical specifications by generating text proposals from a continuously updated corpus of millions of existing German tender documents, provides semantic search and an AI assistant for targeted research, structures market data for digitalised market exploration across product categories, and guides the creation of contracts and standard documents without media discontinuity. By supporting product-neutral, unambiguous specifications, the tool reduces the scope for specifications tailored to a single supplier and improves the quality and comparability of bids. Authorities report time savings of up to 90% in the preparation of tender drafts. As of mid-2025, 166 municipalities had requested the municipal licence and 2,140 individual user licences had been issued.

cases.source_description: In August 2020, the UK government's Home Office abandoned an ADM system called the "Streaming tool" that assessed the risk of visa applicants. The algorithm faced legal challenges from the Joint Council for the Welfare of Immigrants (JCWI) and Foxglove, as it was believed to perpetuate racism and bias in the visa system. The algorithm suffered from "feedback loop" issues, where past bias and discrimination influenced future outcomes. It prioritized applicants from predominantly white countries and subjected people from other nations to a more rigorous review process. In response to the criticism, the Home Office announced plans to redesign the ADM system, explicitly addressing concerns about unconscious bias and the use of nationality in the new system.

cases.context: Zenter fir d'Lëtzebuerger Sprooch (ZLS – Centre for Luxembourgish Language); Non-governmental; Cultural services.; Luxembourg
cases.implementation: At operational level, the project strengthens the data foundation behind Luxembourgish speech technology, enabling better automatic transcription for public, educational, cultural and administrative uses.
cases.outcome: UNKNOWN; 원천의 기대효과와 별도 관측 성과는 구분해야 합니다.
cases.source_description: Luxembourgish is central to the country’s linguistic identity, but speech-recognition technologies often perform better for larger languages with more abundant training data. “Sproocherkennung fir d’Lëtzebuergescht” addresses this gap by improving the speech-to-text capabilities of schreifmaschinn.lu, an AI-based transcription tool developed by the Zenter fir d’Lëtzebuerger Sprooch. The operational problem is that accurate speech recognition requires high-quality synchronised audio and text data, representing different speakers, accents, contexts and recording situations. The existing dataset already provides a foundation for Luxembourgish transcription, but broader and more diverse training material is needed to improve recognition quality and spelling accuracy. The initiative expands the hypersynchronised audio-text dataset from 55 hours to 80 hours, with two main objectives: diversifying the range of speakers and situations represented in the data, and improving orthographic accuracy in the generated transcription. At operational level, the project strengthens the data foundation behind Luxembourgish speech technology, enabling better automatic transcription for public, educational, cultural and administrative uses. It also supports digital inclusion by making spoken Luxembourgish more usable in digital environments, from accessibility tools to language-learning resources and public-service interfaces. The expected impact is more accurate Luxembourgish speech-to-text, stronger support for multilingual digital services and greater visibility of Luxembourgish in AI-enabled communication systems. The initiative is relevant because it treats language resources as strategic digital infrastructure for public-sector innovation and linguistic diversity.
